text:
會試錄序
天順癸未春二月禮部會試
天下貢士遇風火之變弗克
成
皇上旣懲有司不恪乃命移試于
秋八月而以明年甲申三月
賜廷對焉秋期且至尚書臣夔
===

則臣獻臣淳臣俁臣守陳臣健
臣元禎臣軒臣𤦺臣清臣熈臣
誠臣瑛監試官則臣洪臣愷
而綱維其事則臣給實任之
于時士之負才藝就試者幾

會試錄序

天順癸未春二月，禮部會試天下貢士，遇風火之變，弗克成。皇上旣懲有司不恪，乃命移試于秋八月，而以明年甲申三月賜廷對焉。秋期且至，尚書臣夔以考試官請，上命臣時、臣溥典文衡。其同考官則臣獻、臣淳、臣俁、臣守陳、臣健、臣元禎、臣軒、臣𤦺、臣清、臣熈、臣誠、臣瑛，監試官則臣洪、臣愷，而綱維其事則臣給實任之。于時士之負才藝就試者幾
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the second month of spring in the guiwei year of the Tianshun reign (1463), when the Ministry of Rites conducted the Metropolitan Examination for the tribute scholars (gongshi) of the empire, it encountered a disaster of wind and fire and could not be completed. After His Majesty punished the responsible officials for their negligence, He ordered the examination postponed to the eighth month of autumn, and decreed that the Palace Examination be granted in the third month of the following, jiashen year (1464). As the autumn date approached, the Minister, Your Servant [Yao] Kui 姚夔, petitioned for the appointment of the Examiners. His Majesty ordered Your Servant [Chen] Shi 陳時 [Note: Peng Shi 彭時] and Your Servant [Qian] Pu 錢溥 to preside over the literary evaluations. As for the Associate Examiners, they were Your Servant [Si] Xian 司獻, Your Servant [Ni] Chun 倪淳, Your Servant [Tong] Yu 童俁, Your Servant [Yang] Shouchen 楊守陳, Your Servant [Liu] Jian 劉健, Your Servant [Zhang] Yuanzhen 張元禎, Your Servant [Wang] Xuan 王軒, Your Servant Yao 𤦺 [Xu Yao 徐𤦺], Your Servant [Zhou] Qing 周清, Your Servant [Qin] Xi 秦熈, Your Servant [Zhao] Cheng 趙誠, and Your Servant [Jiang] Ying 江瑛; the Monitoring Censors of the Examination (監試官) were Your Servant [Focus/Jiao] Hong 洪 and Your Servant [Zhang] Kai 愷; and as for the overall administration of the affair, Your Servant [Yao] Kui [written 給 in text] truly undertook the responsibility. At that time, the scholars endowed with talent and literary skill who presented themselves for the examination numbered nearly…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
三千人臣笇暨內外諸執事
恊心竭誠各共廼職嚴防範
精去取得才藝之優者二百
五十人爰錄其名以
聞且將傳示天下後世為来者
勸遵舊典也臣竊觀自古聖
帝明王之治天下率以用賢
===
為本賢才盛衰治道之隆替
繫焉洪惟我
太祖高皇帝肇造
鴻基法古為治養賢以學校而
取之必於科目其設科也每
三載一試會試則例以鄉試
之明年其於甲子為辰戌丑

三千人〔臣〕等暨內外諸執事
協心竭誠各共厥職嚴防範
精去取得才藝之優者二百
五十人爰錄其名以
聞且將傳示天下後世為來者
勸遵舊典也〔臣〕竊觀自古聖
帝明王之治天下率以用賢
為本賢才盛衰治道之隆替
===
繫焉洪惟我
太祖高皇帝肇造
鴻基法古為治養賢以學校而
取之必於科目其設科也每
三載一試會試則例以鄉試
之明年其於甲子為辰戌丑
punctuated: 三千人。臣笇暨內外諸執事，恊心竭誠，各共廼職，嚴防範，精去取，得才藝之優者二百五十人。爰錄其名以聞，且將傳示天下後世，為来者勸，遵舊典也。臣竊觀自古聖帝明王之治天下，率以用賢為本，賢才盛衰，治道之隆替繫焉。洪惟我太祖高皇帝肇造鴻基，法古為治，養賢以學校，而取之必於科目。其設科也，每三載一試，會試則例以鄉試之明年，其於甲子為辰、戌、丑、
translation_en:
… three thousand men. Your servants [?] and the various officials in the inner and outer compounds united our hearts and exhausted our sincerity, each reverently fulfilling his duties. We maintained strict precautions and made discerning selections, obtaining two hundred and fifty men of superior talent and accomplishment. Thereupon we recorded their names to report to the Throne, and will furthermore circulate them throughout the realm and to future generations as an encouragement for those to come, in accordance with the old statutes.

Your servant humbly observes that since antiquity, when sage emperors and enlightened kings governed the realm, they invariably took the employment of the worthy as their foundation; upon the flourishing or decline of worthy talent depends the rise or fall of good governance. Reflecting deeply on how our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu), first established the great foundation and modeled himself on antiquity to govern: he nurtured the worthy through schools and invariably selected them through the examination system. In establishing the examinations, a test was held once every three years; the Metropolitan Examination was by rule held in the year following the Provincial Examination, which in the sexagenary cycle falls on the years of chen, xu, chou, and …

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
末也行之既久得人輔治亦
已盛矣通前後諸科論之惟
永樂甲申為尤盛焉盖當是
時
太宗文皇帝初正大統故試士易
癸未以甲申逮至于今六十
年矣夫十日十二子相配數
窮六十窮則變變則通通即
復盛之機也而移試之期適
際其會豈非
皇上聖德神謨切於求賢圖治故
一弛張變通間遂有以應
天心協
祖德振文運於復興而隆太平萬
alt_text:
未世行之既久得人輔治彌
已盛矣通前後諸科論之惟
永樂甲申為尤盛焉蓋當是
時
太宗文皇帝初正大統故試士易
癸未以甲申逮至于今六十
年矣夫十日十二子相配數
===
窮六十窮則變變則通通即
復盛之機也而移試之期適
際其會豈非
皇上聖德神謨切於求賢圖治故
一弛張變通間遂有以應
天心協
祖德振文運於復興而隆太平萬
punctuated: 末也。行之既久，得人輔治亦已盛矣。通前後諸科論之，惟永樂甲申為尤盛焉。盖當是時，太宗文皇帝初正大統，故試士易癸未以甲申。逮至于今，六十年矣。夫十日十二子相配，數窮六十；窮則變，變則通，通即復盛之機也。而移試之期，適際其會，豈非皇上聖德神謨，切於求賢圖治，故一弛張變通間，遂有以應天心、協祖德，振文運於復興，而隆太平萬
translation_en: …wei [years]. Having been practiced for a long time, the recruitment of capable men to assist in governance has indeed flourished. Speaking of all the examination sessions earlier and later as a whole, only that of the jiashen year of the Yongle reign (1404) was especially flourishing. For at that time, Emperor Taizong Wen had just acceded to the Great Succession, and therefore in examining the scholars changed the session from the guiwei year (1403) to the jiashen year (1404). Coming down to the present, sixty years have passed. Now, the ten heavenly stems and twelve earthly branches combine with one another until their number is exhausted at sixty; when exhausted, there is change; with change, there is continuity; and continuity is the very pivot of returning to flourishing. That the rescheduling of the examination date happens to coincide with this juncture—is it not because His Majesty’s sagely virtue and divine counsels are earnestly devoted to seeking worthies and planning for good governance, so that in a single act of relaxing or tightening, of changing and adapting, he is able to respond to the mind of Heaven, harmonize with the virtue of the Ancestors, rouse the literary fortune to revival, and exalt for ten thousand [generations] the great peace’s…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
世之彙於方來也歟非偶然
也士之階此以進者固榮幸
矣行當益自感激淬礪以平
昔所抱負者擇竒約粹祗俟
廷對而發焉庶有以顯
文明之運於今日也雖然知之
非難而行為難知而弗行是
===
謂徒知雖有言也奚足尚哉
惟於聖賢性命道德之微已
習知其說而發乎文者皆允
蹈之實踐之使性得心成積
於己為正學見於用為真才
然後可以建功立業輔世長
民並極而經緯天地制作禮
alt_text:
世之稟於方來也歟非偶然
也士之階此以進者固榮幸
矣行當益自感激淬礪以平
昔所抱負者擇奇約粹祗俟
廷對而發焉庶有以顯
文明之運於今日也雖然知之
非難而行爲難知而弗行是
===
謂徒知雖有言也奚足尚哉
惟於聖賢性命道德之微已
習知其說而發乎文者皆允
蹈之實踐之使性得心成讀
於己爲正學見於用爲真才
然後可以建功立業輔世毫
興節極而經緯天地制作禮
punctuated: 世之彙於方來也歟？非偶然也。士之階此以進者，固榮幸矣；行當益自感激淬礪，以平昔所抱負者，擇竒約粹，祗俟廷對而發焉，庶有以顯文明之運於今日也。雖然，知之非難，而行為難。知而弗行，是謂徒知，雖有言也，奚足尚哉？惟於聖賢性命道德之微，已習知其說而發乎文者，皆允蹈之、實踐之，使性得心成，積於己為正學，見於用為真才，然後可以建功立業，輔世長民，並極而經緯天地、制作禮
translation_en: … the gathering of Worthies for ten thousand generations in the ages to come? This is no mere coincidence. The scholars who ascend by this step to advance in their careers are indeed honored and fortunate. Going forward, they ought to be all the more moved to gratitude and temper themselves, selecting the finest and distilling the purest of the aspirations they have long cherished, and respectfully awaiting the Palace Examination to set them forth—so that they may make manifest the flourishing literary fortune of the present day. Even so, to know is not difficult; it is action that is difficult. To know and yet not act is what is called empty knowledge; even if one has fine words, how could that be worthy of esteem? Only when, with regard to the subtleties of the sages' and worthies' teachings on human nature, destiny, the Way, and virtue—whose doctrines they have already thoroughly learned and expressed in writing—they truly tread that path and put it into actual practice, so that their nature is realized and their mind perfected, accumulating within themselves as orthodox learning and manifesting in application as genuine talent: only then can they establish merit and accomplish great deeds, assist the age and govern the people, and at the highest level order heaven and earth and institute rites…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
樂以□宏至治追復隆古之
太平將無不可韓子所謂本
深而末茂實大而聲宏者此
之謂也是惟有志者自勉焉
勉之而底使人皆稱曰是科
得人之盛超今邁古不其偉
歟否則徒冒
===
寵榮非世所貴也盍相與圖之
中憲大夫太常寺少卿兼翰
林院學士彭時謹序
alt_text:
樂以協宏化遹追隆古之
太平將無孚可韓子所謂本
深而末茂實大而聲宏者此
之謂也是惟有志者自勉焉
勉之而又使人皆稱曰是科
得人之盛超今邁古不其偉
歟否則徒冒
===
寵榮非世所貴也盍相與圖之
中憲大夫太常寺少卿兼翰
林院學士彭時謹序
punctuated:
樂，以□宏至治，追復隆古之太平，將無不可。韓子所謂「本深而末茂，實大而聲宏」者，此之謂也。是惟有志者自勉焉。勉之而底，使人皆稱曰：「是科得人之盛，超今邁古。」不其偉歟？否則，徒冒寵榮，非世所貴也。盍相與圖之？

中憲大夫、太常寺少卿兼翰林院學士彭時謹序。
translation_en:
…and music, so as to [?] and expand the supreme governance and recover the great peace of high antiquity—nothing will be impossible. What Master Han [Han Yu 韓愈] meant by "when the root is deep, the branches are luxuriant; when the substance is great, the renown is vast" refers to this very thing. This rests solely upon those with aspiration exerting themselves. If they exert themselves to the utmost, causing everyone to praise them, saying, "The abundance of talent obtained in this examination surpasses the present and outstrips antiquity"—would that not be magnificent? Otherwise, merely claiming imperial favor and glory in vain is not what the world values. Why not strive together toward this end?

Respectfully prefaced by Peng Shi 彭時, Grand Master exemplar (zhongxian dafu), Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (taichang si shaoqing), and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy (hanlin yuan xueshi).

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Seventh Year of the Tianshun Reign (1463)

Administrator of the Tribute Examination (知貢舉官):
Li Shao 李紹, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Right Vice Minister of Rites. (Courtesy name Keshu 克述, a native of Anfu County, Jiangxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the guichou year [1433].)

Examiners:
Peng Shi 彭時, Grand Master Exemplar, Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. (Courtesy name Chundao 純道, a native of Anfu County, Jiangxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the wuchen year [1448].)

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
仁者先難而後獲可謂仁矣
誠身有道不明乎善不誠乎身矣誠者天
之道也誠之者人之道也
何謂善何謂信曰可欲之謂善有諸己之
謂信充實之謂美充實而有光輝之謂
大大而化之之謂聖聖而不可知之之
謂神樂正子二之中四之下也
===
易
先天而天弗違後天而奉天時天且弗違
而況於人乎
六四安節亨象曰安節之亨承上道也九
五甘節吉往有尚象曰甘節之吉居位
中也
夫乾其靜也專其動也直是以大生焉
唯神也故不疾而速不行而至

仁者先難而後獲，可謂仁矣。
誠身有道，不明乎善，不誠乎身矣。誠者，天之道也；誠之者，人之道也。
「何謂善？何謂信？」曰：「可欲之謂善，有諸己之謂信，充實之謂美，充實而有光輝之謂大，大而化之之謂聖，聖而不可知之之謂神。樂正子，二之中、四之下也。」

易：
先天而天弗違，後天而奉天時。天且弗違，而況於人乎？
六四，安節，亨。象曰：安節之亨，承上道也。九五，甘節，吉，往有尚。象曰：甘節之吉，居位中也。
夫乾，其靜也專，其動也直，是以大生焉。
唯神也，故不疾而速，不行而至。

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books:
"The humane person puts what is difficult first and places the reward afterward; this may be called humanity."
"There is a way to make the self sincere: if one is not clear about what is good, one cannot make the self sincere. Sincerity is the way of Heaven; making oneself sincere is the way of human beings."
"'What is meant by "good"? What is meant by "trustworthy"?' Mencius said: 'What is desirable is called good; having it within oneself is called trustworthy; having it filled to capacity is called admirable; having it filled to capacity and shining forth is called great; being great and transforming others through it is called sage; being sage and beyond comprehension is called numinous. Yuezhengzi 樂正子 is in the middle of the first two and below the last four.'"

Classic of Changes (Yi):
"When he precedes Heaven, Heaven does not contradict him; when he follows Heaven, he respects the timing of Heaven. If even Heaven does not contradict him, how much less will human beings?"
"Six in the fourth place: Content with restraint; success. The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) says: 'The success of being content with restraint' comes from accepting the way of the superior. Nine in the fifth place: Sweet restraint; auspicious; going brings esteem. The Commentary on the Images says: 'The auspiciousness of sweet restraint' comes from occupying the central position."
"As for Qian, in its stillness it is concentrated, and in its movement it is straight; therefore it generates vastness."
"Only because it is numinous does it make haste without hurrying and arrive without traveling."

既明且哲，以保其身，夙夜匪解，以事一人。人亦有言：「柔則茹之，剛則吐之。」維仲山甫，柔亦不茹，剛亦不吐。

translation_en:
“Goodness has no constant master, but accords with what can be unified. Cause the myriad surnames all to say, ‘Great indeed are the king’s words!’ and also to say, ‘Unified indeed is the king’s mind!’”

“By means of virtue make manifest their goodness. If the state is good, it rests with all of you.”

“Now the people will depend on your reverently following your accomplished father, continuing what you have heard and clothing yourself in his virtuous words. Go and extensively seek out the ways of the former wise kings of Yin, thereby protecting and governing the people. You must broadly and distantly reflect upon the aged and accomplished men of Shang, settling your mind so as to understand how to instruct. Furthermore, seek out and learn the ways followed by the ancient former wise kings, thereby pacifying and protecting the people.”

“Practicing virtue, the mind is at ease and daily becomes more excellent; practicing deceit, the mind toils and daily becomes more clumsy. Dwelling in favor, think of danger, and never be without awe; if you are not in awe, you will fall into what is dreadful. Promote the worthy and yield to the able, and all the officials will be in harmony; when they are not in harmony, governance becomes confused. If those you recommend are equal to their offices, that is your ability; if you recommend someone unfit, you fail in your duty.”

Book of Odes (Shi)

“Taking the yearling pigs for themselves, and presenting the large boars to the Duke.”

“Both intelligent and wise, he thereby protects his person; early and late never slackening, so as to serve the One Man. People also have a saying: ‘If it is soft, swallow it; if it is hard, spit it out.’ Yet Zhong Shanfu neither swallows the soft nor spits out the hard.”

“The Marquis of Han came to audience; with his great jade tablet, he entered for audience with the king. The king bestowed upon the Marquis of Han a fine dragon-banner with plumed crest, a bamboo-mat carriage screen and ornamented yoke-bar, a dark dragon-robe and red slippers, breast-plates and carved…”

…frontlets; a leather-bound crossbar, a shallow tiger-skin cover, and reins of leather with gold rings [note: the transcription reads 韓奕 for 鞹靷 "leather-bound crossbar" by attraction to the ode title "Han Yi"]. "The people of Jin and the Jiang Rong defeated Qin at Yao"; "The people of Jin defeated the Di at Ji"; "The people of Jin, the people of Chen, and the people of Zheng attacked Xu" [Thirty-third year of Duke Xi]; "The Marquis of Jin attacked Wei"; "Gongsun Ao met the Marquis of Jin at Qi" [First year of Duke Wen]; "Gongsun Ao met the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Earl of Zheng, and Shi Hu of Jin to make a covenant at Chuilong" [Second year of Duke Wen]; "Yang Chufu of Jin led an army to attack Chu in order to rescue Jiang" [Third year of Duke Wen].

Record of Rites (Liji):
"One may dwell in high and bright places, one may gaze afar, one may ascend hills and mounds, one may reside on terraces and pavilions."
"Now as for ritual, the former kings used it to carry on the Way of Heaven and to regulate the feelings of men."
"Heaven is high and Earth is low; the myriad things are scattered and distinct, and thus ritual regulations are put into practice. Flowing without cease, uniting and transforming together, and thus music arises therein. Generating in spring and growing in summer are benevolence (ren); harvesting in autumn and storing in winter are righteousness (yi). Benevolence is akin to music, and righteousness is akin to ritual. Music promotes harmony, following the spirit and complying with Heaven; ritual distinguishes what is appropriate, settling the earthly souls and complying with Earth. Therefore the sages created music to respond to Heaven and instituted ritual to match Earth. When ritual and music are clear and complete, Heaven and Earth fulfill their proper functions."
"Therefore the gentleman deliberates on the Way by starting from himself, and establishes laws by reference to the people."

Five Policy Questions

Question: The Book of Changes (Yi) states: "Observe the cultural patterns of humanity in order to transform and perfect all under heaven." In antiquity, Yao 堯, Shun 舜, Yu 禹, Tang 湯, King Wen 文, and King Wu 武 were all rulers who excelled at governance. In transforming and perfecting all under heaven, did they indeed do so through the cultural patterns of humanity, or did they have some other way? 聖聖相承皆法二帝三王以為治而敷言垂訓

太祖高皇帝時則有律令大誥在

聖製輝煌徧布海宇其皆有關於人文歟究
其所至真可以化成天下歟方今
皇上政述
===
祖宗心潛往聖躬行大孝以先天下是又克盡
人文之大端也夫上有好者下必有甚
焉者矣天下之人豈無觀感興起捷於
影響者歟如是而世不丕變治不古若
則化成之言有不足信也且易有之曰
聖人久於其道而天下化成自
祖宗以来近百年矣今豈非化成之時歟如其
時也其可制禮作樂以宣人文為萬世
之法歟諸生服膺

translation_en:
… dynasty, sacred sage has succeeded sacred sage; all have modeled themselves on the Two Emperors and Three Kings in governing, setting forth words and handing down instructions as bright as the sun and stars. In the time of the Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu, the Hongwu Emperor), there were the Statutes and Ordinances (Lüling) and the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao); in the time of the Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wen (Taizong, the Yongle Emperor), there were the Unseen Rewards for Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi) and the True Records of Filial Piety and Obedience (Xiaoshun shishi); and in the time of the Proclaiming Ancestor, Emperor Zhang (Xuanzong, the Xuande Emperor), there was the Book of the Five Human Relationships (Wulun shu). These imperial compositions shine brilliantly and are distributed throughout the realm—do they all pertain to human culture? When we examine their ultimate reach, can they truly transform and perfect the world?

At present, His Majesty continues the governance of his ancestors, immerses his mind in the past sages, and personally practices great filial piety to lead the world—this, too, is able to fulfill the great fundamentals of human culture. Now, whatever a superior loves, those below will surely pursue even further. Among the people of the world, how could there not be those who observe and are moved to rise up, more swiftly than a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound? If, despite this, the age is not greatly transformed and governance does not match antiquity, then the words about transforming and perfecting would not be worthy of belief. Moreover, the Book of Changes (Yi) says: "The sage perseveres long in his Way, and the world is transformed and perfected." Since the time of our imperial ancestors, it has been nearly a hundred years; is the present not indeed the time of transformation and perfection? If this is the time, can rites be instituted and music created so as to propagate human culture and establish a standard for ten thousand generations? You students have cherished in your hearts …

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
聖訓欽仰
聖德有素矣願詳陳之以考化成之效
問易書詩春秋禮記所載皆聖道也然不
能無可疑者焉易有三兆三易矣何一
名又有含三之義書有今文古文矣何
東漢又有中文之書詩有六義四始矣
何五際終始則有改變之政春秋三傳
謂事備於左氏例明於公羊而義精于
穀梁矣何以見其失之誣失之亂而失
===
之鑿乎禮有為經為傳之異又有三千
三百條之說矣何以五禮皆肇於三皇
而謂之五始歟晉韓宣子見易象與魯
春秋而曰周禮盡在魯矣吾乃今知周
公之德與周之所以王然爻象既作於
周公而班固則曰人更三聖謂羲文孔
子也何不及於周公春秋既始於周公
何以假天子二百四十二年之行事乃
復修於孔子也禮在魯矣即禮之經與

聖訓，欽仰聖德有素矣，願詳陳之，以考化成之效。

問：《易》、《書》、《詩》、《春秋》、《禮記》所載，皆聖道也，然不能無可疑者焉。《易》有「三兆」、「三易」矣，何一名又有含三之義？《書》有今文、古文矣，何東漢又有中文之書？《詩》有「六義」、「四始」矣，何「五際」終始則有改變之政？《春秋》三傳，謂事備於左氏、例明於公羊、而義精于穀梁矣，何以見其失之誣、失之亂、而失之鑿乎？《禮》有為經、為傳之異，又有「三千」、「三百」條之說矣，何以五禮皆肇於三皇而謂之「五始」歟？晉韓宣子見《易象》與《魯春秋》，而曰：「周禮盡在魯矣，吾乃今知周公之德與周之所以王。」然爻象既作於周公，而班固則曰「人更三聖」，謂羲、文、孔子也，何不及於周公？《春秋》既始於周公，何以假天子二百四十二年之行事，乃復修於孔子也？禮在魯矣，即《禮》之經與？
translation_en:
… the Sacred Instructions and have long revered the Sacred Virtue. Please set forth your views in detail so that we may examine the efficacy of transformative cultivation.

Question: What is recorded in the Book of Changes (Yi), the Book of Documents (Shu), the Book of Odes (Shi), the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), and the Record of Rites (Liji) is all the Way of the Sages; yet they cannot be without points of doubt. In the Changes there are already the "Three Divination Cracks" (sanzhao) and the "Three Changes" (sanyi); why does the single name [Yi] also contain the three meanings [easy, changing, and constant]? In the Documents there are already the New Text and Old Text versions; why in the Eastern Han was there also a "Middle Text" (zhongwen) version of the Documents? In the Odes there are already the "Six Principles" (liuyi) and the "Four Beginnings" (sishi); why is it that at the end and beginning of the "Five Junctures" (wuji) there are changes of governance? As for the Three Commentaries to the Spring and Autumn Annals, it is said that historical events are complete in Zuo (Zuoshi), precedents are clear in Gongyang, and moral principles are refined in Guliang; how then can one see where they err in fabrication, err in disorder, and err in forced interpretation? In the Rites there is the distinction between what constitutes Classic (jing) and what constitutes Commentary (zhuan), and there is also the theory of the "three thousand" and "three hundred" articles; why is it that the Five Rites all originated with the Three Sovereigns and are called the "Five Beginnings" (wushi)? When Han Xuanzi 韓宣子 of Jin saw the Images of the Changes (Yixiang) and the Spring and Autumn Annals of Lu (Lu Chunqiu), he said: "The Rites of Zhou are all in Lu! Only now do I know the virtue of the Duke of Zhou and how Zhou came to rule as true king." Yet since the line statements (yao) and images (xiang) were composed by the Duke of Zhou, why did Ban Gu 班固 say that "the men passed through three sages"—meaning Fuxi 伏羲, King Wen 文王, and Confucius 孔子—without mentioning the Duke of Zhou? Since the Spring and Autumn Annals originated with the Duke of Zhou, why was it again revised by Confucius, borrowing the sovereign's deeds over two hundred and forty-two years? And as for the rites that were in Lu—were they the Classic of Rites itself? …

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
何後世以為瀆亂不經作論難□排之
歟又何謂周禮乃周公致太平之迹啓
人主乙夜之覽歟然經皆作於聖人垂
之萬世而無弊者何以曰三代無文人
六經無文法而所謂文人與文法猶有
待於後之作者否歟此皆有可疑者願
相與明之
問古之為人臣者莫重於相相之職所以
佐理萬機統百官而均四海也故相得
===
其人則君心正而國勢尊賢才用而天
下寧豈輕也哉昔人論相者或以德量
稱或以氣節言或以才能舉皆未足以
盡其職惟先儒有以四事考之者於理
為當其目尚可得而聞歟三代以上若
臯陶伯益伊傅周召之流於四事固全
盡矣其實亦可槩舉歟三代而下稱治
者類曰漢唐其能致治謂非輔相得人
可乎然漢相名矣功莫著於蕭曹丙魏

punctuated:
何後世以為瀆亂不經，作論難□排之歟？又何謂《周禮》乃周公致太平之迹，啓人主乙夜之覽歟？然經皆作於聖人，垂之萬世而無弊者，何以曰「三代無文人，六經無文法」，而所謂文人與文法，猶有待於後之作者否歟？此皆有可疑者，願相與明之。
問：古之為人臣者，莫重於相。相之職，所以佐理萬機，統百官而均四海也。故相得其人，則君心正而國勢尊，賢才用而天下寧，豈輕也哉？昔人論相者，或以德量稱，或以氣節言，或以才能舉，皆未足以盡其職。惟先儒有以四事考之者，於理為當，其目尚可得而聞歟？三代以上，若臯陶、伯益、伊、傅、周、召之流，於四事固全盡矣，其實亦可槩舉歟？三代而下，稱治者類曰漢、唐，其能致治，謂非輔相得人可乎？然漢相名矣，功莫著於蕭、曹、丙、魏，
translation_en:
…Why then did later generations regard it as disorderly and uncanonical, composing treatises of refutation to [?] reject it? And why again was it said that the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) was the trace by which the Duke of Zhou brought about Great Peace, inspiring the ruler's perusal during the second watch of the night? Yet the Classics were all composed by sages and handed down for ten thousand generations without flaw; why then is it said that "the Three Dynasties had no literary men, and the Six Classics had no rules of composition," and do what are called "literary men" and "rules of composition" still await writers of later times or not? All of these are matters open to doubt; I wish to clarify them together with you.

Question: In antiquity, among those who served as ministers, none was more important than the Chief Minister (xiang). The office of Chief Minister exists to assist in governing the myriad affairs of state, to direct the hundred officials, and to bring harmony to the four seas. Therefore, when the right man is found for Chief Minister, the ruler's mind is rectified and the state's authority is exalted, worthy talents are employed and the realm is at peace—how could this be taken lightly? Those in the past who discussed Chief Ministers sometimes praised them for moral capacity, sometimes spoke of them in terms of integrity and principle, and sometimes cited them for talent and ability, yet none of these suffices to exhaust the duties of the office. Only when a former Confucian scholar examined them by means of four criteria was the principle properly met; may the specific items thereof still be heard? In the Three Dynasties and earlier, figures such as Gao Yao, Bo Yi, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao certainly fulfilled all four criteria completely; can the substance of their achievements also be summarized? From the Three Dynasties onward, those who speak of good governance generally name the Han and the Tang. Could it be said that their ability to bring about good governance was not due to finding the right men as assisting ministers? Yet among the renowned Chief Ministers of the Han, none had achievements more illustrious than Xiao He, Cao Shen, Bing Ji, and Wei Xiang; …

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
以四事考之其得有幾歟至漢之再興
也有能備此四事者而成功反不逮蕭
曹之偉其何故歟唐相衆矣名莫顯於
房杜姚宋以四事稽之其失有幾歟及
唐之中微也有不愧此四事者而致治
反不若姚宋之盛其何因歟大抵為相
者貴聞大學之道也之數公者將謂其
已學歟則業不全乎四事以為未學歟
則功已冠於一時不知其何術以成功
===
何由而失學也諸君子強學以待問必
有定見宜明辨之以發所蘊毋徒曰載
諸簡冊而已
問夷為邊患雖聖世不能免而况下此者
乎其下得備邊之策者莫善於西漢建
武以来則不及亦莫善於唐初天寶以
後則不然善莫備於勢得其要兵得其
強食得其足而將得其良也何以見其
備是四者而為善與失是四者而為不

以四事考之，其得有幾歟？至漢之再興也，有能備此四事者，而成功反不逮蕭、曹之偉，其何故歟？唐相衆矣，名莫顯於房、杜、姚、宋，以四事稽之，其失有幾歟？及唐之中微也，有不愧此四事者，而致治反不若姚、宋之盛，其何因歟？大抵為相者，貴聞大學之道也。之數公者，將謂其已學歟，則業不全乎四事；以為未學歟，則功已冠於一時。不知其何術以成功、何由而失學也？諸君子強學以待問，必有定見，宜明辨之，以發所蘊，毋徒曰載諸簡冊而已。

問：夷為邊患，雖聖世不能免，而况下此者乎？其下得備邊之策者，莫善於西漢，建武以来則不及；亦莫善於唐初，天寶以後則不然。善莫備於勢得其要、兵得其強、食得其足，而將得其良也。何以見其備是四者而為善，與失是四者而為不
translation_en:
…when examined against these four criteria, how many of them did they fulfill? When the Han was restored, there was one capable of fulfilling all four criteria, and yet his achievements did not match the greatness of Xiao He 蕭何 and Cao Can 曹參—what was the reason for this? The chief ministers of the Tang were numerous, and none were more renowned in name than Fang Xuanling 房玄齡, Du Ruhui 杜如晦, Yao Chong 姚崇, and Song Jing 宋璟; when investigated against these four criteria, in how many of them did they fall short? When the Tang fell into mid-dynastic decline, there were those who were worthy of these four criteria, and yet the governance they achieved did not match the flourishing age of Yao Chong and Song Jing—what was the cause of this? Broadly speaking, what is valued in a chief minister is having heard the Way of the Great Learning (Daxue). As for these several gentlemen, if one were to say they had already engaged in such learning, their accomplishments did not fully encompass the four criteria; if one considers them not to have learned, their merits already crowned their own eras. I do not know by what art they achieved their success, or from what cause they fell short in learning. You gentlemen have striven in your studies while awaiting inquiry and must hold settled views; you should clearly distinguish these matters in order to bring forth your accumulated learning, and not merely repeat what is recorded in the historical texts.

Question: That foreign tribes pose a menace on the frontiers is something even an age of sage rulers cannot avoid—how much less those ages that fall below it! Among those later ages that attained sound policies for frontier defense, none was better than the Western Han, whereas from the Jianwu era (25–56 CE) onward it was not equaled; likewise, none was better than the early Tang, whereas after the Tianbao era (742–756) this was no longer so. Excellence in defense is never more complete than when the strategic topography secures its key points, the troops attain their strength, provisions attain sufficiency, and the generals are of fine caliber. How can one see that fulfilling these four conditions constitutes excellence, and that failing in these four conditions constitutes a lack of…

者而得其道諸士子應賓興而來皆懷
用世之材者試為我言之以觀素蘊
問天下之務可言者多矣始以最切者相
與論之民惟邦本任牧民之責者守令
也守令非其人則民不安民不安則無
punctuated:
善？就是四者論之，又以何者爲先乎？可舉其人以實之乎？論者謂自古無無上策，雖周宣之盛，僅得中策耳。西漢、唐初以降，宜無足取者，何唐太宗自謂得上策歟？抑所謂上策者，在聖世則有歟？方今天下一家，四夷賓服，固已軼漢、唐矣。近惟南蠻弗率，是寇之小者也，嘗命將以征之，尚未見其斂迹；北虜靡寧，是寇之大者也，嘗嚴兵以拒之，即已致其來庭。然不知因其來庭，可弛兵以息民乎？究其未斂迹，可益兵以窮治乎？兵散恐墮掩襲之計，兵聚又費粮餉之給，然則行何者而得其道？諸士子應賓興而來，皆懷用世之材者，試爲我言之，以觀素蘊。
問：天下之務可言者多矣，姑以最切者相與論之。民惟邦本，任牧民之責者，守令也。守令非其人則民不安，民不安則無
translation_en:
…unsound? And in discussing these four factors, which among them should take priority? Can you cite specific individuals to substantiate this? Commentators have maintained that since antiquity there has been no supreme policy [for dealing with the barbarians—reading 無上策 for 無無上策 [?]], and that even at the height of King Xuan of Zhou's reign, he achieved only a middling policy. From the Western Han and early Tang onward, there should be nothing worth adopting; why then did Emperor Taizong of Tang claim for himself that he had attained the supreme policy? Or does what is called a supreme policy exist only in a sagely age? At present, all under Heaven is a single family and the four barbarian peoples submit in allegiance, which indeed already surpasses the Han and Tang. Recently, only the southern蠻 (Man) tribes have been unruly; these are minor bandits, yet although generals have been commissioned to campaign against them, they have not yet been seen to restrain their tracks. The northern虜 (Lu) caitiffs have been unsettled; these are major bandits, yet once troops were strictly deployed to repel them, it promptly brought them to come to court in submission. Even so, because they have come to court, can we relax our military preparedness in order to give rest to the people? Or examining those who have not yet restrained their tracks, should we increase the troops in order to pursue and suppress them to the end? If the troops are dispersed, one fears falling into a scheme of surprise attack; if the troops are massed, it wastes the supply of grain rations. Which course of action, then, will attain the proper way? You scholars have come in response to the call of the examination and all cherish talents useful to the world; try to set this forth for me, so that I may observe the learning you have long accumulated.

Question: Among the affairs of the realm, there are many that could be discussed; let us for now discuss together those that are most urgent. The people are the foundation of the state, and those who bear the responsibility of shepherding the people are the Prefects and Magistrates (shouling). If the Prefects and Magistrates are not the right men, the people will not be at peace; if the people are not at peace, there is no way…

以成内治此理也亦勢也今法禁非不
嚴仁卹非不至而守令之貪墨者不少
齊民之窮困者加多何歟軍以衛民任
領軍之責者將校也將校非其人則軍
不精軍不精則無以禦外侮此勢也亦
理也今選求非不切簡練非不數而將
校之智勇兼全者寡軍士之強弱不齊
者衆何歟且軍民相資缺一不可何民
每自私怠軍餉而不顧軍恒自守視民
===
患而不卹而為之長者恬不知戒歟凡
若此者皆司文武之柄者所欲急聞而
變通之也茲欲使守令皆秉廉潔之操
齊民舉有富安之樂將校咸兼智勇之
才軍旅悉負強壯之氣彼此相視猶一
體然將何法以處之激勸通融以為
國家長治久安之規殆必有要道也諸士子
致用有日矣宜考古之所可法與今之
所當行者詳著于篇以俟夫

punctuated: 以成内治，此理也，亦勢也。今法禁非不嚴，仁卹非不至，而守令之貪墨者不少，齊民之窮困者加多，何歟？軍以衛民，任領軍之責者，將校也。將校非其人，則軍不精；軍不精，則無以禦外侮，此勢也，亦理也。今選求非不切，簡練非不數，而將校之智勇兼全者寡，軍士之強弱不齊者衆，何歟？且軍民相資，缺一不可，何民每自私，怠軍餉而不顧，軍恒自守，視民患而不卹，而為之長者恬不知戒歟？凡若此者，皆司文武之柄者所欲急聞而變通之也。茲欲使守令皆秉廉潔之操，齊民舉有富安之樂，將校咸兼智勇之才，軍旅悉負強壯之氣，彼此相視猶一體然，將何法以處之？激勸通融，以為國家長治久安之規，殆必有要道也。諸士子致用有日矣，宜考古之所可法與今之所當行者，詳著于篇，以俟夫
translation_en: …whereby to achieve internal order; this is both principle and the natural course of events. Nowadays, legal prohibitions are not unstrict and benevolent relief is not unforthcoming, yet prefects and magistrates who are corrupt and venal are not few, and commoners who are impoverished and distressed grow ever more numerous—why is this? The military exists to protect the people, and those who bear the responsibility of commanding the military are the generals and officers. If the generals and officers are not the right men, then the troops will not be elite; if the troops are not elite, then there will be no means to fend off external aggression—this is both the natural course of events and principle. Nowadays, selection and recruitment are not unearnest and inspection and training are not infrequent, yet generals and officers who combine both wisdom and courage are few, and soldiers who are uneven in strength and weakness are many—why is this? Moreover, the military and the people depend upon one another, and neither can be dispensed with. Why is it that the people are ever selfish, neglecting military provisions without regard, while the soldiers constantly look only after themselves, viewing the people's distress without compassion, and those who serve as their superiors remain unconcerned and fail to take warning? All matters such as these are what those who hold the reins of civil and military authority eagerly wish to hear about and adapt to circumstances. Now, if we wish to cause prefects and magistrates all to uphold incorruptible integrity, the common people all to enjoy the pleasures of wealth and peace, generals and officers all to combine the talents of wisdom and courage, the armed forces all to possess vigorous and robust morale, and both sides to regard one another as a single body, by what method shall we manage this? To rouse and encourage them and bring about mutual accommodation, so as to form a plan for the state's long-term governance and enduring peace, there must surely be an essential way. You gentlemen will soon be put to practical use; you should examine what can be taken as a model from antiquity and what ought to be put into practice today, setting it forth in detail in your essays, so as to await…

translation_en:
First Session
The Four Books

"The humane person puts what is difficult first and what is to be gained last; this may be called humaneness." (Analects 6.22)
By Peng Jiao 彭敎

Associate Examiner Supervising Secretary Huang comments: This essay analyzes the principle clearly and thoroughly, and its phrasing is concise and apt. It is the work of a seasoned hand; it is fitting to single it out for publication.
Associate Examiner Supervising Secretary Tong comments: Those in the examination hall writing on this topic generally spoke in terms of the efficacy of "overcoming the self and returning to ritual propriety" or "holding fast to reverence and practicing reciprocity," which grew tiresome. Finding this essay late in the reading, with its expressive diction and fluent reasoning that transforms the commonplace into the marvelous, I know the author must be a scholar of deep fundamental attainment; it is especially worthy of recommendation.
Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Li comments: The mind of the humane person is inherently difficult to describe. In the examination hall, candidates either spoke of concrete affairs, or of abstract principles, or set forth vague generalities, quite missing the essential purport. This piece alone grasps the truth with genuine immediacy and has the words sufficient to bring it forth; it is especially fitting to transcribe and publish it.
Examiner Academician Qian comments: Humaneness is utmostly difficult to speak of, yet this piece is able to fuse the ideas harmoniously into a fine composition; the author must be one who has devoted his mind to the learning of principle (lixue).
Examiner Academician Peng comments: Most who wrote on this topic missed the essential purport; this piece alone grasped it.

Only when the mind of the humane person is unencumbered by selfish interest does the Way of humaneness lie nowhere outside of this. Indeed, putting what is difficult first and what is to be gained last is the mind of the humane person; having this mind and being unencumbered by selfish interest, is not the Way of humaneness made complete right here? title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
旨深矣思昔聖人之意若曰常人於行事之際
必先計其功效是以已私間乎仁矣惟仁者則
不然其於行事也必先其事之所難而後其效
之所得焉何也盖行已接物莫非事也凡事之
難者理不可以速成而仁者心恒先之則不底
于成有不止矣曷嘗輙計其效而他求哉處常
應變亦莫非事也凡事之難者理不可以苟就
而仁者心恒先之則不至于就有不舎矣曷嘗
輙計其功而他適哉謂之曰先難則非特先之
===
而已雖一瞬息之頃不少忽焉謂之曰後獲則
非特後之而已雖一念慮之間不少存焉夫先
所難而後所獲如此非其心不累於私者乎惟
一私不存萬理明淨是以心之本體純粹而不
雜其大用也周流而無間可謂心德全而仁道
即此而在矣然此語必因樊遲有計獲之失而
告之使能因是而自勉焉何患乎不至於仁哉
雖然聖人之語每因人而變化顏子嘗問仁矣
則告之以克已復禮是因其資之剛明欲其明

punctuated: 旨深矣。思昔聖人之意，若曰：常人於行事之際，必先計其功效，是以已私間乎仁矣。惟仁者則不然，其於行事也，必先其事之所難，而後其效之所得焉。何也？盖行已接物，莫非事也。凡事之難者，理不可以速成，而仁者心恒先之，則不底于成有不止矣，曷嘗輙計其效而他求哉？處常應變，亦莫非事也。凡事之難者，理不可以苟就，而仁者心恒先之，則不至于就有不舎矣，曷嘗輙計其功而他適哉？謂之曰「先難」，則非特先之而已，雖一瞬息之頃，不少忽焉；謂之曰「後獲」，則非特後之而已，雖一念慮之間，不少存焉。夫先所難而後所獲如此，非其心不累於私者乎？惟一私不存，萬理明淨，是以心之本體純粹而不雜，其大用也周流而無間，可謂心德全而仁道即此而在矣。然此語必因樊遲有計獲之失而告之，使能因是而自勉焉，何患乎不至於仁哉？雖然，聖人之語，每因人而變化。顏子嘗問仁矣，則告之以「克已復禮」，是因其資之剛明，欲其明
translation_en: … its meaning is profound indeed. Reflecting on the intent of the Sage in the past, it is as if he said: When ordinary people undertake affairs, they invariably calculate the results and benefits first; thus they allow their personal selfishness to come between them and benevolence (ren). Only the benevolent person is not so. In undertaking affairs, he invariably puts first what is difficult in the affair, and puts last the results to be gained from it. Why is this? Because conducting oneself and dealing with others are all affairs. In all difficult affairs, by principle they cannot be quickly accomplished; yet the mind of the benevolent person constantly puts them first, and so unless he reaches completion, he will never stop. When has he ever lightly calculated the results and sought after something else? Managing normal situations and responding to emergencies are likewise all affairs. In all difficult affairs, by principle they cannot be carelessly achieved; yet the mind of the benevolent person constantly puts them first, and so unless he reaches achievement, he will never give up. When has he ever lightly calculated the功 (merit/achievement) and turned elsewhere? Calling it "putting the difficult first" means not merely putting it first, but even for the space of a single blink or breath, never slightly neglecting it. Calling it "putting the gain last" means not merely putting it last, but even in a single passing thought, never slightly harboring it. Now, putting what is difficult first and what is gained last in this manner—is this not having a mind unencumbered by selfishness? Only when not a single trace of selfishness remains and the myriad principles are bright and pure is the fundamental substance of the mind pure and unadulterated, and its great functioning pervasive and without gap. One may say that the virtue of the mind is complete, and the Way of benevolence resides right here. Yet these words must have been spoken to Fan Chi because he had the fault of calculating gains; if he could take this to heart and exert himself, what worry would there be that he would not attain benevolence? Even so, the words of the Sage always varied according to the person. Yanzi [Yan Hui] once asked about benevolence, and he told him "overcome the self and return to propriety"; this was because his natural disposition was firm and clear-sighted, so he wanted him to clearly …

… and resolute, wishing for him to overcome selfishness through clear decisiveness. Zhonggong once asked about humaneness, and the Master told him to maintain reverence and practice reciprocity; this was because of his grave and substantial natural endowment, wishing for him to forget selfishness through self-cultivation. As for Fan Chi, who was coarse and inclined toward profit, the Master told him this, wishing in turn for him to eliminate the selfishness in his mind through his engagement in affairs. Alas! Nothing harms humaneness more than selfishness; scholars who set their minds on humaneness must begin by overcoming and eliminating their own selfishness.

"There is a way to make oneself sincere: if one does not understand what is good, one will not be sincere in oneself. Sincerity is the Way of Heaven; making oneself sincere is the Way of Man."

Lin Pin

Associate Examiner, Historiographer劉 (Liu) comments: In this topic, "Sincerity is the Way of Heaven" is spoken of in terms of the real principle with which human beings are endowed. Most writers in the examination hall based their arguments on the Way of Heaven above and the virtue of the sage, which quite misses the original purport. This essay not only shows a genuine comprehension, but its diction and reasoning throughout are pure and correct, making it superior to the other compositions.

Associate Examiner, Historiographer 楊 (Yang) comments: For a topic from the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), the difficulty lies not in marshaling words, but in attaining the principle. This essay excels in principle, and therefore I record it.

Examiner, Academician 錢 (Qian) comments: This essay discusses sincerity and grasps its fundamental purport; it deserves to be selected.

Examiner, Academician 彭 (Peng) comments: The analysis of principle is clear; without thorough prior study and mastery, one could not reach this level.

When the Doctrine of the Mean discusses making oneself real [sincere], it lies in exhausting principle; having stated that what is naturally without any lack of reality is the inherent state of Heavenly principle, it further states that seeking to attain that reality is the proper duty of human affairs. For […][?] is simply reality and nothing more. Principle issues from Heaven and is never without sincerity; yet in man, there is […][?]…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
□□□□□□□于明善以誠身豈可不知其所
自哉中庸以在下位者推言素定之意謂夫君
子獲上治民信友順親既皆本於身之誠然欲
誠其身者惡可襲取而強為哉其道在明乎善
而已盖不能格物致知以窮其理則未能察於
人心天命之本然而真知至善之所在其於好
善也必不能如好好色惡惡也必不能如惡惡
臭雖欲勉焉以誠其身而身不可得而誠矣誠
身本於明善如此則是善也豈無所自哉盖本
===
一理之出于天而賦于人耳是故理出於天者
為命賦於人者為性是性也曰仁曰義渾然真
實而無妄曰禮曰知粹然至實而無偽然其無
偽無妄也自然而然不假修為非天理之本然
而何故曰誠者天之道也若夫仁義之性未能
真實無妄也而欲其真實無妄禮知之性未能
至實無偽也而欲其至實無偽然欲其無偽無
妄也勉然而然必假修為非人事之當然而何
故曰誠之者人之道也然則得於天者本無不

translation_en: … [?] in illuminating the good in order to make one's person sincere, how could one not know whence it originates? In the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), when extending the discussion of the meaning of prior preparation from the perspective of one in a subordinate position, it is said that for the noble man, winning the confidence of his superiors, governing the people, being trusted by his friends, and being obedient to his parents are all rooted in the sincerity of his own person. Yet if one wishes to make one's person sincere, how can this be seized through outward imitation or forced effort? The way lies simply in illuminating the good. For if one is unable to investigate things and extend knowledge so as to exhaust their principles, then one cannot discern the original nature of the human mind and the Mandate of Heaven, nor truly know where the highest good resides. In loving the good, one will certainly be unable to love it as one loves a lovely sight; in hating evil, one will certainly be unable to hate it as one hates a foul odor. Though one may strive to make one's person sincere, one's person cannot be made sincere. Since making the person sincere is thus rooted in illuminating the good, how could this goodness be without a source? Indeed, it is rooted in the single principle that issues from Heaven and is endowed in human beings. Therefore, principle as it issues from Heaven is the Mandate, and as it is endowed in human beings is human nature. As for this nature, what are called benevolence and righteousness are wholly real and free from falsehood; what are called propriety and wisdom are purely genuine and free from artifice. Yet their being free from artifice and falsehood comes about of itself, without depending on cultivation or effort—what is this if not the original state of Heavenly principle? Thus it is said: "Sincerity is the Way of Heaven." As for when the nature of benevolence and righteousness is not yet wholly real and free from falsehood, and one desires it to be wholly real and free from falsehood; or when the nature of propriety and wisdom is not yet purely genuine and free from artifice, and one desires it to be purely genuine and free from artifice—wishing it to be free from artifice and falsehood comes about through exertion, and must depend on cultivation and effort. What is this if not the proper duty of human affairs? Thus it is said: "Attaining sincerity is the Way of man." If this is so, then what is received from Heaven originally has no principle that is not…

text:
實之理而在乎人者乃有不實之心君子其可
不以誠身為貴歟身既誠則順親信友獲上治
民將無施而不可矣抑又論之子思道學之傳
實得之曾子故其書多與大學相表裏其曰明
善即大學之格物致知也其曰誠身即大學之
誠意正心修身也盖明善誠身為知行之要聖
賢相傳以教人者不外乎此厥後孟子又筆之
於書以示門人益可見其淵源之有自矣有志
于道者尚其勉焉
===
何謂善何謂信曰可欲之謂善有諸己之
謂信充實之謂美充實而有光輝之謂大

… principle that is not real, whereas what rests with man may involve a mind that is not real. How then could the noble man not value making the person sincere? Once the person is sincere, then in obeying one's parents, being trusted by friends, gaining the confidence of superiors, and governing the people, there will be nothing one undertakes that does not succeed. Furthermore, if we discuss it further, Zisi 子思 actually received the transmission of the Learning of the Way from Zengzi 曾子; therefore, his book largely forms an exterior and interior counterpart to the Great Learning (Daxue). What he calls "clarifying the good" is namely the "investigating things" and "extending knowledge" of the Great Learning; what he calls "making the person sincere" is namely the "making the intentions sincere," "rectifying the mind," and "cultivating the person" of the Great Learning. Indeed, clarifying the good and making the person sincere are the essentials of knowledge and action, and what the sages and worthies transmitted from one to another in order to teach people goes no further than this. Afterwards, Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) also wrote these words down in his book to show his disciples, from which one can see all the more that this transmission had a definite source. May those who set their minds on the Way exert themselves in this!

"What is meant by 'the good'? What is meant by 'the true'?" Mencius replied: "What is desirable is called the good; having it in oneself is called the true; being filled with it to the full is called the beautiful; being filled with it to the full and shining forth with splendor is called the great; being great and transforming with it is called the sagely; being sagely and beyond comprehension is called the spiritual. Yuezhengzi 樂正子 is in the middle of the first two, and below the last four."

德之盛者日益盛仁之熟者日益熟不思而得

目所能盡心思所能及矣夫自可欲之善以至
於不可知之神充一理以至於極隨所至而異

致將與顏子之合仁與智具體聖人者並稱雖

… seamlessly transforms it, so that his greatness leaves no visible trace—this is called being a "sage" (sheng). Being a sage means that the abundance of his virtue grows ever more abundant, and the maturity of his benevolence grows ever more mature; he apprehends without deliberation and hits the mark without effort. When sageliness reaches the utmost subtlety, to the point where no one can fathom it, this is called being "spirit-like" (shen). Being spirit-like is the ultimate peak of abundant virtue and highest goodness, a subtlety without sound or scent, beyond what ears and eyes can exhaust or what thought can reach. Thus, from the "goodness" (shan) that is desirable, all the way to the "spirit-likeness" that is unknowable, one extends a single principle to its utmost, its name varying according to the stage reached, in just this way. Now as for Yuezhengzi 樂正子, he had desirable goodness, though perhaps what he possessed in himself was not yet completely real, had he fallen short of "trustworthiness" (xin)? Yet even if his trustworthiness fell short—how much less could he attain the realms of the "admirable" (mei), the "great" (da), the "sage" (sheng), and the "spirit-like" (shen), which are the ultimate culmination of extension and fulfillment! Clearly, as a person he stood within the two stages of the good and the trustworthy, and below the four stages of the admirable, the great, the sage, and the spirit-like. Alas! What Haosheng Buhai 浩生不害 asked about was merely Yuezhengzi; yet Mencius 孟子 set forth in order the stages from the good and the trustworthy all the way to the sage and the spirit-like, so as to show that learning must never cease. Had Yuezhengzi heard this and exerted himself therein, the admirable and the great could have been gradually reached; he would have been praised alongside Yanzi 顏子, who combined benevolence and wisdom and embodied the sage in miniature, and even the realms of the sage and the spirit-like would perhaps have been within his reach. What a pity that he was blind to whom he chose to follow and did not know to devote himself to learning—is this not why he stopped at merely being good and trustworthy?

同考試官編修劉批乾卦一題士皆能作而可觀者
鮮是篇說理明而措辭老必熟於經者
同考試官編修楊批此題易甚學者忽之故場中
佳作絕少有指先天後天為羲文之易者蓋玩常喜新之弊此篇得
㫖而其辭奕奕有氣焰又可以振近時學者之習是宜表之
考試官學士錢批聖人與天合道而無間于人者此作發
明治無餘蘊讀之令人起敬
考試官學士彭批此篇發明天人不違之意辭贍理
===
明佳作也
惟天與大人不相違則人於大人不能違夫天
人一道也大人以道為體則天且與之不相違
矣而况於人乎乾文言釋九五大人之德而推
言至此夫大人者與天地合其德與日月合其
明與四時合其序與鬼神合其吉凶者也其有
先於天者盖天雖未為而吾意之所為默與道
契天亦不能違之如禮以義起而恊先王之制
志既先定而致龜筮之從此先天而天弗違大

Comment by Associate Examiner and Historiographer (Bianxiu) Liu: Every scholar is capable of writing on a topic from the Qian hexagram, yet few produce anything worth reading. This essay explains the principles clearly and employs mature phrasing; the author must be thoroughly versed in the Classic.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Historiographer Yang: This topic is extremely simple, so scholars tend to take it lightly, resulting in very few fine compositions in the examination compound. Some even interpreted "preceding Heaven" and "following Heaven" as referring to the Changes (Yi) of Fuxi and King Wen—a failing born of tiring of the familiar and delighting in novelty. This essay grasps the main purport, and its language is radiant and spirited; moreover, it can rouse contemporary scholars from their habits, so it deserves to be singled out for praise.
Comment by Examiner and Academician (Xueshi) Qian: How the sage is united in the Way with Heaven and has no disharmony with man is elucidated with complete clarity [?] in this piece, leaving nothing unexpressed; reading it inspires reverence.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Peng: This essay elucidates the meaning of Heaven and man not acting in opposition; its language is rich and its reasoning clear—an excellent piece.

Because Heaven and the Great Man do not act in opposition to one another, man cannot act in opposition to the Great Man. Now, Heaven and man share a single Way. When the Great Man takes the Way as his substance, even Heaven does not act in opposition to him—how much less will man! In explaining the virtue of the Great Man at the Nine in the Fifth place, the "Words of the Text" (Wenyan) commentary on the Qian hexagram extends its discussion to this point. Now, the Great Man is one who unites with Heaven and Earth in his virtue, unites with the sun and moon in his brilliance, unites with the four seasons in his order, and unites with ghosts and spirits in his good and ill fortune. text:
即天也其有後於天者盖天雖已為而吾知
如是奉而行之亦不違乎天時如天叙有典
五典之是惇天秩有禮而五禮之是庸此後
而奉天時天即大人也夫大人所為天尚不
違之矣况於天生之烝民仰大人左右之者孰
有外其德化而違之乎必將丕應徯志若風雲
之從乎龍虎矣天尊無對且不能違乎大人矣
况於天降之下民望聖人勞来之者孰有阻其
聲教而違之哉必將愛戴歸往若水火之就乎

我之私是以梏於形體而不能相通大人無私

之大人即九二之大人也二之學聚問辨乃德

translation_en:
…[the great man] is himself Heaven. And as for cases where he acts after Heaven: although Heaven has already acted, because he knows it to be so, he upholds and carries it out without opposing Heaven's timing. For instance, when Heaven has ordered the social relationships, he gives weight to the five relationships; when Heaven has instituted the rites, he puts the five rites into practice. This is acting after [Heaven] and upholding Heaven's timing, whereby Heaven is the great man. Now, in what the great man does, even Heaven cannot oppose him; how much less, then, among the multitudes brought forth by Heaven who look up to the great man for guidance and aid, could anyone stand outside his moral transformation and oppose him? They will surely respond grandly and await his will, just as wind and clouds follow the dragon and the tiger. Heaven is supreme and peerless, yet even it cannot oppose the great man; how much less, then, among the common people sent down by Heaven who look to the sage to comfort and encourage them, could anyone obstruct his prestige and teachings and oppose him? They will surely revere and turn to him in allegiance, just as water and fire naturally seek out the wet and the dry. Why is this so? It is because Heaven and humanity originally share no dual principle; ordinary people are merely blinded by the selfishness of ego, and thus are fettered by physical form and unable to communicate with the whole. The great man has no selfishness and takes the Way as his very substance—how could one even speak of a distinction between "self" and "other," or "before" and "after"? Broadly speaking, the great man of the Nine in the Fifth place is the very same great man as that of the Nine in the Second place. In the Second place, gathering through study and discerning through inquiry are the initial steps toward uniting one's virtue with Heaven and Earth; whereas in the Fifth place, uniting one's virtue with Heaven and Earth is the ultimate achievement of gathering through study and discerning through inquiry. For in relation to the Way, the Second place cannot do without exerting effort, whereas the Fifth place is one with the Way as its substance and has no room left for the exertion of effort. Ah! Is this not whereby the great man of the Nine in the Fifth place is able to occupy the position of Heavenly virtue, bring about order throughout the realm, and rouse the gaze of all things?

In the "Limitation" (Jie) hexagram, the yielding line attains correctness and supports the one above, while the firm line matches its position and occupies the center; therefore, both the line statements and the Commentary on the Images clarify them. Now, limitation is one and the same: when a yielding line attains correctness and supports the one above, it results in the success of "contented limitation"; when a firm line matches its position and occupies the center, it results in the auspiciousness of "sweet limitation." In the line statements and the Commentary on the Images, the sages have clarified this thoroughly. In antiquity, when the Duke of Zhou appended the line statements to the "Limitation" hexagram, in every case he drew upon the meaning of limitation. Now, "limitation" means having a bound and stopping. There is no affair that does not have its limitation, and no person can do without limitation; great indeed is the Way of limitation! The Yin line at the fourth place is yielding, compliant, and attains correctness, supporting the Yang line at the fifth place above. 之則豁達而無礙亨通而無滯也爻辭如此而

五居六四之上也四之所以得安節之亨者亦
由其承上之道而無侮慢自賢之失耳且上之
道何道也九五當位以節中正以通其於節也
在已則安行而無所勞苦天下則說從而無所
艱辛故有甘節之象矣占者如之則所為有吉

translation_en: …possesses it without arising from artificial constraint, and therefore has the image of "contented regulation" (an jie). If the diviner is like this, things will be open and unobstructed, smoothly successful and without stagnation. The line statement is thus, and the Commentary on the Images (Xiang zhuan) elaborates upon it, holding that among the line positions some are exalted above and some are humble below, and Nine in the Fifth dwells above Six in the Fourth. The reason why the Fourth obtains the smooth success of contented regulation is also because it upholds the Way of the one above, without the fault of being disrespectful or considering itself worthy. Moreover, what Way is the Way of the one above? Nine in the Fifth occupies the proper position with which to regulate, and is central and correct so as to achieve free flow. In its relation to regulation, in itself it practices it calmly without any toil, and the world gladly follows without any hardship; therefore it has the image of "sweet regulation" (gan jie). If the diviner is like this, what is done will bring good fortune without misfortune, and going forward will bring merit worthy of esteem. The line statement is like this, and the Commentary on the Images elaborates upon it, holding that when the Way of regulation attains the mean it is sweet, and when it exceeds the mean it is bitter, while the fifth position dwells in the center of the upper trigram. The reason why it obtains the good fortune of sweet regulation is truly because it dwells in the center of its position, without the flaws of going too far or falling short. Centrality of position is none other than centrality of the Way. This being so, the Fifth attains the central Way and therefore regulates sweetly with good fortune; the Fourth upholds its central Way and therefore regulates contentedly with smooth success. Does not regulation indeed prize centrality! I have heard it said: the sage thoroughly comprehends regulation, the next keeps to regulation, and the lowest loses regulation. Thoroughly comprehending regulation is the central Way, and the Fifth and Fourth come close to it. Losing regulation suffers from falling short, which is why the Third laments; keeping to regulation often goes so far as to be excessive, which is why the Top repents. Among the ancients, men like Boyi, who was narrow, Liuxia Hui, who was lacking in respect, Jingzhong, under whom it was hard to serve as a superior, and Pingzhong, over whom it was hard to stand as a superior—all missed the mean. …

Only because the function of the Changes reaches the utmost subtlety does it issue forth from the infinitesimal and fill the universe without being fathomable. For whatever is swift through hurrying, or arrives through traveling, can be fathomed; yet as for the marvelous function of the Changes, its issuing forth is swift without hurrying, and its pervasive filling arrives without traveling—how could this be something that men are able to fathom? The numinous is the marvelous function of the Changes: it is nowhere and yet nowhere not present; it does nothing and yet leaves nothing undone. Therefore, …

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
自其發之微而言之凡天下之事速者必疾而
是神之發也則一念方萌而至理已具未嘗待
疾而後速焉所謂發微不可見者也于以通天
下之志志其有不通乎自其充之周而言之凡
天下之事至者必行而是神之充也則隨其所
寓而理無不到未嘗待行而後至焉所謂充周
不可窮者也于以成天下之務務其有不成乎
夫神本無速也無至也而此乃以疾速行至言
者豈以不如是不足以形容其不可測之妙也
===
歟抑考聖人傳易屢言乎神此既曰不疾而速
不行而至矣而他章又曰神无方曰陰陽不測
之謂神曰神也者妙萬物而為言者蓋易不外
乎陰陽而理即在焉理非氣則淪於無而不能
以有為氣非理則滯於有而不能以變化易之
所以生生不已變化無窮者皆理乘乎氣而妙
不可測之為也先儒謂其體則謂之易其理則謂之
道其用則謂之神合此而觀則神之義自明矣

punctuated: 自其發之微而言之，凡天下之事速者必疾，而是神之發也，則一念方萌而至理已具，未嘗待疾而後速焉，所謂「發微不可見」者也。于以通天下之志，志其有不通乎？自其充之周而言之，凡天下之事至者必行，而是神之充也，則隨其所寓而理無不到，未嘗待行而後至焉，所謂「充周不可窮」者也。于以成天下之務，務其有不成乎？夫神本無速也，無至也，而此乃以疾速、行至言者，豈以不如是不足以形容其不可測之妙也歟？抑考聖人傳《易》，屢言乎神。此既曰「不疾而速，不行而至」矣，而他章又曰「神无方」，曰「陰陽不測之謂神」，曰「神也者，妙萬物而為言者」。蓋《易》不外乎陰陽，而理即在焉。理非氣，則淪於無而不能以有為；氣非理，則滯於有而不能以變化。《易》之所以生生不已、變化無窮者，皆理乘乎氣，而妙不可測之為也。先儒謂「其體則謂之易，其理則謂之道，其用則謂之神」，合此而觀，則神之義自明矣。
translation_en:
… speaking in terms of the subtlety of its manifestation: in all affairs of the world, that which is rapid must first be hurried; yet in the manifestation of this spirit, the moment a single thought sprouts, the ultimate principle is already complete—it never waits to be hurried before becoming rapid. This is what is meant by "manifesting the subtle so that it cannot be seen." When this is used to penetrate the wills of all under heaven, could there be any will that is not penetrated? Speaking in terms of the all-pervasiveness of its extension: in all affairs of the world, that which arrives must first travel; yet in the extension of this spirit, wherever it lodges, there is nowhere that principle does not reach—it never waits to travel before arriving. This is what is meant by "extending all-pervasively so that it cannot be exhausted." When this is used to accomplish the affairs of all under heaven, could there be any affair that is not accomplished?

Now, spirit inherently has neither rapidity nor arrival. That it is spoken of here in terms of hurrying and rapidity, traveling and arriving—is it not because without doing so, one could not adequately describe the marvel of its unfathomability? Moreover, if we examine how the Sage transmitted the Book of Changes (Yi), he spoke repeatedly of spirit. Here he already says, "rapid without hurrying, arriving without traveling"; yet in other chapters he also says, "spirit has no spatial restriction," "that which is unfathomable in yin and yang is called spirit," and "spirit is that which is spoken of as working wondrously in all things." For the Changes is nothing other than yin and yang, and principle resides right within them. Without vital force (qi), principle would sink into non-being and be unable to act; without principle, vital force would stagnate in concrete form and be unable to transform. The reason the Changes generates and regenerates unceasingly and transforms inexhaustibly is entirely the doing of principle riding upon vital force in a wondrous and unfathomable way. A former Confucian scholar said: "As to its substance, it is called change (yi); as to its principle, it is called the Way (dao); as to its function, it is called spirit (shen)." When we view these together, the meaning of "spirit" becomes self-evident.

大臣告君，既勉以一德之工夫，復期以一德之感應，盖君心之德即民心之德也。人君一德之工夫既盡於己，又寧不致夫斯民感應之大哉？昔伊尹告太甲之言也，謂夫人君取善之要，固當博而求之於不一之善，尤當約而會之於至一之理。彼親親而仁民，仁之善也；從兄而敬長，義之善也。仁義之善雖有萬端，豈可執一□□
translation_en:
"Goodness has no constant master, but accords with what can be unified; cause the myriad people all to say, 'Great are the King's words!' and also to say, 'Unified is the King's mind!'"

Ge Xiao 戈潚

Comment by Associate Examiner and Supervising Secretary Huang: This essay depicts the effort of pure virtue and the principle of stimulus and response. Neither verbose nor sketchy, it captures the intent of Yi Yin's counsel to Tai Jia, and deserves to be selected.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Supervising Secretary Tong: On this topic, most writers forcibly tacked the preceding text onto the phrase "goodness has no constant master." None surpassed this essay in explaining the principles clearly.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler Li: This topic is inherently easy to understand, yet among the candidates in the examination compound, most let rhetoric prevail over principle. If one seeks an essay that thoroughly integrates the commentary and annotations into its composition, there is only this piece.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Qian: It elucidates the purport of pure virtue and its stimulus and response; its conciseness and purity are commendable.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Peng: Clear, lucid, and well worth reading; he must be a skilled writer.

When a great minister counsels his ruler, having urged upon him the effort of cultivating pure virtue, he again looks forward to the stimulus and response brought about by that pure virtue, for the virtue of the ruler's mind is none other than the virtue of the people's minds. Once the ruler has fully exerted the effort of pure virtue within himself, how could he fail to bring about the great response of the people? Such were the words spoken of old by Yi Yin 伊尹 in counseling Tai Jia 太甲. He meant that the essential way for a ruler to adopt what is good is surely to seek it broadly among the manifold forms of goodness, yet even more importantly to condense and bring them together in the principle of supreme unity. Now, being affectionate to one's kin and benevolent toward the people is the goodness of humanity; following one's elder brothers and respecting elders is the goodness of righteousness. Although the goodness of humanity and righteousness has a myriad manifestations, how could one cling to a single [to rule them?]…

text:
哉要必融而會之俾仁義之善皆合於吾心至
一之理可也恭敬辭讓之節文禮之善也是非
邪正之分别知之善也禮知之善雖有萬殊又
豈可以執一而主之哉要必貫而通之皆有以
協于吾心至一之理可也夫人君之為善如此
非一德之工夫而何人君惟其心之一故其發
諸言也大由是羣黎百姓非一人也莫不咸曰

punctuated: 哉？要必融而會之，俾仁義之善皆合於吾心至一之理可也。恭敬辭讓之節文，禮之善也；是非邪正之分别，知之善也。禮知之善雖有萬殊，又豈可以執一而主之哉？要必貫而通之，皆有以協于吾心至一之理可也。夫人君之為善如此，非一德之工夫而何？人君惟其心之一，故其發諸言也大。由是羣黎百姓，非一人也，莫不咸曰：「大矣哉，吾王之言乎！」言而謂之大，則溥博廣大而于帝其訓，蕩蕩平平而皇極敷言也。萬姓見其言之大，又能知其心之一。吾見庶民小子，非一夫也，莫不又曰：「一哉，吾王之心乎！」心而謂之一，則純一不雜而該括萬善，精粹無間而統會萬理也。夫斯民之頌上如此，又非一德之感應而何？抑考伊尹告老而去，恐太甲德不純一及任用非人，上文既告以用人之一，而此則告以脩德之一，下文又告以一德之效，無非欲太甲純一其德，以為用人為治之本也。吁！古之大臣，忠愛其君也有如是夫！
translation_en: … [rely on?] In short, he must blend and synthesize them, causing the goodness of benevolence and righteousness to all accord with the supremely unified principle of our mind; only then is it right. The ritual regulations and refinements of respect and yielding are the goodness of propriety; the distinctions between right and wrong, crooked and upright, are the goodness of wisdom. Although the goodness of propriety and wisdom has ten thousand differences, how could one again hold fast to a single aspect and make it the master? In short, he must thread them together and penetrate them, so that all have the means to harmonize with the supremely unified principle of our mind; only then is it right. Now, when a ruler practices goodness like this, what is it if not the effort of pure and constant virtue? Because the ruler's mind is unified, when he issues it forth in words, they are great. From this, the multitude of black-haired people and the hundred surnames—not just a single person—all without exception say: "How great are the words of our king!" For words to be called great means they are all-embracing, vast, and great, taking the Supreme Lord as their instruction, broad and level, spreading forth the words of the August Ultimate. When the myriad surnames see the greatness of his words, they are also able to know the oneness of his mind. We see the common people and the young—not just a single man—all without exception saying further: "How unified is the mind of our king!" For a mind to be called unified means it is pure and unadulterated, encompassing ten thousand goodnesses, refined and seamless, integrating ten thousand principles. Now, when this people praise their superior like this, what is it if not the resonant response to pure and constant virtue? Moreover, if we examine when Yi Yin 伊尹 announced his retirement on account of old age and was departing, he feared that Tai Jia's 太甲 virtue would not be pure and unified and that he might employ the wrong men. In the preceding passage he had already instructed him on constancy in employing men, here he instructs him on constancy in cultivating virtue, and in the following passage he further instructs him on the efficacy of pure and constant virtue. None of this was anything other than desiring Tai Jia to make his virtue pure and unified, taking it as the foundation for employing men and effecting governance. Ah! How loyal and loving toward their ruler were the great ministers of antiquity—even to such a degree as this!

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
克明德遂以明德望之謂夫爾文考之子也今
往治民將在祗遹文考而已是故不侮鰥寡文
考明德之事也汝豈不聞之乎汝敬述其事宜
繼其所聞而服行之使文考之德言皆見之於
躬行庸庸祗祗亦文考明德之事也汝又不聞
之乎汝祗述其事宜紹其所聞而佩服之使文
考之德言皆見之於實踐如是則汝之德明而
民可治矣然未可以自足也又當博求於古焉
彼殷先哲王若成湯非明德之君乎成湯顧諟
===
明命以撫綏萬邦是可法也汝往必廣博以求
之法其明德而用之於政則可以保治其民商
耇成人若伊尹非明德之臣乎伊尹咸有一德
以道覺斯民亦可法也汝又大遠以思之法其
明德以安汝之心則知所以訓迪其民如是則
汝之德益明而政斯立矣然亦未可以自足也
尤當等而上之別求於古焉古先哲王之明德
者莫堯舜若也堯之平章百姓舜之咸寧萬邦
豈不可法乎汝求知其理行其事用以康保乎

… was able to make bright his virtue, and accordingly he looked to him to make bright his own virtue, saying: You are the son of our accomplished late father [King Wen]; now as you go forth to govern the people, your task lies simply in reverently following our accomplished late father. Therefore, not showing contempt for widowers and widows was a matter of our accomplished late father's bright virtue—have you not heard of it? In reverently continuing his affairs, you ought to succeed to what you have heard and put it into practice, causing the virtuous words of our accomplished late father all to be manifest in your personal conduct. Employing the employable and revering the venerable were also matters of our accomplished late father's bright virtue—have you not heard of them as well? In reverently continuing his affairs, you ought to carry on what you have heard and take it to heart, causing the virtuous words of our accomplished late father all to be manifest in actual practice. If you act thus, your virtue will be made bright and the people can be governed.

Yet you must not be self-satisfied with this; you should also seek broadly in antiquity. Those former wise kings of Yin, such as Tang the Successful (Cheng Tang 成湯)—was he not a ruler of bright virtue? Tang the Successful kept his eye constantly on the bright mandate of Heaven so as to pacify the myriad states; this is worthy of emulation. When you go forth, you must seek broadly after the example of such kings, emulating their bright virtue and applying it to governance, so that you may protect and govern your people. The aged and accomplished men of Shang, such as Yi Yin 伊尹—was he not a minister of bright virtue? Yi Yin possessed pure and constant virtue, awakening this people by means of the Way; he too is worthy of emulation. You should also reflect deeply and far back upon such men, emulating their bright virtue so as to settle your own mind, and then you will know how to instruct and guide your people. If you act thus, your virtue will become ever brighter and your governance will thereby be established.

Yet even with this you must not be self-satisfied; still more should you ascend a step further and seek elsewhere in antiquity. Among the ancient former wise kings who made bright their virtue, none could match Yao 堯 and Shun 舜. … the people of Wei. If you do thus, there will be no learning in which you do not advance, no virtue that is not made illustrious, and no governance that is not brought to completion. Alas! Having reverently followed your Cultured Deceased Father [King Wen], you also broadly seek out the kings of Shang—from this it can be seen that the Way has no ultimate exhaustion; having thought far back upon the worthies of Shang, you also separately seek out the ancient sages—from this it can be seen that learning has no stopping point. This is what is meant by "the gentleman remembers many words of antiquity and deeds of the past in order to accumulate his virtue." And how could the Way of governance lie outside of this? In general, the Way of governance consists of nothing more than the two ends of virtue and punishment. Virtue serves to show encouragement and is the root of moving the people; punishment serves to show warning and is the instrument for restraining the people. When King Wu charged Kangshu, his intention was盖 like this. From "reverently follow your Cultured Deceased Father" onward, he wished him to make illustrious his virtue; from "reverently clarify your punishments" onward, he further wished him to be cautious with punishments. If Kangshu could truly make illustrious his virtue and be cautious with punishments, then the Way of governance would be exhausted—what difficulty would there be in governing the people of Yin?

"Practicing virtue, the mind is at ease and daily becomes more admirable; practicing hypocrisy, the mind toils and daily becomes more clumsy. Dwelling in favor, think of peril, and in all things be reverently fearful; if you are not fearful, you will enter into that which is to be feared. Advance the worthy and yield to the capable, and the numerous officials will be [harmonious] [?]; when they are not harmonious, governance becomes disordered [?]. Recommend those who are capable of their offices, and it is your capability; nominate those who are not the right men, and you are unequal to your duty."

考試官學士彭批成王申戒卿士以處己用人之道篇中發

處己用人之道哉昔者成王申戒卿士之意若
曰爾卿士皆有祿位者也可不知所以恭儉乎
恭儉實得於己是作德也作德則中外惟一心
逸而日休休焉恭儉矯飾於外是作偽也作偽
則揜護不暇心勞而日著其拙焉誠偽之驗如

位則當思危辱之憂無所不致其祗畏可也苟或
不畏則不知恭儉而入于可畏之中矣食此厚祿則

誠偽異其驗，固當嚴處己之戒；義利殊其效，尤當任用人之責。蓋處己莫先於敬畏，而用人當舉夫賢能。苟或不知所畏，而舉非其人，豈大臣處己、用人之道哉？昔者成王申戒卿士之意若曰：爾卿士皆有祿位者也，可不知所以恭儉乎？恭儉實得於己，是作德也；作德則中外惟一，心逸而日休休焉。恭儉矯飾於外，是作偽也；作偽則揜護不暇，心勞而日著其拙焉。誠偽之驗如此，爾其可不嚴處己之戒耶？是故位高祿厚，固為寵盛矣，而寵盛則憂患或由之以生。爾居此高位，則當思危辱之憂，無所不致其祗畏可也；苟或不畏，則不知恭儉，而入于可畏之中矣。食此厚祿，則
translation_en:
… concern employing others. This essay threads them together with the doctrines of reverence and frugality, and of righteousness and profit; it merits selection.

Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler Li commented: This topic has quite a few threads and is difficult to encompass. This essay constructs its text on the basis of the commentary; its wording and reasoning are detailed and thorough, which is delightful.

Examiner and Academician Qian commented: Going back and forth clearly and fluently, it captures the intent of the admonition delivered to the noble-officials at the time.

Examiner and Academician Peng commented: King Cheng admonished the noble-officials regarding the way to conduct oneself and employ others; the exposition in this essay is utmost.

Since sincerity and falsity differ in their verification, one ought certainly to be strict in the admonition regarding how to conduct oneself; since righteousness and profit differ in their effects, one ought especially to shoulder the responsibility of employing others. For in conducting oneself, nothing comes before reverent awe, and in employing others, one ought to recommend the worthy and capable. If perhaps one does not know what to stand in awe of, and recommends the wrong person, how could that be the way of a great minister in conducting himself and employing others?

In antiquity, the intent of King Cheng's admonition to the noble-officials was as if to say: You noble-officials are all holders of emoluments and positions; how can you not know whereby to be reverent and frugal? When reverence and frugality are genuinely attained within oneself, this is practicing virtue; when one practices virtue, inside and outside are one, the mind is at ease, and day by day it is admirably composed. When reverence and frugality are falsely adorned on the outside, this is practicing falsity; when one practices falsity, one has no leisure to cover up and protect oneself, the mind toils, and day by day its clumsiness becomes more manifest. Such are the verifications of sincerity and falsity—how can you not be strict in the admonition regarding how to conduct yourselves?

Therefore, when position is high and emolument generous, favor is certainly abundant; yet when favor is abundant, anxiety and calamity may arise therefrom. Dwelling in this high position, you ought to ponder the anxiety of peril and disgrace, and leave nothing toward which you do not extend your reverent awe; if perhaps you are not in awe, you will not know reverence and frugality, and will enter into what is to be feared. Consuming this generous emolument, …

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
當思危辱之患無所不畏斯可也茍或不
畏則不能恭儉而入于可畏之內矣一念不謹
而危辱至焉可不以是爲戒哉然嚴於處己固
事君之道而以人事君尤大臣之責彼推賢讓
能所以爲義也義則庶官是效濟濟相讓而和
焉蔽賢害能所以爲利也利亦庶官是效爭論
功能而不和焉庶官不和則政庬而不修事雜
而不理矣義利之效如此其可不任用人之責
耶然用人惟在薦舉而薦舉則不可以不慎若
===
爾所舉之人能脩其官是亦惟爾能勝其任矣
所薦者或非其人是亦惟爾不能勝其任矣一
舉用間而己之賢否係焉可不以是爲責哉成
王之戒卿士如此其意切矣大抵保祿位非難
而本於恭儉爲難薦賢才非難而出於公義爲
難成王申戒卿士既告以保祿位之道欲其以
己而事君復告以薦賢才之道欲其以人而事
君制治保邦之要端在此矣其政治洽於當時
成功垂於後世而爲守成之令主也宜哉

translation_en:
… should ponder the peril of danger and disgrace, and only by holding everything in awe will you be safe; if by chance you lack awe, you will be unable to be reverent and frugal, and will fall into that which is truly to be feared. When a single unguarded thought brings on danger and disgrace, how can you not take this as a warning? Yet while strictness in conducting oneself is indeed the way to serve the ruler, serving the ruler by bringing forward worthy men is even more the responsibility of a great minister. Promoting the worthy and yielding to the capable is how one acts out of righteousness; when there is righteousness, all the officials imitate it, yielding to one another with dignified bearing and dwelling in harmony. Obstructing the worthy and harming the capable is how one acts out of selfish profit; when there is selfish profit, all the officials likewise imitate it, wrangling over merit and ability and falling into discord. When the officials are not in harmony, governance becomes disordered and uncultivated, and affairs become muddled and unmanaged. Since the effects of righteousness and selfish profit are such as this, how can you not shoulder the responsibility of employing men? Yet employing men lies solely in recommendation, and in making recommendations one cannot but be cautious. If the man you recommend is able to fulfill his office, then you yourself have proved equal to your charge; if the one you recommend happens not to be the right man, then you yourself have failed to prove equal to your charge. Since in a single act of recommendation and appointment your own worthiness or unworthiness is at stake, how can you not take this as your responsibility?"

Such was King Cheng's admonition to his noble officers; his intent was earnest indeed. On the whole, preserving one's emolument and rank is not difficult, whereas rooting them in reverence and frugality is difficult; recommending worthy talents is not difficult, whereas doing so out of public righteousness is difficult. In repeatedly admonishing his noble officers, King Cheng first instructed them in the way of preserving emolument and rank, wishing them to serve their ruler through their own persons; and then he instructed them in the way of recommending worthy talents, wishing them to serve their ruler through others. The essentials of securing order and preserving the state truly lie right here. That his governance pervaded his own age, that his achievements were handed down to posterity, and that he became an exemplary sovereign of consolidation—how fitting indeed!

translation_en:
Classic of Poetry (Shijing): "The one-year-old boar we keep for ourselves; the three-year-old boar we present to the Duke."
Ma Shi 馬軾
Comment by Associate Examiner and Secretary Song: This essay vividly portrays the endless sincerity with which the people of Bin loved their superiors. Moreover, the brushwork is vigorous and antique, with an abundance of rhetorical spirit; it ought to be placed in the front ranks.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Director Liu: It expresses the affection of the people of Bin for their superiors as though the author had placed himself right in their shoes. Few pieces like this are to be found in the examination compound; without a doubt, he should be selected for high honors.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Compiler Zhang: In the examination compound, most brushes were cramped. Even among those who occasionally managed to elaborate on this topic, their writing was prolix and rambling. Only this piece is concise and antique, and its brushwork is bold and robust; therefore I have selected it.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Qian: In depicting the loyal and loving sentiments of the people of Bin, a warm and genial spirit is clearly visible. Moreover, its diction and tone are seasoned and poignant, and judging from his first-session essays as a whole, one looks upon him as having no equal ahead of him.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Peng: Across all seven essays, the writing rises and falls with rhythmic cadence—something impossible except for one who has long savored the finest blossoms of literature. Throughout the entire examination compound, none surpasses him.
To be sparing toward oneself while generous toward one's superiors—this was the heart with which the ancients loved their ruler. Indeed, the ancients' love for their ruler was present at all times. The smaller beasts they kept privately as their own possession, while the larger ones they presented to their superiors. How could a heart so devoted to loving the ruler ever be exhausted? Rightly did the Duke of Zhou recount this to instruct the King. I imagine the people of Bin, on the day when the great cold had arrived and after their martial exercises had been resumed: "Our furs are bright and warm," already having wherewith to make…

哉盖将奉其大於君不忍自厚也豕之大者研
也豕之大宜可以自私則曰獻豳民豈真不愛
其大哉盖欲致吾誠於君不忍不厚也吁一獸
之微而必擇以奉上如此其愛上之心何其至
