公子裳矣，而豕之微，亦不欲私之；取彼狐狸，既有以為公子裘矣，而豕之賤，亦必以奉之。夫其所以奉之者，又豈無所擇哉？彼豕之小者，豵也；豕之小宜可以及人，則曰私。豳民豈真愛其小哉？盖将奉其大於君，不忍自厚也。豕之大者，研也；豕之大宜可以自私，則曰獻。豳民豈真不愛其大哉？盖欲致吾誠於君，不忍不厚也。吁！一獸之微，而必擇以奉上如此，其愛上之心何其至哉！雖然，豳民之愛其君不止於此。方春則有殆及同歸之歎，西成則有勸趨藏氷之勞，以至殺羔以獻，舉酒而祝，亦莫非愛上之意。所以然者，則上以是施之，下以是報之也。不然，則民將胥讒之不暇，而何好愛之有？此正周公告戒之意，讀者所當知也。
韓侯入覲，以其介圭，入覲于王。王錫韓侯，淑旂綏章，簟茀錯衡，玄衮赤舄，鉤膺鏤錫，鞹靫淺幭，偉革金厄。韓侯出祖，出宿于屠。顯父餞之，清酒百壺。其殽維何？炰鼈鮮魚。
translation_en:
… skirts for the young lords, yet even something as paltry as a pig they do not wish to keep for themselves. "To take those foxes and wildcats"—they already have these to make fur garments for the young lords, yet even something as lowly as a pig they must present to him. Moreover, in presenting them, how could they do so without making a careful selection? A small pig is a yearling (*zong*). Since a small pig is suitable for ordinary people, the poem says they "keep it for themselves." Do the people of Bin truly prefer the small one? Rather, because they intend to present the large one to their lord, they cannot bear to be generous to themselves. A large pig is a full-grown boar (*jian* [written 研 for 豣]). Although one might well wish to keep a large pig for oneself, the poem says they "offer it up." Do the people of Bin truly not care for the large one? Rather, because they wish to express their sincerity toward their lord, they cannot bear not to be generous to him. Ah! Even in the trifling matter of a single beast, they unfailingly make a selection to present to their superior like this—how utmost is their devotion to their superior!

Even so, the love that the people of Bin bear for their lord does not stop here. In the spring, there is the sigh of "almost going home with him"; at the autumn harvest, there is the toil of urging one another to hasten to the work and to store the ice; and finally, slaughtering lambs to offer up and raising goblets of wine to pray for his longevity—none of this is anything other than devotion to their superior. The reason it is so is that the superior bestows such grace upon them, and the inferiors repay him in kind. Otherwise, the people would scarcely have enough time to rail at one another in mutual resentment—what affection and love could there be? This is precisely the meaning of the Duke of Zhou's admonition, which the reader ought to understand.

"The Marquis of Han came to court; with his greatjade tablet, he came in audience before the King. The King bestowed upon the Marquis of Han a fine banner with plumed ornaments, a bamboo-mat screen and an inlaid yoke-bar, a dark robe embroidered with dragons and red slippers, breast-hooks and carved frontlets, a leather-covered leaning-board and a tigerskin dash-covering, and bridle-reins with gilt rings [? 偉革金厄 for 鞗革金厄]. The Marquis of Han went forth and offered the sacrifice to the Spirit of the Road; he went forth and lodged for the night at Tu. Xianfu gave him a farewell feast, with a hundred jars of clear wine. What were the meats? Roasted turtle and fresh fish. …"

同考試官主事宋　批〔塲中作者多漫遠可取此獨〕〔鋪叙簡當且說出王寵韓侯之意殆無餘蘊宜表出之〕
同考試官郎中劉　批〔作長題而措詞簡古理趣沖融〕
同考試官編修張　批〔此篇簡嚴能道詩人之意與尋〕〔常篹註者不侔〕
考試官學士錢　批〔此言君之待臣而致寵錫之厚意〕〔非老學之士不能宜寘高選〕
===
考試官學士彭　批〔詞簡意高一結尤見筆力〕〔明詞皂非他作可儷也〕
詩人之美賢侯來朝而膺寵錫之厚歸國而膺
寵餞之隆夫諸侯來朝以歸　王者厚其錫而降
其餞亦一時盛事也詩人作為歌詩以暢達其
美不亦宜哉昔者韓侯初立來朝始受王命而
歸詩人作此以送之如此吾想韓侯為藩屏之
臣當覲君之際以其介圭而舞蹈于龍衮之前
執其寶玉而俯伏于冕旒之下盡以之合瑞□□
punctuated:
其蔌維何？維筍及蒲。其贈維何？乗馬路車。
同考試官主事宋批：場中作者多漫漶可厭，此獨鋪叙簡當，且説出王寵韓侯之意，殆無餘蘊，宜表出之。
同考試官郎中劉批：作長題而措詞簡古，理趣冲融，非老學之士不能，宜寘高選。
同考試官編修張批：此篇簡嚴，𨓏道詩人之意，典𥼶宅箋註者不侔。
考試官學士錢批：此言君之待臣而致寵錫之厚，意明詞𥼶，非他作可儷也。
考試官學士彭批：詞簡意高，一結尤見筆力。
詩人之美賢侯，来朝而膺寵錫之厚，歸國而膺寵餞之隆。夫諸侯来朝以歸，王者厚其錫而修其餞，亦一時盛事也。詩人作為歌詩以暢達其美，不亦宜哉！昔者韓侯初立来朝，始受王命而歸，詩人作此以送之如此。吾想韓侯為藩屏之臣，當覲君之際，以其介圭而拜瞻于龍衮之前，執其寳玉而俯伏于冕旒之下，盖以之合瑞于
translation_en:
…“What are the vegetables? Bamboo shoots and sweetflag. What are the parting gifts? Teams of horses and state carriages.”

Comment by Associate Examiner and Secretary (zhushi) Song: Among the writers in the examination hall, most arerambling and tedious. This essay alone lays out the narrative concisely and fittingly, and moreover brings out the meaning of the King’s favor toward the Marquis of Han until almost nothing is left unexpressed. It deserves to be singled out for distinction.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Director (langzhong) Liu: Treating a long quotation as the topic, its phrasing is concise and archaic, and its reasoning and spirit are harmonious and well-integrated. None but a scholar of mature learning could have written this; it should be placed in a high rank.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Historiographer (bianxiu) Zhang: This essay is concise and rigorous, directly expressing the intention of the poet; in its classic elegance, it is not on the same level as those that merely rely on [?] commentaries and annotations.

Comment by Examiner and Academician (xueshi) Qian: This speaks of how a ruler treats his minister and bestows lavish favors and gifts upon him. Its meaning is clear and its diction elegant; no other composition can match it.

Comment by Examiner and Academician (xueshi) Peng: The diction is concise and the conception lofty; the concluding section especially shows the vigor of the brush.

The poet praises the worthy marquis, who comes to court and receives lavish favors and gifts, and who returns to his state and is honored with a grand farewell banquet. Now, when a feudal lord comes to court and then returns home, for the true king to bestow generous gifts upon him and prepare a farewell feast for him is indeed a grand occasion of the age. For the poet to compose a song to give full expression to its beauty—is this not fitting indeed! In ancient times, when the Marquis of Han was first invested and came to court, upon his first receiving the King’s charge and returning home, the poet composed this to see him off in such a manner. I imagine the Marquis of Han, as a minister serving as a bulwark of the realm, at the moment of his audience with his lord: presenting his great jade tablet, he bows and gazes up before the dragon robe; holding fast his precious jade, he prostrates himself beneath the tasseled crown, using it to match his tally of authority with…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
王也於是王者不惟錫之以交龍之淑旂表旂
之綏章而又錫以蔽車之竹簟錯文之車衡有
所謂玄衮赤舄之錫者所以華其身也有所謂
鉤膺鏤錫之錫者所以飾其馬也至若鞹持靷
焉淺覆式焉鞗革而掞以金環焉皆車馬之飾
也亦無不舉以錫之則其恩寵不已厚哉然王
者不惟厚恩寵於其來朝之日而已及韓侯之
歸國也導所往而出祖至於屠而暫宿則又命
顯父之卿行餞贈之禮焉夫餞必有酒曰清酒
===
百壺蓋及眾也而又有炰鱉鮮魚為之殽焉殽
有炰鱉鮮魚則其味嘉矣殽必有蔌曰維筍及
蒲蓋示儉也而又有乘馬路車為之贈焉贈有
乘馬路車則其儀備矣是其寵餞不已隆哉吁
厚其錫於來覲之日隆其餞於歸國之時王者
之待諸侯何其至歟雖然懷諸侯之道不獨有
周王者然也書不云乎車服以庸易不云乎錫
馬蕃庶則懷諸侯之道行之尚矣周王舉而行
之此其所以為盛也歟

王也於是王者不惟錫之以交龍之淑旂表旂
之綏章而又錫以簟車之竹簟錯文之車衡有
所謂玄袞赤舄之錫者所以華其身也有所謂
鉤膺鏤鍚之錫者所以飾其馬也至若鞹持鞹
馬淺幭弍馬鞗革而搤以金環馬皆車馬之飾
也亦無不舉以錫之則其恩寵不已厚弍然王
者不惟厚恩寵於其來朝之日而已及韓侯之
歸國也尊所往而出祖至於屠而暫宿則又命
顯父之卿行餞贐之禮焉夫餞必有酒曰清酒
===
百壺蓋及衆也而又有魚鼈鮮魚為之殽焉殽
有魚鼈鮮魚則其味嘉矣殽必有蔌曰維筍及
蒲蓋示儉也而又有乘馬路車為之贈焉贈有
乘馬路車則其儀備矣是其寵餞不已隆弍吁
厚其錫於來覲之日隆其餞於歸國之時王者
之待諸侯何其至歟雖然懷諸侯之道不獨有
周王者然也書不云乎車服以庸易不云乎錫
馬蕃庶則懷諸侯之道行之尚矣周王舉而行
□其所以為盛也歟
punctuated: 王也。於是王者不惟錫之以交龍之淑旂、表旂之綏章，而又錫以蔽車之竹簟、錯文之車衡。有所謂玄衮赤舄之錫者，所以華其身也；有所謂鉤膺鏤錫之錫者，所以飾其馬也。至若鞹持靷焉，淺覆式焉，鞗革而掞以金環焉，皆車馬之飾也，亦無不舉以錫之，則其恩寵不已厚哉！然王者不惟厚恩寵於其來朝之日而已，及韓侯之歸國也，導所往而出祖，至於屠而暫宿，則又命顯父之卿行餞贈之禮焉。夫餞必有酒，曰「清酒百壺」，蓋及眾也；而又有炰鱉鮮魚為之殽焉，殽有炰鱉鮮魚，則其味嘉矣。殽必有蔌，曰「維筍及蒲」，蓋示儉也；而又有乘馬路車為之贈焉，贈有乘馬路車，則其儀備矣。是其寵餞不已隆哉！吁！厚其錫於來覲之日，隆其餞於歸國之時，王者之待諸侯，何其至歟！雖然，懷諸侯之道，不獨有周王者然也。《書》不云乎：「車服以庸。」《易》不云乎：「錫馬蕃庶。」則懷諸侯之道，行之尚矣，周王舉而行之，此其所以為盛也歟！
translation_en:
… the king. Thereupon, the true king not only bestowed upon him a fine banner emblazoned with intertwined dragons and a plume-tassel emblem at the top of the flagstaff, but also bestowed a bamboo mat to screen his carriage and a carriage yoke painted with intersecting patterns. There were the gifts spoken of as the dark dragon-robe and red slippers, wherewith to adorn his person; and there were the gifts spoken of as the breast-plate hooks and carved frontlets, wherewith to ornament his horses. As for the bare leather covering the trace-ring, the tiger skin covering the leaning-board, and the leather reins tipped with gilt rings—all these being ornaments for his carriage and horses—there was none that he did not take up and bestow upon him. Was not the favor and grace shown to him generous indeed!

Yet the true king did not merely lavish generous favor and grace upon him on the day he came to court. When the Marquis of Han was returning to his state, after offering the sacrifice to the Spirit of the Road to guide his journey and going out to lodge briefly at Tu, the king further commanded the noble Xianfu to perform the rites of farewell banquet and parting gifts. Now, a farewell banquet must have wine: it says, "a hundred jars of clear wine," which was so as to reach the whole retinue; and there were also roast turtle and fresh fish to serve as meats—when the meats include roast turtle and fresh fish, the flavors are fine indeed. With meats there must also be vegetables: it says, "bamboo shoots and sweetflag," which was to demonstrate frugality; and there were also teams of four horses and state carriages to serve as parting gifts—when the parting gifts include teams of horses and state carriages, the ceremonial is complete indeed. Was not this favored farewell grand indeed!

Alas! Bestowing generous gifts upon him on the day he came for audience, and holding a grand farewell for him at the time of his return to his state—how consummate was the way the true king treated the feudal lords! Even so, the Way of cherishing the feudal lords was not practiced by the kings of Zhou alone. Does not the Book of Documents (Shu) say, "Carriages and robes are given according to merit"? And does not the Book of Changes (Yi) say, "He bestows horses in great numbers"? Thus the Way of cherishing the feudal lords had been practiced since antiquity; the king of Zhou took it up and put it into practice—is not this why his reign was so flourishing!

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
既備乃奏簫管備舉喤喤厥聲肅雝和鳴
先祖是聽我客戾止永觀厥成
同考試官主事宋批〔通場不能說出自古功德之盛發揚〕
〔於樂作之時此作得之而詞旨愈見健美健羡〕
同考試官郎中劉批〔頌義能形容有周作樂氣象非泥〕
〔於章句者也允宜錄出〕
同考試官編修張批〔首篇規模宏大詞氣雄渾必老於〕
〔學者難以場屋文字目之〕
===
考試官學士錢批〔此言樂音之盛而致祖與客之難感者〕
〔而感之甚得其旨〕
考試官學士彭批〔詞氣簡勁不為委靡瑣細之語得非〕
〔佳士乎可喜可喜〕
器備而聲和神格而人悅此可見一代之盛也
蓋功成作樂自古為然樂器備而聲無不和神
明格而人無不悅則一代功業之盛豈不於斯
而可見乎昔有周當四方無虞之日而作樂以
告乎祖者如此想其登歌之際虡業鐘鼓之雜

既備乃奏，簫管備舉。喤喤厥聲，肅雝和鳴，先祖是聽。我客戾止，永觀厥成。

同考試官主事宋批：〔通場不能說出自古功德之盛發揚〕〔於樂作之時，此作得之，而詞旨愈見健美健羡。〕
同考試官郎中劉批：〔頌義能形容有周作樂氣象，非泥〕〔於章句者也，允宜錄出。〕
同考試官編修張批：〔首篇規模宏大，詞氣雄渾，必老於〕〔學者，難以場屋文字目之。〕
考試官學士錢批：〔此言樂音之盛，而致祖與客之難感者〕〔而感之，甚得其旨。〕
考試官學士彭批：〔詞氣簡勁，不為委靡瑣細之語，得非〕〔佳士乎？可喜可喜！〕

器備而聲和，神格而人悅，此可見一代之盛也。蓋功成作樂，自古為然。樂器備而聲無不和，神明格而人無不悅，則一代功業之盛，豈不於斯而可見乎？昔有周當四方無虞之日，而作樂以告乎祖者如此。想其登歌之際，虡業鐘鼓之雜…
translation_en:
"When all are ready, the performance begins; the panpipes and double-flutes are all raised up. Resounding is their sound, reverently and harmoniously blending; the royal ancestors give ear to it. Our guests have arrived, long to witness this grand completion." [Book of Odes, "You gu" 有瞽]

Comment by Associate Examiner, Bureau Secretary Song: [Throughout the examination hall, candidates were unable to articulate how the flourishing of achievements and virtue since antiquity is manifested at the moment music is performed. This essay captures it, and its phrasing and purport appear all the more vigorous, admirable, and enviable.]
Comment by Associate Examiner, Bureau Director Liu: [This exposition of the Sacrificial Odes succeeds in depicting the grand spirit of the Zhou dynasty's music-making; the author is not one bogged down in mere chapter-and-verse exegesis. It is truly fitting to select this for publication.]
Comment by Associate Examiner, Historiographer Zhang: [This opening essay is grand in scale and vigorous in tone; the author must be a seasoned scholar, and it is difficult to regard this merely as standard examination-hall writing.]
Comment by Examiner, Academician Qian: [This passage speaks of how the grandeur of musical sound moves both the ancestors and the royal guests—who are otherwise difficult to move—and it grasps the meaning of the text exceptionally well.]
Comment by Examiner, Academician Peng: [The diction and spirit are concise and forceful, avoiding listless or trivial phrasing. Is he not a fine scholar? Most delightful, most delightful!]

When the instruments are complete and the sounds are harmonious, the spirits draw near and men rejoice—herein may be seen the flourishing of an entire dynastic era. Indeed, that music is instituted once great achievements are brought to completion has been so since antiquity. When the musical instruments are fully prepared so that no sound lacks harmony, and when the divine spirits draw near so that no person fails to rejoice, can the magnificence of an era's achievements and enterprises not be witnessed right here? Of old, when the house of Zhou enjoyed a time of peace free from anxiety throughout the four quarters, such was the music it performed to announce its accomplishments to the royal ancestors. One imagines that at the moment the singers ascended the hall, as the stands, crossbeams, bells, and drums were variously…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
陳靴磬柷敔之咸備于焉而摶拊之則凡編竹
而為之簫無不作矣于焉而戛擊之則凡并兩
而吹之管無不舉矣斯時也以天下太和之休
播而為喤喤之聲翕如純如無滛窪也以四方
熙皥之治發而為肅雝之音敫如繹如無怠懣
也彼其先祖之幽若難以格今也是假是享而
聽其美則樂有以通乎幽矣先代之後若難以
悅今也永觀厥成而無所厭則樂有以和乎人
矣吁功成作樂而感格乎幽明如此有周功業
===
何其盛哉嗟夫功成作樂其来尚矣堯之時黎
民於變而作大章舜之時四夷来王而作大韶
禹之樂大夏湯之樂大濩是皆昭一代之德也
况周之積功累仁非一世矣其作樂以合於祖
夫豈不宜此詩人所以播諸歌頌萬世之下讀
之者宛然身際當時之盛
春秋
王人子突救衛〔莊公六年〕季子来歸〔閔公元年〕楚
屈完来盟于師〔僖公四年〕吳子使札来聘〔襄公〕
alt_text:
陶匏磬柷圉之咸備于焉而搏拊之則凡編竹
而爲之簫無不作矣于焉而戛擊之則凡弁兩
而吹之管無不舉矣斯時也以天下太和之休
播而爲喤喤之聲翕如純如皦如繹如無滯
□韓之治發而爲肅雝之音皦如繹如無滯
也彼其先祖之幽若難以格今也是假是享而
聽其矣則樂有以通乎幽矣先代之後若難以
悅令也永觀厥成而無所斁則樂有以和乎人
矣吁功成作樂而感格乎幽明如此有周功業
===
何其盛哉嗟夫功成作樂其來尚矣堯之時黎
民於變而作大章舜之時四夷來王而作大韶
禹之樂大夏湯之樂大濩是皆昭一代之德也
况周之積功累仁非一世矣其作樂以合於祖
夫豈不宜此詩人所以播諸歌頌萬世之下讀
之者究然身際當時之盛
春秋
王人子突救衛〔莊公六年〕季子來歸〔閔公元年〕楚
□宛來盟于師〔僖公四年〕吳子使札來聘〔襄公〕
punctuated:
陳，靴、磬、柷、敔之咸備。于焉而摶拊之，則凡編竹而為之簫，無不作矣；于焉而戛擊之，則凡并兩而吹之管，無不舉矣。斯時也，以天下太和之休，播而為喤喤之聲，翕如、純如，無滛窪也；以四方熙皥之治，發而為肅雝之音，敫如、繹如，無怠懣也。彼其先祖之幽，若難以格，今也是假是享，而聽其美，則樂有以通乎幽矣；先代之後，若難以悅，今也永觀厥成，而無所厭，則樂有以和乎人矣。吁！功成作樂，而感格乎幽明如此，有周功業何其盛哉！嗟夫，功成作樂，其来尚矣。堯之時，黎民於變而作《大章》；舜之時，四夷来王而作《大韶》；禹之樂《大夏》，湯之樂《大濩》，是皆昭一代之德也。况周之積功累仁，非一世矣，其作樂以合於祖，夫豈不宜？此詩人所以播諸歌頌，萬世之下，讀之者宛然身際當時之盛。

春秋
「王人子突救衛」〔莊公六年〕，「季子来歸」〔閔公元年〕，「楚屈完来盟于師」〔僖公四年〕，「吳子使札来聘」〔襄公…
translation_en:
…arrayed, and the pellet-drums [read 鞉 for 靴], stone chimes, starter boxes (zhu), andwooden tiger-stoppers (yu) were all completely provided. When they were struck and patted, all the panpipes (xiao) made of bound bamboo sounded forth without exception; when they were tapped and beaten, all the double-pipes (guan) blown in pairs were raised up in play without exception. At that moment, the blessings of supreme harmony throughout the realm were broadcast into resplendent sounds—blended together and pure, without licentiousness or hollowness; the tranquil and radiant governance over the four quarters was expressed as solemn and harmonious tones—clear and continuous, without slackness or dissonance. Those spirits of the ancestors in the unseen realm might seem difficult to reach, yet now they draw near, accept the offerings, and listen to the beauty of the performance—thus the music has the power to communicate with the unseen! The descendants of the former dynasties might seem difficult to please, yet now they long behold this musical completion without ever tiring of it—thus the music has the power to bring harmony to men! Ah! To compose music upon the achievement of merit and thereby move both the unseen and the manifest in such a manner—how magnificent were the achievements of the House of Zhou! Alas, composing music upon the achievement of merit is a practice of great antiquity. In the time of Yao, the black-haired people were transformed and he composed the Great Brilliance (Dazhang); in the time of Shun, the four barbarian tribes came to acknowledge his kingship and he composed the Great Succession (Dashao); the music of Yu was the Great Xia (Daxia), and the music of Tang was the Great Protection (Dahuo)—all of these made illustrious the virtue of an entire dynasty. How much more so for the Zhou, whose accumulation of merit and benevolence spanned more than a single generation! In composing music to present in the ancestral temple, how could this not be fitting? This is why the poet broadcast it in songs of praise, so that ten thousand generations later, those who read it feel as though they are personally witnessing the splendor of that era.

Associate Examiner and Bureau Director Ouyang comments: Those in the examination hall who wrote on this topic mostly treated the four men as inner and outer grandees, while others paired Qu Wan 屈完 and Ji Zha 季札 in their discussion; all of them missed the meaning of the Classic. This essay not only makes clear distinctions, but also judges the four men by whether they "accorded with righteousness" or "exceeded the mean" in order to determine praise and blame. It is truly beyond the reach of the other essays.

Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler Wang comments: The historiographical phrasing for these four men represents special strokes of the brush in the entire Classic. This essay bases its argument on Master Hu's commentary and threads it together with the two words "righteousness" (yi 義) and "the mean" (zhong 中), which especially shows learning and insight.

Examiner and Academician Qian comments: Those who study the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu 春秋) nowadays mostly discard the commentaries and follow their own whims to take shortcuts; how could they know to seek it in earnest for lifelong use? This essay is able to remember the original commentary traditions on the four men and judge their right and wrong, causing the Sage's historiographical principles to appear resolutely beyond the words. It is truly solid learning, and deserves to be placed first in this Classic.

Examiner and Academician Peng comments: This essay discusses the merits and faults of the four men very aptly, and its prose has a mature vigor. It is superior to all the other compositions and deserves to be the best in the Spring and Autumn Annals.

For affairs that accord with righteousness, the Spring and Autumn Annals invariably alters its wording to show praise; for conduct that exceeds the mean, the Spring and Autumn Annals specially abbreviates its terms to show criticism. This impartiality of the Sage in granting praise and condemnation is what makes it a model for ten thousand generations. Why is this so? "Righteousness" means that an affair accords with what is proper. As for the three men, how indeed did they accord with righteousness so as to be praised in the Spring and Autumn Annals? When Wei 衛 was embroiled in the crisis of Qianmou 黔牟, Zitu 子突 received the royal command and went to rescue it; when Lu 魯 suffered the disaster of Qingfu 慶父, Jiyou 季友 relied on the Hegemon's order to return; when Chu 楚 was subjected to the punitive expedition of the eight states, Qu Wan went as an envoy to the battle lines…

… expeditionary lines to seek a peace settlement. At those times, had Zi [tu] calculated affairs in terms of success or failure and delayed the army without advancing, or had [Ji] You and [Qu] Wan not taken the altars of soil and grain to heart and exhausted their loyalty in the service they rendered, how would that have been righteous? Fortunately, Zitu arrived and Heaven’s punishment was thereby carried out; Ji You returned and the people’s hopes were thereby comforted; Qu Wan came and amity with the hegemon was thereupon accomplished. Royal law was reasserted in the aftermath of the collapse of sovereign authority, and the position of the state was stabilized on a day when the people were terrified—whose achievement was this? The Sage considered that within, among the Central States, and without, among the four barbarian peoples, those who abandoned ritual and flouted the law followed one after another in succession; now, that these three men regulated affairs with righteousness in such a manner was truly as delightful as the sound of footsteps in an empty valley. Therefore, he did not record them according to the standard precedent, but recorded one by his style name, one with the title ‘Master’ (zi), and one with his clan name—was this not altering the wording to show praise? In praising them, he praised the fact that their deeds accorded with righteousness.

As for centrality (zhong), it means neither exceeding nor falling short; how then did [Ji] Zha exceed centrality so as to be criticized in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)? Now, Shoumeng had four sons and wished to establish Zha as his heir, and Zhufan and his brothers agreed to pass the succession in order down to Zha. At that time, had Zha placed himself in the position of Jili and accepted the state without declining, he would have attained centrality. Why then did he cling to the integrity of Zizang and remain blind to the Way of the Mean—knowing how to preserve himself as something lofty while not bearing in mind the weight of the ancestral temple and the altars of state, knowing how to decline a state to keep himself pure while not knowing that domestic troubles ought to be pitied—until in the end he hid himself away in Yanling and thereby fostered the steps toward disorder? Whose fault was this? The Sage considered that the highest can adapt their integrity to circumstances (dajie), and the next best can hold fast to their integrity (shoujie); holding fast to integrity is the conduct of an ordinary man, whereas adapting integrity is truly what a worthy does. … [?] the intention of [treating him as] a worthy? Therefore, on the occasion of his coming on a mission of friendly inquiry, [the Spring and Autumn Annals] did not group him under the precedent of the three worthies [Jiyou,仲遂/叔肸 etc., i.e.季子/仲子/叔子], but specially grouped him under the precedent of recording Jiao [of Chu] and Shu [of Qin]—was this not abbreviating the wording in order to indicate censure? Censuring him was the means of censuring his conduct for going beyond the Mean. The Sage established an impartial standard for ten thousand generations, either [granting?] it or withholding it—how could this not be brilliantly clear! Even so, the worthiness of the three men needs no discussion; yet someone might doubt why, since Jizha's yielding and the yielding of Boyi and Shuqi arose from the very same heart, the Sage alone did not regard him as worthy and instead demoted him—why is that? Alas! This is not so. The virtue of Shuqi did not equal that of Boyi, whereas the worthiness of Jizha surpassed that of his brothers [the older sons of Shoumeng]; therefore, Boyi and Shuqi's yielding the state was achieving benevolence, whereas Jizi's declining the state gave rise to disorder. Although the yielding was the same, the times were different. One who does not unite his virtue with Heaven and Earth and attain the Timely Mean is not sufficient to participate in this.

禮迭講於尊王春秋必嚴君臣之分好特講於
爭伯春秋必謹華夷之防夫春秋謹嚴之書也
安得不因齊之尊周吳之長晉而變文以示法
哉慨夫周自東遷以來名分之在人心也微矣
尚何望君臣之復正耶乃今惠王溺愛齊桓會
===
世子以弭難襄王致胙齊桓會宰孔以修禮首
止之後植大本於危疑葵丘之會肅天威於咫
尺然世子也無王命而下會諸侯宰孔也以三公
而出與諸侯會桓公之尊宰孔若無異乎世子
也春秋宜紀實書之而獨殊會世子何耶聖人
以謂子鄭雖未立儲君也宰孔雖用事相臣也
君之於臣猶天尊地卑其位定矣而可紊乎
故於首止以殊會書葵丘以列會書一尊之一

哉嘅夫周自東遷以來名分之在人心也微矣
尚何望君臣之復正耶乃今惠王溺愛齊桓會
===
世子以弭難襄王致胙齊桓會宰孔以修禮蓋
止之後植大本於危疑葵丘之會肅天威於咫
尺然世子也無王命而下會諸侯宰孔也以三公
而出與諸侯會桓公之尊宰孔若無異乎世子
也春秋宜紀實書之而獨殊會世子何耶聖人
以謂子鄭雖未立儲君也宰孔雖用事相臣也
君之於臣猶天尊地卑其位定矣而可紊乎
故於首止以殊會書葵丘以列會書一尊之一
抑之其嚴於君臣之分為何如若夫吳自稱王
punctuated:
正名分而已。近時學者多忽此不講，凴以己意牽合經傳，求為高大之論，不幾於侮聖言乎？此篇理勝而文不浮，足以矯其弊矣。
考試官學士錢批：此作以謹嚴立法，甚得《春秋》之旨。
考試官學士彭批：此篇文理兼至，蓋嘗用心於是經者也。
禮迭講於尊王，《春秋》必嚴君臣之分；好特講於爭伯，《春秋》必謹華夷之防。夫《春秋》，謹嚴之書也，安得不因齊之尊周、吳之長晉，而變文以示法哉？慨夫周自東遷以來，名分之在人心也微矣，尚何望君臣之復正耶？乃今惠王溺愛，齊桓會世子以弭難；襄王致胙，齊桓會宰孔以修禮。首止之後，植大本於危疑；葵丘之會，肅天威於咫尺。然世子也，無王命而下會諸侯；宰孔也，以三公而出與諸侯會。桓公之尊宰孔，若無異乎世子也。《春秋》宜紀實書之，而獨殊會世子，何耶？聖人以謂子鄭雖未立，儲君也；宰孔雖用事，相臣也。君之於臣，猶天尊地卑，其位定矣，而可紊乎？故於首止以殊會書，葵丘以列會書，一尊之，一抑之，其嚴於君臣之分為何如！若夫吳自稱王
translation_en:
… and rectify names and statuses—nothing more. Recent scholars mostly neglect this without discussing it, relying on their own notions to forcibly piece together the Classic and its commentaries, seeking to make grandiose arguments; does this not come close to insulting the words of the Sage? In this essay, the reasoning prevails and the prose is not superficial; it is sufficient to rectify such abuses.

Comment by Examiner Academician Qian [Qian Pu 錢溥]: This composition establishes its structure with rigor and strictness, grasping well the purport of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu).

Comment by Examiner Academician Peng [Peng Shi 彭時]: This essay achieves excellence in both style and principle; it is surely by one who has applied his mind deeply to this Classic.

When rites were repeatedly practiced in honoring the King, the Spring and Autumn Annals unfailingly enforced the distinction between ruler and minister; when amicable meetings were specially held in contending for hegemony, the Spring and Autumn Annals unfailingly guarded the boundary between Chinese and barbarian. Now, the Spring and Autumn Annals is a book of rigor and strictness; how could it not alter its wording to display the standard in response to Qi's honoring of Zhou and Wu's claiming precedence over Jin?

Alas! Ever since the eastern relocation of the Zhou, the sense of names and statuses in men's hearts had grown faint; how could one still hope that the relationship of ruler and minister would be rectified again? Yet now, when King Hui wasblinded by partial affection, Duke Huan of Qi met with the Heir Apparent to avert disaster; when King Xiang bestowed the sacrificial meat, Duke Huan of Qi met with Chief Minister Kong (Zai Kong 宰孔) to cultivate ritual propriety. After the meeting at Shouzhi, the great foundation of the state was planted amidst peril and doubt; at the meeting of Kuiqiu, the royal majesty was revered as if within a foot's breadth. Yet the Heir Apparent went down to meet with the feudal lords without a royal command, while Chief Minister Kong, as one of the Three Dukes, went out to meet with the feudal lords. Duke Huan's honoring of Chief Minister Kong seemed no different from his honoring of the Heir Apparent. The Spring and Autumn Annals ought to have recorded the facts as they were; why, then, did it single out the meeting with the Heir Apparent for special phrasing? The Sage considered that although Prince Zheng (Zi Zheng 子鄭) had not yet been enthroned, he was the heir to the ruler; and although Chief Minister Kong held authority, he was a ministerial subject. The relation of ruler to minister is like the exaltedness of Heaven and the lowliness of Earth—their positions are fixed; how can they be confounded? Therefore, at Shouzhi it recorded a "separate meeting" (shuhui 殊會), whereas at Kuiqiu it recorded a "ranked meeting" (liehui 列會)—exalting the one and suppressing the other. How strict indeed was its maintenance of the distinction between ruler and minister!

As for Wu, after it usurped the title of King…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
以後其勢橫溢於中原莫之禦也尚何望華夷
之復辨耶乃今黃池有會夫差寔臨內而晉魯
在焉上而王臣與焉然吳恃周室之長偃然先
軟晉以姬姓之伯俛首後盟諸侯之畏吳有甚
於畏晉也春秋宜據實書之而特殊會吳子何
耶聖人以謂吳人雖強夷狄也晉伯雖衰中國
也中國之與夷狄猶君子之與小人其類殊矣
而可並乎故特先書晉侯而後書及吳子一貴
之一賤之其謹於華夷之辨又何如吁不觀是
止葵丘之書無以知聖人扶持王道之心不觀
黃池之筆無以知聖人憫傷世道之意先儒謂
春秋非聖人莫能修詎不信夫雖然不特此也
他如貴王賤伯命德討罪遏人欲存天理大義
數十炳如日星無非所以垂萬世之戒噫以是
防民其後猶有次世子於三恪之下位單于於
諸侯王上而不以為異者讀經至此寧不為之
三嘆
晉人及姜戎敗秦于殽晉人敗狄于箕

punctuated:
以後，其勢橫溢於中原，莫之禦也，尚何望華夷之復辨耶？乃今黃池有會，夫差寔臨，內而晉、魯在焉，上而王臣與焉。然吳恃周室之長，偃然先軟；晉以姬姓之伯，俛首後盟。諸侯之畏吳，有甚於畏晉也。《春秋》宜據實書之，而特殊會吳子，何耶？聖人以謂吳人雖強，夷狄也；晉伯雖衰，中國也。中國之與夷狄，猶君子之與小人，其類殊矣，而可並乎？故特先書晉侯，而後書「及吳子」。一貴之，一賤之，其謹於華夷之辨又何如！吁！不觀是止、葵丘之書，無以知聖人扶持王道之心；不觀黃池之筆，無以知聖人憫傷世道之意。先儒謂「《春秋》非聖人莫能修」，詎不信夫！雖然，不特此也。他如貴王賤伯、命德討罪、遏人欲、存天理，大義數十，炳如日星，無非所以垂萬世之戒。噫！以是防民，其後猶有次世子於三恪之下，位單于於諸侯王上，而不以為異者。讀經至此，寧不為之三嘆！
晉人及姜戎敗秦于殽，晉人敗狄于箕，
translation_en:
… afterward, its power overflowed into the Central Plains with none able to resist it; how could one still hope for the distinction between Chinese and barbarian to be maintained again? Now, at the meeting of Huangchi, Fuchai personally attended; from within, Jin and Lu were present, and from above, the King's minister participated. Yet Wu, presuming upon its seniority in the lineage of the House of Zhou, arrogantly took precedence in sipping the blood of the covenant [? 先軟, error for 先歃], while Jin, though hegemon of the Ji clan, bowed its head and swore the covenant afterward. The feudal lords feared Wu even more than they feared Jin. The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) ought to have recorded this according to the facts, yet why did it specially record meeting the Viscount of Wu as a separate, secondary party? The Sage considered that although the people of Wu were strong, they were barbarians; and although the hegemon of Jin was in decline, it was of the Central States. The relation of the Central States to the barbarians is like that of the noble man to the petty man; their categories are distinct—how could they be placed on a par? Therefore, he specially wrote "the Marquis of Jin" first, and afterward wrote "and the Viscount of Wu." Honouring the one and demeaning the other—how scrupulous too was his care in distinguishing between Chinese and barbarian! Alas! Without examining the records of Shoushi [? 是止, error for 首止] and Kuiqiu, one has no way to know the Sage's heart in upholding the Kingly Way; without examining the brush-strokes at Huangchi, one has no way to know the Sage's intent in grieving over the way of the world. Former Confucians said, "None but a sage could have compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals"—how could we not believe this! Even so, it is not only this. Other great principles—such as honouring the King and demeaning the hegemons, rewarding virtue and punishing crime, curbing human desires and preserving Heavenly Principle—number in the dozens and shine as brightly as the sun and stars, all of them meant to hand down warnings for ten thousand generations. Alas! Even with such dikes to restrain the people, in later ages there were still those who ranked the Heir Apparent below the Three Revered Guests (sanke) and placed the Chanyu above the feudatory kings without considering it strange. Reading the Classic to this point, how can one not heave a threefold sigh over it!

"The men of Jin and the Jiang Rong defeated Qin at Yao; the men of Jin defeated the Di at Ji; …"

translation_en:
… The men of Jin, the men of Chen, and the men of Zheng invaded Xu. [Thirty-third year of Duke Xi.] The Marquis of Jin invaded Wei. Gongsun Ao met the Marquis of Jin at Qi. [First year of Duke Wen.] Gongsun Ao met the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Earl of Zheng, and Shi Hu of Jin to make a covenant at Chuilong. [Second year of Duke Wen.] Yang Chufu of Jin led an army to invade Chu in order to rescue Jiang. [Third year of Duke Wen.]

Zhang Xianhua 張獻華

Comment by Associate Examiner and Director (langzhong) Ouyang: For this topic, the original commentary and notes are very clear and reliable, yet writers neglected their memorized learning and did not know what to take as their main thesis; those who occasionally grasped it were constrained by the momentum of their prose and unable to bring it out fully. This essay alone stands apart from the rest of the compositions—it has decisive judgment and vigor of brush. We record it to serve as a model for scholars.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler (xiuzhuan) Wang: He thoroughly synthesizes the meaning of the commentary, and his prose is sufficient to bring it out—truly a standout in the examination hall.

Comment by Examiner and Academician (xueshi) Qian: The import of the Classic is clear, and the vigor of the brush is concise and strong; it is a fine piece of work.

Comment by Examiner and Academician (xueshi) Peng: The prose is grand and the meaning clear; the successes and failures of Duke Xiang of Jin are thus made manifest here.

When his prestige was repeatedly extended abroad, the succession of the hegemony was continued; when his counsels repeatedly failed within, the governance of the hegemony was impaired. This is why Duke Xiang of Jin, in inheriting the hegemony, was keen at the beginning yet negligent at the end. How could the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) not record these events in full to convey its meaning? Consider in the past, when Jin reached the reign of Duke Xiang, who rose in succession to Duke Wen: the hearts of the people were not yet united, and external troubles repeatedly arose—Qin was powerful in the west, the Di grew emboldened in the north, and Chu flourished in the south. If the enemies were let loose for a moment, the calamity would surely extend for several generations; how could that suffice to manifest the illustriousness of the former ruler? Fortunately, he was able to carry on his enterprise and was bold in taking action: in summer [?狄]…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
夏此衄襲鄭之秦秋率師而翦侵齊之狄冬則
連陳鄭之兵以離黨楚之許秦狄挫而中國之
勢已安許人服而荆楚之焰復熄墨縗即戎雖
可譏也而威靈以之大振忘親毒民雖足誚也
而風采為之一新一年之間三強悉退此其所
以有伯者之畧而能繼文之統歟雖然使襄公
不貴速成而圖全于終不志近利而慮患于遠
豈不益有光於其先乎奈何外患甫息舉動即
異怒衛不朝也告諸侯以致伐疆衛戚田也偕
===
公孫以同會垂隴之役以士縠合三國而主盟
救江之行以處父率偏師而伐楚稔私忿以討
衛則損其威棄政柄以會敖則毀其列士縠主
盟而拳散處父救江而謀怠氣已驕盈豈能敦
至誠于不息政多乖舛無以收永譽于諸侯不
越二載事不逮初此規模所以不足而終非文
之比歟嗟夫銳始而忽終伯心之常也於晉襄
乎何尤獨以桓文同一伯也晉襄能繼文之統
宋襄不能率桓之烈何哉蓋宋欲抑齊而啓亂

translation_en: …In summer, here[?] [at Xiao] he routed Qin, which had made a surprise attack on Zheng; in autumn, he led an army to crush the Di, who had invaded Qi; and in winter, he joined the forces of Chen and Zheng to detach Xu, which had sided with Chu. Once Qin and the Di were checked, the position of the Central States was already secure; once the people of Xu submitted, the flames of Jing-Chu were again extinguished. Taking to the battlefield in mourning garments stained black was indeed open to criticism, yet his martial prestige was greatly roused thereby; forgetting his parent and afflicting the people was indeed worthy of blame, yet his bearing was wholly renewed by it. Within a single year, all three powerful rivals retreated—was this not why he possessed the strategy of a hegemon and was able to continue the succession of Duke Wen? Even so, had Duke Xiang not prized quick success but planned for perfection at the end, and had he not set his mind on immediate gain but taken thought for troubles far off, would he not have added even greater lustre to his predecessor? How was it that no sooner had external threats subsided than his conduct immediately changed? Angered that Wei did not come to court, he notified the feudal lords so as to mount a punitive expedition; in demarcating the fields of Qi in Wei, he joined the duke’s grandson [Gongsun Ao] at a joint meeting. In the campaign of Chuilong, he used Shi Hu to bring together three states and preside over the covenant; in the expedition to relieve Jiang, he used [Yang] Chufu to lead a partial force to attack Chu. Harboring private resentment in punishing Wei impaired his authority; relinquishing the handle of governance to meet with [Gongsun] Ao ruined his proper rank; with Shi Hu presiding over the covenant, authority[?] was dispersed, and with Chufu relieving Jiang, his counsels grew slack. Once his spirit had grown proud and self-satisfied, how could he cultivate utmost sincerity without ceasing? When his governance was full of perversities and errors, he had no means to win lasting renown among the feudal lords. Within no more than two years, his achievements fell short of their beginning—was this not why his scope was inadequate and why in the end he was no match for Duke Wen? Alas! To be keen at the start and negligent at the end is the constant nature of the hegemon’s mind; what special blame is there to lay upon Duke Xiang of Jin? Yet considering that Duke Huan [of Qi] and Duke Wen [of Jin] were alike hegemons, why was Duke Xiang of Jin able to continue the succession of Duke Wen, whereas Duke Xiang of Song was unable to follow up the illustrious achievements of Duke Huan? It is because Song wished to suppress Qi and so opened the disorder…

text:
處非其所而何以順陽氣之大壮哉月令仲夏
記先王順時之政如此謂夫仲夏之月陽極於
午而長養之氣方殷火旺於離而文明之象斯
著凡人於此可不順陽明之時而居高明之所
乎彼其寒氣総至其皆入室秋固然矣而今則
宜居於崇顯之地曰為改嵗入此室處冬固尔
矣而今則宜止於爽塏之域夫惟崇顯之是居
則所眺者必及於廣遠爽塏之是止則所望者
不蔽於淺近盖居高明斯可以遠眺望故也然
===

峙而高者為山平而人可陵者為陵此自然高

之以開明其心目封土為臺臺之有木者為榭

哉盖將藉之以宣泄其志意所以然者以陽氣

punctuated: 處非其所，而何以順陽氣之大壮哉？《月令》仲夏記先王順時之政如此。謂夫仲夏之月，陽極於午而長養之氣方殷，火旺於離而文明之象斯著。凡人於此，可不順陽明之時，而居高明之所乎？彼其「寒氣総至，其皆入室」，秋固然矣；而今則宜居於崇顯之地。「曰為改嵗，入此室處」，冬固尔矣；而今則宜止於爽塏之域。夫惟崇顯之是居，則所眺者必及於廣遠；爽塏之是止，則所望者不蔽於淺近。盖居高明，斯可以遠眺望故也。然而欲遠眺望，又可不或升山陵、或處臺榭乎？夫峙而高者為山，平而人可陵者為陵，此自然高明之所也。陟彼山陵，豈徒事乎般遊哉？盖欲資之以開明其心目。封土為臺，臺之有木者為榭，此人為高明之所也。處彼臺榭，豈欲縱乎逸豫哉？盖將藉之以宣泄其志意。所以然者，以陽氣在上，無非順之以適乎居處之宜爾。雖然，不特居處為然也。門閭毋閉，以防有壅塞之虞；關市毋索，以慮無寛大之政；暴布則恐以小功干盛
translation_en:
…one is dwelling in an improper place, and how then could one accord with the great vigor of the yang vital force? Thus it is that the "Monthly Ordinances" (Yueling) in its section on mid-summer records the former kings' governance in accordance with the seasons.

It means that in the month of mid-summer, yang reaches its zenith at the wu position, and the vital force of growth and nourishment is at its height; fire flourishes in the li trigram, and the emblem of brightness and civilization becomes manifest. At such a time, how could anyone fail to accord with the season of bright yang and dwell in high and bright places? As for the saying, "When the cold air arrives in full force, all enter their chambers," that is certainly true of autumn; yet now one ought to dwell in lofty and prominent places. And as for the saying, "The year is changing, let us enter and dwell in these chambers," that is certainly so of winter; yet now one ought to reside in airy and elevated precincts. Only by dwelling in what is lofty and prominent will one's gaze surely reach far and wide; only by residing in what is airy and elevated will one's view not be obstructed by what is shallow and near. For it is by dwelling in high and bright places that one is able to gaze into the distance.

Yet if one wishes to gaze into the distance, how could one not either ascend mountains and hills or reside in terraces and pavilions? That which stands towering and high is a mountain, and that which is broad and can be scaled by men is a hill; these are places that are naturally high and bright. In ascending those mountains and hills, is one merely engaging in pleasure-seeking excursions? Rather, one wishes to rely on them to open and brighten one's mind and eyes. Piled-up earth forms a terrace, and a terrace with wooden structures upon it is a pavilion; these are places made high and bright by human effort. In residing in those terraces and pavilions, does one wish to indulge in idle ease? Rather, one intends to make use of them to vent and refresh one's thoughts and feelings. The reason for this is that the yang vital force is above, and all of this is simply a matter of according with it so as to suit what is proper in one's dwelling place.

Even so, this is true not only of one's dwelling place. Gates and village portals are not to be kept shut, lest there be the danger of obstruction and blockage; barriers and markets are not to make exactions, lest there be a lack of generous and magnanimous governance; in bleaching cloth in the sun, one fears offending the flourishing [yang] with petty work…

已久而此猶以王政紀事說者謂月令祖先王
而成書夫豈不信
天高地下萬物散殊而禮制行矣流而不

… yang; and in applying punishments, there was concern lest yin affairs suppress the yang vital force. Therefore, within the span of a single month, warnings were repeatedly issued. Thus, in issuing governmental ordinances in accordance with the bright yang force, the former kings may truly be said to have left no aspect unattended in the application of their minds. Indeed, by that era, kingly governance had long ceased to be practiced, yet this text still recorded affairs in terms of kingly governance. When commentators say that the Monthly Ordinances (Yueling) was compiled by modeling itself on the former kings, how could that not be credible?

"Heaven is high and earth is low; the myriad things are scattered and differentiated, and thus the regulations of ritual operate. Flowing without cease, uniting in common and transforming, music arises therein. Spring's stirring and summer's growth are benevolence; autumn's harvesting and winter's storing are righteousness. Benevolence is akin to music, and righteousness is akin to ritual. Music thickens harmony, leading the celestial spirits and following Heaven; ritual distinguishes what is fitting, settling the terrestrial spirits and following Earth. Therefore, the sages created music to respond to Heaven and instituted ritual to match Earth. When ritual and music are luminous and complete, Heaven and Earth fulfill their proper functions."

Cao Keng 曹鍷

Comment by Associate Examiner and Bureau Director Wu: This composition bases its argument entirely on the commentary of Master Chen [Chen Hao 陳澔], expressing it in warm and lustrous language. title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
禮樂本於造化者有貫通之妙禮樂作於聖人
者有參贊之功甚矣禮樂在天地間一和序之
理貫通而已然則聖人寓禮樂之精微於制作
者又豈不足以參贊乎造化哉且夫兩儀定位
而有高下之形品彙咸亨而有散殊之迹此造
化示人以自然之序而禮之原已肇於此矣周
流而有不息之機合同而有化醇之妙此造化
示人以自然之和而樂之本已基於此矣惟其
合同也故春而作興夏而長養者天地生物之
===
仁惟其散殊也故秋而收斂冬而歸藏者天地
成物之義仁主發生一陽氣之運行氣行而同
和者近似於統同之樂義主裁制一陰氣之凝
寂質具而異序者近似於辨異之禮樂不徒近
而樂能厚其氣之同循其陽氣之伸而行於天

Rites and music, as rooted in the creative transformations of nature, possess the subtlety of pervading interconnection; rites and music, as created by the sages, possess the merit of assisting in cosmic transformation. Profound indeed is it that rites and music between Heaven and Earth are simply pervaded by a single principle of harmony and order! Since this is so, how could the sages' lodging of the subtle essence of rites and music within their institutions fail to suffice in assisting the creative transformations of nature?

Moreover, when the Two Modes [Heaven and Earth] establish their positions, there are the forms of high and low; when the myriad categories of things all flourish, there are the traces of dispersion and distinction. In this way, creative nature reveals to humankind the spontaneous order of things, and the origin of rites has already been initiated here. Circulating everywhere with an unceasing mechanism, uniting together with the marvel of generative fusion—in this way, creative nature reveals to humankind the spontaneous harmony of things, and the foundation of music has already been established here. Precisely because of this uniting together, what stirs and arises in spring and what grows and nourishes in summer is the benevolence of Heaven and Earth in generating things; precisely because of this dispersion and distinction, what gathers in autumn and what returns to storage in winter is the righteousness of Heaven and Earth in bringing things to completion. Benevolence presides over generation and sprouting, which is entirely the movement of yang qi; as qi moves and harmonizes in unity, it closely resembles music, which unites what is common. Righteousness presides over regulation and restraint, which is entirely the condensation and stillness of yin qi; as physical substance takes form and is ordered in distinction, it closely resembles rites, which differentiate what is distinct. Yet music does not merely resemble this: music is able to enrich the commonality of qi, following the expansion of yang qi to operate in Heaven—this is what is meant by "music manifests the Great Beginning." And rites do not merely resemble this: rites are able to differentiate the distinctions among things, gathering the contraction of yin qi to take form on Earth—this is what is meant by "rites reside in the completion of things." Because the principles of rites and music arise from spontaneity, they fill the universe and flow everywhere, reaching every height and penetrating every depth like this. 契妙理，以一身而當重任。知樂之原於天也，作為五聲六律之樂，以應助乎天之生物；知禮之本於地也，制為三千三百之禮，以配合乎地之成物。聖人禮樂之精微寓於制作者，既煥乎其昭晰，又郁乎其完美。則是以裁成其道，輔相其宜，將見天位乎上，而陰陽寒暑之和平；地位乎下，而草木鳥獸之咸若，無不各得其職矣。雖然，黃鐘大呂、弦歌干揚，樂之末節也，而本不在是；陳尊俎、列籩豆、以升降為禮者，禮之末節也，而本不在是。禮樂之本在天地，而其用也則貫乎陰陽。不有聖人，抑孰能發天地之蘊而成贊助之功哉？吁！童者舞之，有司者掌之，不足以語此。

「是故君子議道自己，而置法以民。」

… accords with this subtle principle, and in his own person shoulders the heavy responsibility. Knowing that music originates in Heaven, he creates music with the five notes and six pitch-pipes to respond to and assist Heaven's generation of things; knowing that ritual is rooted in Earth, he institutes the three thousand major and three hundred minor rules of ritual to correspond to Earth's completion of things. When the subtle essence of the sage's ritual and music is lodged in his institutions and creations, it is at once brilliantly clear and richly perfected. Thus, by regulating and completing their Way and assisting what is fitting for them, one will see Heaven take its place above, with yin and yang, cold and heat in harmony, and Earth take its place below, with plants and trees, birds and beasts all thriving in compliance—none failing to fulfill its proper function. Even so, the huangzhong and dalü pitch-pipes, singing to stringed instruments, and brandishing shields and battle-axes are merely the minor details of music, and its root does not lie in them; setting out goblets and sacrificial stands, arranging bamboo and wooden vessels, and treating ascending and descending the hall as ritual are merely the minor details of ritual, and its root does not lie in them. The root of ritual and music lies in Heaven and Earth, and their functioning runs through yin and yang. Without the sage, who indeed could bring forth the profound stores of Heaven and Earth and accomplish the work of assisting them? Ah! Youths who perform the dances and functionaries who manage the ceremonies are not worthy of discussing this.

"Therefore the superior man deliberates on the Way starting from himself, and establishes laws according to the people."

Comment by Associate Examiner Historiographer Wang: It brings out the subtle intent of the sage in deliberating on the Way and establishing laws. Scraping away crudity and mediocrity, its brilliance shines forth—not to be compared with those who compose essays merely from rote memorization.

When the sage discusses the Way, he必ず roots it in his own person, whereas when he establishes laws, he adapts them to other people. For the Way does not permit the slightest compromise, whereas laws must be sought that are easy to put into practice. When the sage discusses the Way above and displays laws to those below, how could he not draw upon what is innate in his own nature while adapting to what the common people are capable of? This chapter of the Record on Example (Biaoji) continues the preceding passage and extends its meaning, saying that the Way of fully realizing benevolence is something none but a sage can achieve, whereas the method of seeking benevolence is something even the multitude can strive after. Therefore, in this matter the sage 반드시 discusses the Way on the basis of himself, and establishes laws on the basis of the people. Why is this? To love benevolence without desire, and to hate lack of benevolence without fear—this is what he himself is capable of. When he deliberates upon the Way according to what he himself is capable of, his words are intimate and exact without lapsing into accommodation, and his discussions are supremely fitting without erring through compromise. Because he himself is able to fulfill his nature, what he speaks of strives to reach the ultimate principle; because he himself is able to realize his bodily form, what he puts forth necessarily attains utmost subtlety. In this manner, nothing of the Way is left unexhausted. To love benevolence out of desire, and to hate lack of benevolence out of fear—this is what the people are capable of. When he establishes laws according to what the people are capable of, he follows the reach of their talents without forcing upon them things that are difficult to practice, and accommodates the capacity of their strength without demanding of them overly lofty conduct. He enables them to attain it for themselves so that all the people can follow it, and guides them with great ease so that everyone can reach it. In this manner, no law fails to be put into practice. Alas! The Way is constant and unchanging, and deliberating upon it from oneself is how the ultimate standard [is established?]…

…whereby the ultimate standard is established; laws adapt and change according to people, and establishing them on the basis of the common people is whereby the governance of the people is carried out. Were it not a sage who embodies the constant and exhausts all transformations, who could participate in this? Examining further the following passage, which says, "He whose heart is naturally at peace in benevolence is but one person in the world," we see that no one other than a sage is sufficient to possess benevolence as his very nature. The tradition says, "If one sets his mind on benevolence, he will be free from evil," which means that the multitude can all practice benevolence. Thus, the sage discusses the Way on the basis of his own nature, and establishes laws on the basis of what the multitude can do, because he exhausts benevolence in himself while wishing that all others strive toward benevolence. Alas! That "benevolence has long been difficult to achieve, and only the gentleman is capable of it" is truly for good reason!

世於雍熙制作之盛超越百王禮樂之懿
卓冠百代放勲光于四表文軌同乎萬方
聖人在天子之位自生民以來未有如今日也
於戲盛哉愚也沐浴膏澤于茲有年敢以
今日之盛證先儒之言可乎盖嘗論之當
===
制作之任必有其德又有其位如今日之
聖天子至矣使徳焉而無位固不敢為借曰為
之不過自專而已不尊不信如制作何使
焉而無德將何以為借曰為之不過自用
而已無徵不信如制作何此先儒所以謂
作禮樂者必聖人在天子之位也聖人在
天子之位則其聰明睿知足以居臨馭之
尊仁義禮智足以周天下之用身為律
度之□體用與道義之全統萬邦而百官

駿德配天，飛龍御極，陶吾民於嘉靖，囿斯世於雍煕。制作之盛，超越百王；禮樂之懿，卓冠百代。放勲光于四表，文軌同乎萬方。聖人在天子之位，自生民以來，未有如今日也。於戯，盛哉！愚也沐浴膏澤于兹有年，敢以今日之盛證先儒之言，可乎？

蓋嘗論之，當制作之任，必有其德，又有其位，如今日之聖天子，至矣。使德焉而無位，固不敢為；借曰為之，不過自專而已。不尊不信，如制作何？位焉而無德，將何以為？借曰為之，不過自用而已。無徵不信，如制作何？此先儒所以謂「作禮樂者，必聖人在天子之位」也。

With magnificent virtue matching Heaven, the flying dragon ascends the supreme throne, molding our people in auspicious tranquility and encompassing this age in harmonious prosperity. The flourishing of his institutions surpasses the hundred kings; the excellence of his rites and music stands supreme above a hundred generations. His far-reaching merits shine to the four extremities of the earth, and written scripts and carriage gauges are unified across the ten thousand regions. "A sage occupies the position of Son of Heaven"—since the birth of mankind, there has never been a time like today. Ah, how magnificent! I, in my simplicity, have been bathed in this rich grace for years now; may I venture to use the magnificence of today to verify the words of the former Confucian scholar?

Let us consider the matter: to bear the responsibility of creating institutions, one must possess both the virtue and the position—just like our sage Son of Heaven today, who represents the ultimate perfection. Suppose one has the virtue but lacks the position: he certainly would not dare to act; and even supposing he did act, it would amount to nothing more than presuming upon authority on his own. Not being in a position of honor, he would not be trusted—what then could he do about creating institutions? Suppose one has the position but lacks the virtue: wherewithal would he act? And even supposing he did act, it would amount to nothing more than relying on his own arbitrary will. Lacking attestation, he would not be trusted—what then could he do about creating institutions? This is why the former Confucian scholar said, "He who creates rites and music must be a sage occupying the position of Son of Heaven."

When a sage occupies the position of Son of Heaven, his intelligence, perspicacity, and wisdom are sufficient to occupy the exalted station of ruling and governing, and his benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom are sufficient to meet the needs of the entire world. His person and voice serve as the great standard and measure, and in substance and function he embodies the completeness of the Moral Way and righteousness. He governs the myriad states, and the hundred officials…

translation_en: … take him as their model, and when he pacifies the Four Seas, the six domains submit to his virtue. Attaining equilibrium, he has the means to bring into equilibrium all that is out of equilibrium in the world; attaining harmony, he has the means to harmonize all that is out of harmony in the world. Exercising the subtlety of his spirit and mind, he exhausts the comprehensiveness of regulations and institutions. When he institutes rites, that by which he distinguishes superior and inferior and settles the minds of the people is in every respect utterly complete and thorough; when he creates music, that by which he calms their feelings and broadcasts their customs is in every respect utterly good and utterly beautiful. Applied among the people of the districts and extended to the states and realms, he harmonizes and rectifies them so that none dare diverge; practiced in the royal court and extended throughout the Four Seas, he makes them uniform and united so that none dare differ. Because of this, there is no one in the world who does not say: "How admirable! In the creations and institutions of our Sage, that by which he establishes the supreme standard for us is complete. Turning solely toward this supreme standard, could we ever be remiss? If even being remiss is impermissible, how much less unspoken criticism and private disputation!" And there is no one who does not say: "How great! In the creations and institutions of our Son of Heaven, that by which he displays the model for us is comprehensive. Hastening to follow his commands and act upon them, would we ever dare fall behind? If we dare not even fall behind, how much less practice divergent governance and different customs!" Thereby one may test them against the Three Kings and find no error; thereby one may set them up before Heaven and Earth and find no contradiction. In the unseen realm, one may verify them before the ghosts and spirits without doubt; in the distant future, one may wait a hundred generations for a sage without perplexity. text:
代三禮五禮之制□□漢武之作制度考
文之事若堯若舜固此德此位也若湯若
武亦此德此位也是以措之當代而致隆
垂之萬世而無弊成周之季聖王不作可
當制作之任者唯吾夫子而已然有德無
位托諸空言雖損益之大凡徒兆於為邦
之言而不世之事業卒未見於東周之盛
也下洎漢唐宋其間願治之君或有志於
制作亦不過因陋就簡而已蓋不能不有
===
待於今日也雖然今日之盛厥亦有由洪
惟我
太祖高皇帝創制立法聿新一代之命
太宗文皇帝潤色昭宣丕顯重光之治至我
皇上復登大寶益弘敷賁推明而光大之若昔
成周之業雖大備於文武之世而郁郁之
文卒成於累世之餘此今日所以能致若
是之盛也歟

translation_en:
… [Later, during the Three] Dynasties, in the establishment of the Three Rites and the Five Rites, the creations of [Shao and Hu?] [?] and the martial accomplishments of the Han [or: King Wu's creations of the Shao and Wu dances?], and the matters of ordering institutions and examining the written script: rulers like Yao and Shun certainly possessed both this virtue and this position; rulers like Tang and King Wu likewise possessed both this virtue and this position. Therefore, when they implemented these in their own age, they brought about prosperity, and when they handed them down for ten thousand generations, there were no defects. By the end of the flourishing Zhou, sage-kings no longer arose, and the only one capable of bearing the responsibility of creating institutions was our Master [Confucius]. Yet he possessed the virtue without the position, and so entrusted his ideas to empty words. Although the general outlines of what to abrogate and what to add were merely prefigured in his remarks on governing a state, his extraordinary enterprise was never finally realized in the flourishing of an Eastern Zhou. Coming down to the Han, Tang, and Song, although among them there were sovereigns who desired good governance and at times aspired to create institutions, they did no more than make do with existing crudities and settle for simplicity. Indeed, it could not but wait until today! Even so, today's flourishing also has its origin. Humbly reflecting on our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao [the Hongwu Emperor], he created institutions and established laws, initiating the mandate of a new era; the Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wen [the Yongle Emperor], embellished and brilliantly proclaimed them, grandly manifesting governance of renewed splendor; and down to Our Sovereign Majesty, who has again ascended to the Great Treasure [the throne], he has even more broadly spread and adorned them, extending, clarifying, and glorifying them. It is just like the enterprise of the flourishing Zhou of old: although it was greatly prepared in the eras of Kings Wen and Wu, its resplendent cultural pattern was finally brought to completion only after several generations. Is this not why today we are able to attain such flourishing as this!

===
篇關鍵可見筆力其嘗用心於古作者歟
制大事者必有其本而又有其具可也無其本
則大事不立無其具則大事不行然則制大事
者惡可苟焉而已夫大事者何禮與樂也禮以
定民分樂以和民心皆吾民日用之不可缺者
彼其先天下之憂者孰不欲為之更張以陶吾
民然而無其具則不尊不信而民弗從矣執天
下之柄者亦孰不欲為之損益以淑吾民然而
無其本則無徵不信而民不從矣是故孔孟先

He who would institute great affairs must possess their foundation, and only when he also possesses their instruments will it suffice. Without their foundation, great affairs cannot be established; without their instruments, great affairs cannot be carried out. This being so, how could he who would institute great affairs simply go about it casually? Now, what are great affairs? They are ritual and music. Ritual serves to fix the people's stations, and music serves to harmonize the people's hearts; both are indispensable to the daily necessities of our people. As for those who are first to worry about the world's troubles, who among them does not wish to reform and restring them so as to mold our people? Yet if they lack the instruments, they are neither revered nor trusted, and the people will not follow. And as for those who hold the handle of authority in the world, who among them does not likewise wish to subtract from and add to them so as to improve our people? text:
天下之憂者何棲遲於鄒魯而不聞其更
張有其本無其具故也辛受執天下之柄
者何寂寥於千載而未聞其損益有其具
無其本故也無其本而作者為愚愚固不
可也無其具而作者為僭僭亦不可也然
則可當其任者其惟聖人在天子之位乎
聖人者道全而德備義精而仁熟本之大
莫加焉天子之位者高麗乎九重俯視乎
萬方具之大莫加焉以是至大之本而藉

一樂之作隨布而隨悅不必徙木以立信

敬之如神明故德不加於孔孟而功邁之
位不大於辛受而功邁之天下之人皆秩
秩乎倫理正而分義明以為有禮也而不
知聖人在天子之位有以使之也皆熙熙

也而信之如金石不必縣首以示戒也而
敬之如神明故德不加於孔孟而功過之
位不大於辛受而功邁之天下之人皆秩
秩乎倫理之而分義明以為有禮也而不
知聖人在天子之位有以使之也皆熙熙
乎恩誼焉而和氣洽以為有樂也而不知
聖人在天子之位有以致之也書以記□□
punctuated: 天下之憂者，何棲遲於鄒、魯而不聞其更張？有其本無其具故也。辛受執天下之柄者，何寂寥於千載而未聞其損益？有其具無其本故也。無其本而作者為愚，愚固不可也；無其具而作者為僭，僭亦不可也。然則可當其任者，其惟聖人在天子之位乎！聖人者，道全而德備，義精而仁熟，本之大莫加焉。天子之位者，高麗乎九重，俯視乎萬方，具之大莫加焉。以是至大之本，而藉此至大之具，是以一禮之制，朝渙而暮從；一樂之作，隨布而隨悅。不必徙木以立信也，而信之如金石；不必縣首以示戒也，而敬之如神明。故德不加於孔、孟，而功邁之；位不大於辛受，而功邁之。天下之人，皆秩秩乎倫理正而分義明，以為有禮也，而不知聖人在天子之位，有以使之也；皆熙熙乎恩誼篤而和氣洽，以為有樂也，而不知聖人在天子之位，有以致之也。書以記實，
translation_en:
… anxieties of the world, yet why did they linger in Zou and Lu without anything being heard of their instituting reforms? It was because they possessed the foundation [moral virtue] without the instrument [imperial authority]. Xin Shou [King Zhou of Shang] held the handle of authority over the world, yet why has he remained devoid of achievement across a thousand years without anything being heard of his making adjustments to tradition? It was because he possessed the instrument without the foundation. To initiate institutions without the foundation is folly, and folly is certainly unacceptable; to initiate institutions without the instrument is usurpation, and usurpation is likewise unacceptable. This being so, as for who can shoulder this responsibility—is it not solely a sage who occupies the throne of the Son of Heaven!

A sage is complete in the Way and perfected in virtue, refined in righteousness and mature in benevolence; nothing can surpass the greatness of such a foundation. The throne of the Son of Heaven is loftily arrayed in the ninefold palace enclosures, looking down upon the myriad regions; nothing can surpass the greatness of such an instrument. Taking this supreme foundation and availing oneself of this supreme instrument, whenever a single ritual is instituted, it is proclaimed in the morning and obeyed by evening; whenever a single piece of music is created, no sooner is it promulgated than it brings delight. There is no need to move a wooden pole to establish credibility, yet the people trust in it like metal and stone; there is no need to hang up heads to display a warning, yet they revere it like the spirits and gods. Therefore, though his virtue does not exceed that of Confucius and Mencius, his achievements surpass theirs; though his position is no greater than that of Xin Shou, his achievements surpass his. The people of the world are all orderly, with human relationships rectified and distinctions of duty made clear; they take this to be the presence of ritual, without realizing that it is the sage on the throne of the Son of Heaven who has caused it to be so. They are all joyful and content, with kindness and friendship deepened and harmonious vital energy permeating everywhere; they take this to be the presence of music, without realizing that it is the sage on the throne of the Son of Heaven who has brought it about. Writing is used to record realities, …

博矣哉車以載行不出戶而合轍引重致
遠以濟不通其利遠矣哉若是者皆以聖
人在天子之位故也蓋聖人者必假乎位
而後行故曰聖人之大寶曰位民亦必有
聖人在位而後信故曰聖人作而萬物覩
維昔唐虞三代之時禮樂明備治化昭彰
皆以聖人在天子之位故也自秦而下有
其德而無其位者鮮矣有其位而有其德

punctuated:
不相約而自同，百官以察，萬民以治，其機博矣哉！車以載行，不出戶而合轍，引重致遠，以濟不通，其利遠矣哉！若是者，皆以聖人在天子之位故也。蓋聖人者必假乎位而後行，故曰：「聖人之大寶曰位。」民亦必有聖人在位而後信，故曰：「聖人作而萬物覩。」維昔唐、虞、三代之時，禮樂明備，治化昭彰，皆以聖人在天子之位故也。自秦而下，有其德而無其位者鮮矣，有其位而有其德者尤鮮，是以禮樂之制不傳。恭惟天朝列聖相承，皆大有為之主，是以禮樂之原淑乎人心，禮樂之化通乎天下，正所謂聖人在天子之位而制禮作樂者。愚何幸身際其盛！謹論。

表
沈正
擬宋蘇軾進唐陸宣公奏議表
translation_en:
…without prior agreement they naturally become uniform; through it the hundred officials are examined and the myriad people are governed—how broad is its mechanism! Carriages are used to carry things in transit: without leaving one's door, their wheel-ruts match on the road, drawing heavy loads and reaching distant places to relieve lack of communication—how far-reaching is their benefit! That things are like this is all because a sage occupies the throne of the Son of Heaven. Indeed, a sage must rely upon the throne before his Way can be put into practice; hence it is said: "The great treasure of the sage is called the throne." The people likewise must have a sage on the throne before they place their trust; hence it is said: "The sage arises and all creatures behold him." In antiquity, during the times of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties, rites and music were bright and complete, and ordering transformation was gloriously manifest—all because sages occupied the throne of the Son of Heaven. From the Qin dynasty downward, those who possessed the virtue without possessing the throne have been few, and those who possessed both the throne and the virtue have been rarer still; therefore the institutions of rites and music were not transmitted. Reverently considering our Celestial Dynasty, where a succession of sacred emperors have inherited one from another, all of them sovereigns of great achievement, the source of rites and music has purified human hearts, and the transformation of rites and music has pervaded the entire realm. This is truly what is meant by a sage occupying the throne of the Son of Heaven and instituting rites and creating music. How fortunate am I, in my humble person, to witness such flourishing times! I respectfully offer this discourse.

Memorial
Shen Zheng 沈正
An Imitation of the Song-Dynasty Official Su Shi's 蘇軾 Memorial Presenting the Memorials and Deliberations of Duke Xuan of the Tang, Lu Zhi 陸贄 (Tang Lu Xuangong zouyi 唐陸宣公奏議)

Your servant [Su] Shi humbly reflects: Fond of questioning and employing the mean, the sage emperor inaugurated the flourishing governance of the Yu dynasty [of Shun]; studying antiquity and seeking instruction, the worthy ruler restored the grand peace of the Yin age. Although governance is decided solely within the imperial mind, insight must draw upon the old canons. Now, I humbly encounter Your Majesty [〇〇〇〇], intelligent, resolute, and upright, civil, martial, sagely, and divine. Your virtue accords with Chonghua [Shun], capably continuing the great enterprise of the late Emperor; ascending to the Great Treasure [the throne], You comprehensively seek the grand plans of past sages. Near words are not disdained even from grass- and firewood-gatherers; how would small merits be cast aside like turnip or radish greens? Your servant [Su] Shi unworthily holds an office of deliberation and counsel, yet has no way to fulfill his hoped-for repayment; searching widely for the writings of worthies and wise men, I still hope to offer some aid. I humbly reflect that the Tang minister Lu Zhi was endowed by Heaven with unadorned loyalty, and cherished in his heart the ordering of the state and relief of the people. Formerly serving as an "Inner Chief Councilor" [Hanlin Academician], he took charge of drafting imperial edicts for an era; standing independent in the central court, he upheld the cardinal principles and constant virtues during the restoration of the dynasty. punctuated: 天人三策，識陳時病；進白皆仁義之談，啓沃君心，亹亹盡帝王之學。奉天之詔一下，挽人心於已離；興元之疏屢陳，回天命於復續。慮邊患必條其六失，敷治要則動以萬言。生民休戚之所關，中夏盛衰之攸繫。精忠貫乎金石，炳炳如丹；嘉謨載於簡編，昭昭若鑒。雖不究用於當世，而實有待於明時也。臣夙已潛心，久益玩味，爰繕寫以成帙，仍以次而類編，上徹九重之深，少塵乙夜之覽。篇雖富，舉其綱而目自隨；言雖詳，挈其本而末可見。誠人君之藥石，寔治化之鹽梅。彼經史之格言，非不載夫至道；而兵民之急務，則莫切於是書。寓於目而運之心，庶有符於一得；采其言而達之政，豈無裨於萬機？伏望聖學緝熙，並光明於日月；
translation_en: …the three policy essays on Heaven and Humanity, insightfully setting forth the ills of the age; his submissions to the throne were all discourses on benevolence and righteousness, enlightening and enriching the ruler's mind, tirelessly exhausting the learning of emperors and kings. Once the decree from Fengtian was issued, it won back people's hearts when they had already become alienated; as the memorials from Xingyuan were repeatedly presented, they restored the Mandate of Heaven so that it continued anew. When concerned about frontier troubles, he invariably itemized their six failings; when setting forth the essentials of governance, he readily ran to ten thousand words. Herein lies what bears upon the weal and woe of the common people, and what determines the flourishing and decline of the Central Realm. His pure loyalty pierces metal and stone, shining brightly like cinnabar; his fine counsels are recorded in bamboo slips and volumes, clear and luminous as a mirror. Although he was not employed to the fullest in his own age, his work truly awaited an enlightened era. Your servant has long immersed his mind in it, savoring its meaning all the more over time. Accordingly, I have had it transcribed into volumes and arranged in order by category, to reach the depths of the Ninefold Palace and briefly occupy Your Majesty's perusal during the second watch of the night. Though its chapters are abundant, if one raises the main cord, the meshes naturally follow; though its words are detailed, if one grasps the root, the branches become visible. It is truly medicinal stone for a ruler of men, and verily the salt and plum of governing transformation. Those maxims of the Classics and Histories do not fail to record the Ultimate Way, yet for the urgent affairs of the military and the people, nothing is more pertinent than this book. If you rest your eyes upon it and revolve it in your mind, perhaps it will accord with some modest insight; if you adopt its words and extend them into governance, how could it be without benefit to the myriad affairs of state? I humbly hope that Your Sacred Learning will continue in bright illumination, matching the brilliance of the sun and moon;…

天地人皆有文。日月星辰，天之文也；山川草木，地之文也；君臣父子之親之義，則人之文也。昔者堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武，人之至而文之備者也，而其所以治天下，亦不過以此而已。觀夫堯以克明峻德而致黎民之於變，舜以慎徽五典而致百姓之親睦，禹之敷文命，湯之修人紀，文王之所以咸和萬民，武王之所以撫綏萬方，何莫不本於人文哉！降自嬴秦，人文大否，或寄於頰舌，或廢於干戈，愚固所耻言，而亦不忍言，誠如執事所戒，姑置勿論也。天運循環，無往不復，既晦於千載之前，遂彰於千載之後。惟其晦之也久，故其彰之也隆。洪惟我朝□□相承，法二帝、三王以為治，

Examiner and Instructor Peng's comment: In the replies to the five policy questions, the matters are judged with decisiveness and the prose adheres to proper standards. They truly match the vigor of the brush shown in the first two sessions, and are by no means the result of an accidental stroke of luck. Taking this into joint consideration, he deserves to be placed first among the many scholars.

Heaven, Earth, and Man all have their patterns (wen). The sun, moon, stars, and constellations are the patterns of Heaven; the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees are the patterns of Earth; the affection and righteousness between ruler and minister, father and son, are the patterns of Man (renwen, human culture). In antiquity, Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu represented the pinnacle of humanity and the perfection of culture, and that by which they governed All under Heaven was nothing more than this. Consider how Yao, by being able to make illustrious his lofty virtue, brought about the transformation of the black-haired people; how Shun, by carefullybeautifying the Five Cardinal Duties, brought about affection and harmony among the hundred surnames; how Yu spread his cultural mandate abroad; how Tang cultivated the human moral bonds; and that by which King Wen brought universal harmony to the myriad people, and King Wu pacified the myriad regions—which of these was not rooted in human culture? Coming down from the time of the Ying-clan Qin dynasty, human culture fell into great obstruction, either consigned to mere glibness of tongue or ruined by weapons of war. This is something I am certainly ashamed to speak of and also cannot bear to speak of; truly, as Your Reverence the Examiner has cautioned, let us set it aside and not discuss it. The cycle of Heaven revolves, and there is no going forth without a return. Having been obscured a thousand years ago, it has consequently been made manifest a thousand years later. Precisely because its obscuration was long, its manifestation is glorious. Humbly reflecting upon Our Dynasty, [the sacred Emperors?] have succeeded one another, modeling themselves on the Two Emperors and Three Kings to effect good governance. …

奎章宸翰徧布於海宇之間
睿藻天葩昭回於雲漢之表若
太祖高皇帝掃除羶穢復我衣冠厥功大矣而
律令大誥汲汲乎播告者恐民之去其人
文也
太宗文皇帝肅清內難奠我鐘虡厥功偉矣而
為善陰騭孝順事實遑遑乎頒示者誘民
之歸於人文也迨夫
宣宗章皇帝則又以君臣父子之倫夫婦長幼
===
朋友之典製為一書名曰五倫則亦豈外
於人文也哉是以四海之內家傳人誦風
移俗美熙熙乎和樂而不孝不弟之不聞
皥皥乎和平而不姻不睦之無有鳳儀獸
舞之治煥如也鳶飛魚躍之天蕩如也化
成之美蓋前有古而後無今矣於戲盛哉
然執事又謂久於其道而天下化成今可
作禮樂否嗟乎周自文武至于成康積德
百年禮樂興焉我

translation_en:
… Their imperial compositions and sovereign calligraphies are spread throughout the realm; Their sagely literary flourishes and heavenly blossoms shine brilliantly beyond the Milky Way. For instance, Grand Progenitor Emperor Gao (Taizu) swept away the rank defilement of the Mongols and restored our proper robes and caps—great indeed was his achievement! Yet his urgent promulgation of the Statutes and Ordinances (Lüling) and the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao) was out of concern that the people might stray from human culture. Grand Ancestor Emperor Wen (Taizong) pacified the internal rebellion and stabilized our dynastic altars—magnificent indeed was his achievement! Yet his eager distribution of the Secret Blessings for Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi) and the True Examples of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi) was to guide the people to return to human culture. Coming down to Ancestor of Proclamation Emperor Zhang (Xuanzong), he further took the moral relations of ruler and minister, father and son, and the canons of husband and wife, elder and younger, and friend and friend, and compiled them into a book entitled the Book of the Five Relationships (Wulun)—how could this, too, be anything external to human culture? Therefore, within the Four Seas, every household transmits them and every person recites them; customs are transformed and mores made beautiful. Joyously harmonious, neither unfilial nor unfraternal conduct is heard of; serenely peaceful, neither failure in affinal obligations nor discord among kin exists. Brilliant is the governance under which phoenixes come to court with poised demeanor and beasts dance; vast is the heaven under which hawks fly and fishes leap! In the beauty of transformative completion, it surpasses antiquity before and knows no peer in the present. Oh, how magnificent!

Yet Your Excellency also quotes, "Long abiding in His way, all under heaven is transformed and perfected," and asks whether rites and music may now be instituted. Alas! text:
朝重熈累洽逮今已將百年矣人文之化既
視成康何如哉歷世之久視成康何如哉
况又恭遇
皇上政述
祖宗心潛往聖躬行大孝以先天下是尤克盡
人文之大端其
德視成康又何如哉人文既洽歷年既久
聖德尤隆于焉而制作禮樂以宣人文以光
祖宗以垂萬世正一代之盛事而時不可失者

朝重熈累洽，逮今已將百年矣。人文之化既視成、康何如哉？歷世之久視成、康何如哉？况又恭遇皇上政述祖宗，心潛往聖，躬行大孝以先天下，是尤克盡人文之大端，其德視成、康又何如哉？人文既洽，歷年既久，聖德尤隆，于焉而制作禮樂，以宣人文，以光祖宗，以垂萬世，正一代之盛事，而時不可失者也，何不宜之有哉？愚也拭目制作于兹有年，雖無謂，尚能執筆以鋪張對天之宏休，如頌周詩人；玄端章甫，願為小相，如孔門之公西赤也。不知執事能進而教之否？謹對。

第二問

同考試官給事中黄批：策學多尚虚文，惟此卷剖析經疑，區畫邊防，通濟兵民，皆卓然有見，而文詞簡古，氣體亦然，試諸政事，必有可觀。「識時務者在俊傑」，吾於此起敬哉！
translation_en:
… Dynasty has enjoyed successive eras of radiant peace and cumulative harmony for nearly a hundred years up to the present. How does the transformation through human culture already compare to that of Kings Cheng and Kang? How does the length of passing generations compare to that of Kings Cheng and Kang? Moreover, we respectfully encounter His Majesty, whose governance follows the Imperial Ancestors, whose mind is immersed in the former sages, and who personally practices supreme filial piety to lead the realm. This especially fulfills the great principles of human culture—how then does His virtue compare to that of Kings Cheng and Kang? Since human culture is already pervasive, the passing of years is already long, and Sacred Virtue is especially exalted, to establish rites and music here and now—so as to proclaim human culture, glorify the Imperial Ancestors, and hand them down for ten thousand generations—is truly the grand enterprise of an era, and an opportunity that must not be lost! How could there be anything inappropriate about it? For years now, this humble one has wiped his eyes in anticipation of the establishment of rites and music. Though of no account, I am still able to take up the brush to extol the vast blessings of responding to Heaven, like the poets who praised the Zhou; or in black robes and ceremonial cap, I wish to serve as a minor liturgical assistant, like Gongxi Chi 公西赤 of Confucius's gate. I do not know whether Your Excellency might advance me and instruct me or not? Respectfully replied.

Second Question

Comment by Associate Examiner and Supervising Secretary Huang 黃: Policy studies mostly prize empty verbiage; this paper alone resolves doubts in the Classics, plans out frontier defense, and brings relief and benefit to both soldiers and civilians, showing outstanding insight throughout. Its diction is concise and archaic, and its vital style is likewise; if tested in actual governance, there will surely be much worth beholding. "Those who understand the affairs of the times are the outstanding heroes"—before this candidate I stand in admiration!

Comment by Associate Examiner Supervising Secretary Feng: When the questions were issued in the policy-essay session and scripts began coming to hand, for days in succession I read through them, and very few answered well. When this script came in at the end, all of its essays were good, and the three policy essays on classical doubts, defending against the northern nomads, and current affairs are especially fluent and clear, backed by evidentiary research and insight—how surging is its spirit! None without a breast capable of swallowing eight or nine Yunmeng marshes could utter such words. Compared with this, are not those who ride upon empty rhetoric while remaining blind to far-sighted understanding mere peddlers of trivial talk?
Comment by Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Li: Advancing the enlightened and selecting with impartiality is assuredly intended to obtain men of solid talent to serve the needs of the times. In this script, all five policy essays are good, and the three on classical doubts, frontier defense, and current affairs are especially extraordinary. Even compared to seasoned clerks deciding points of law, they strike clearly into agreement with human hearts. How could anyone without great aspirations attain to this? Achievements and renown in the world find their omen here. Placed second in this ward [?], let him strive onward!
Comment by Examiner Academician Qian: Late in the reading I obtained these five policy essays and examined them. All proceed from what he has perceived within his own breast; his learning suffices to bring forth the principles, and his words suffice to set out the affairs in full. Truly he must be one whose scholarship has already reached maturity through long cultivation. Standing in the Great Court, how could he lack the aspiration to give a peerless solitary reply?
Comment by Examiner Academician Peng: All five policy essays are good. His itemized replies show outstanding, unrestrained talent and spirit, and his literary brilliance shines forth like the great Tai'e sword drawn from its scabbard, startling the hearts of all who behold it. What he sets forth in the two policy essays on frontier preparedness and current affairs is solidly grounded and practicable, sufficing to show that he is well versed in governance and not merely extraordinary in his writing. Having obtained a scholar such as this, we may present him to the Great Court without failing our trust.
