punctuated: 聖之心，非合異而歸同，亦何以破俗儒之說？此愚於執事之問，敢不悉其意而畧具詞以對？夫自人文肇開，圖書繼出，道載於六經，文備於三代。《易》有《玉兆》、《瓦兆》、《原兆》，又有《連山》、《歸藏》、《周易》，而所謂一名三義，則易者其德也，變易者其氣也，不易者其位也。《書》有孔壁之藏為古文，伏生之授為今文，而又有《中文尚書》，則劉陶推明大、小夏侯、歐陽三家而為之訓詁也。《詩》則有風、雅、頌、賦、比、興之六義，《關雎》、《鹿鳴》、《文王》、《清廟》之四始，而卯酉、午戌亥為陰陽際會之歲，則不能無改變之政焉。《春秋》則事備於左氏而失之誣，例明於公羊而失之亂，義精於穀梁而失之鑿，則又不能無得失之議焉。《禮》有《儀禮》為經，《禮記》為傳，經禮三百、曲禮三千，其條目可謂多矣；又有所謂五始者，以伏羲造琴制皮為嘉禮之始，神農播種飲食為吉禮之始，黃帝有戰、有官、有葬為軍、…
translation_en: … the minds of the sages. Without reconciling differences and bringing them back to unity, how could one refute the theories of vulgar scholars? Thus, in response to Your Excellency's question, how dare I not fully express my thoughts and set forth my words in brief to reply? Now, ever since human culture first dawned and the River Chart and Luo Writing successively appeared, the Way has been recorded in the Six Classics and its textual expression was perfected in the Three Dynasties. For divination and the Changes, there were the Jade Tortoise-Cracks (Yuzhao), Tile Tortoise-Cracks (Wazhao), and Plain Tortoise-Cracks (Yuanzhao), and also the Linked Mountains (Lianshan), Return to the Hidden (Guizang), and the Changes of Zhou (Zhouyi). As for what is called "one name encompassing three meanings," "ease and simplicity" (yi) refers to its virtue, "alternation and change" (bianyi) refers to its vital force, and "invariability" (buyi) refers to its positions. For the Book of Documents (Shu), what was hidden in the wall of Confucius's house is the Ancient Text (guwen), and what was transmitted by Master Fu (Fu Sheng) is the Modern Text (jinwen); and there is also the Middle-Text Book of Documents (Zhongwen Shangshu), in which Liu Tao elucidated the three schools of the Elder and Younger Xiahou and Ouyang to compose an exegetical commentary. For the Book of Odes (Shi), there are the "six principles" of Airs (feng), Odes (ya), Hymns (song), narrative exposition (fu), metaphor (bi), and evocative image (xing), as well as the "four beginnings" of "Guanju," "Luming," "Wen Wang," and "Qingmiao"; and since the mao and you years and the wu, xu, and hai years are the years of juncture between yin and yang, there could not fail to be governance of reform and renewal therein. For the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), historical events are comprehensively recorded in Zuo's tradition (Zuoshi) yet it errs in fabrications, the interpretive rules are clarified in the Gongyang tradition yet it errs in disorder, and the moral principles are refined in the Guliang tradition yet it errs in forced interpretations; thus here too there cannot fail to be discussions of their respective merits and flaws. For the Rites (Li), there is the Etiquette and Ceremonial (Yili) as the classic proper and the Record of Rites (Liji) as the commentary; with three hundred cardinal rites and three thousand detailed rules of demeanor, its articles and headings may indeed be called numerous. There are also what are called the "five beginnings": taking Fuxi's making of the zither and fashioning of deer-skins for betrothals as the beginning of felicitous rites (jiali), Shennong's sowing of seeds and provision of food and drink as the beginning of auspicious sacrificial rites (jili), and the Yellow Emperor's (Huangdi) having warfare, officialdom, and burial as [the foundation] of military, …

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
賓凶禮之經也夫易之為書伏羲畫卦文
王作彖周公繫其爻孔子為之傳而班固
則曰人更三聖而不及周公者父子一道
也春秋之作既始於周公而尤有待於孔
子者蓋王政既衰不能不因魯史之文以
寓一王之法也至若周禮一經本末備具
品式周旋乃周公致太平之迹而唐太宗
所以勤乙夜之覽夫何不經之說出於腐
儒論難之排貽於後世雖其首末未全有
===
以啓紛紛之議論亦經生學子無以稽制
作之精微故也烏虖六經之作道義之懿
惟聖惟賢不以文士名也渾渾噩噩不以
文法名也後世人無體道之實辭非載道
之文班馬馳聲柳韓名世人則文矣於周
孔其云何詭然龍翔蔚然鳳躍法則文矣
於六經其奚若吁道散於三代之餘文弊
於六經之後風雲月露蟬噪蛙鳴良可為
世道惜也然則力追古作之流以變衰陋

punctuated: 賓、凶禮之經也。夫《易》之為書，伏羲畫卦，文王作彖，周公繫其爻，孔子為之傳，而班固則曰「人更三聖」而不及周公者，父子一道也。《春秋》之作，既始於周公，而尤有待於孔子者，蓋王政既衰，不能不因魯史之文，以寓一王之法也。至若《周禮》一經，本末備具，品式周旋，乃周公致太平之迹，而唐太宗所以勤乙夜之覽。夫何不經之說出於腐儒，論難之排貽於後世，雖其首末未全，有以啓紛紛之議論，亦經生學子無以稽制作之精微故也。烏虖！六經之作，道義之懿，惟聖惟賢，不以文士名也；渾渾噩噩，不以文法名也。後世人無體道之實，辭非載道之文。班、馬馳聲，柳、韓名世，人則文矣，於周、孔其云何？詭然龍翔，蔚然鳳躍，法則文矣，於六經其奚若？吁！道散於三代之餘，文弊於六經之後，風雲月露，蟬噪蛙鳴，良可為世道惜也。然則力追古作之流，以變衰陋
translation_en:
… guest, and mourning rituals. Now as for the Book of Changes (Yi) as a work: Fuxi drew the trigrams, King Wen composed the judgments (tuan), the Duke of Zhou appended the line statements (yao), and Confucius wrote the commentaries (zhuan) for it. Yet Ban Gu 班固 said that "it passed through three sages in human history," without mentioning the Duke of Zhou, because father and son shared a single Way. As for the creation of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), although its conventions began with the Duke of Zhou, it especially awaited Confucius; this was because once royal governance had declined, he could not but rely upon the text of the historical records of Lu to lodge the laws of a true king. As for the classic Rites of Zhou (Zhouli), its fundamentals and details are fully complete and its regulations and protocols are comprehensive; it is the trace by which the Duke of Zhou brought about Great Peace, and the reason why Emperor Taizong of Tang 唐太宗 diligently perused it into the second watch of the night. Why then did claims that it is uncanonical issue from pedantic scholars, and refutations and objections get passed down to later generations? Although its beginning and end are incomplete, which gave rise to tangled debates, this is also because students of the classics had no means to investigate the subtleties of its institution.

Alas! In the creation of the Six Classics and the excellence of their moral principles, their authors were solely sages and worthies, not known merely as literary men; vast and unadorned, their works were not known merely for literary technique. In later generations, men lacked the reality of embodying the Way, and their words were not literature that carries the Way. Ban Gu and Sima Qian 司馬遷 won renown, and Liu Zongyuan 柳宗元 and Han Yu 韓愈 were famous in their eras—as men they were indeed literary, yet how do they compare to the Duke of Zhou and Confucius? Wondrously soaring like dragons and resplendently leaping like phoenixes—their techniques were indeed literary, yet how do they measure up to the Six Classics? Alas! The Way dispersed after the Three Dynasties, and literature deteriorated after the Six Classics; writing of wind, clouds, moon, and dew, like the buzzing of cicadas and croaking of frogs, is truly to be lamented for the sake of the Way of the world. This being so, in striving to pursue the tradition of ancient works so as to transform decadent and vulgar…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
之習不能無望於今之宗主文章權衡人
物者
第三問
吳戭
體元者君之職調元者相之任相之任重
矣所以佐理萬機者在是所以撫綏四方
者在是君心正而國勢尊賢才用而天下
寧何莫不本於相之得人哉昔之論相者
有以德量稱德量不足以盡之有以氣節
===
言氣節不足以盡之有以才能舉才能不
足以盡之惟先儒真西山以四事考之於
理為當四事者一曰正己二曰格君三曰
謀國四曰用人是也三代以上臯陶伯益
伊傅周召之流其所以都俞吁咈於廟堂
之上揄揚諷詠於聲歌之際考之詩書槩
可見矣三代而下若蕭曹丙魏之於漢其
功著矣然律以四事則蕭曹雖皆有謀國
之功而起自刀筆未嘗學問己且不正如

punctuated:
之習，不能無望於今之宗主文章、權衡人物者。

第三問
吳戭

體元者，君之職；調元者，相之任。相之任重矣！所以佐理萬機者在是，所以撫綏四方者在是。君心正而國勢尊，賢才用而天下寧，何莫不本於相之得人哉？昔之論相者，有以德量稱，德量不足以盡之；有以氣節言，氣節不足以盡之；有以才能舉，才能不足以盡之。惟先儒真西山以四事考之，於理為當。四事者：一曰正己，二曰格君，三曰謀國，四曰用人是也。三代以上，臯陶、伯益、伊、傅、周、召之流，其所以都俞吁咈於廟堂之上，揄揚諷詠於聲歌之際，考之《詩》、《書》，槩可見矣。三代而下，若蕭、曹、丙、魏之於漢，其功著矣；然律以四事，則蕭、曹雖皆有謀國之功，而起自刀筆，未嘗學問，己且不正，如
translation_en:
… decadent habits, one cannot but place hope in those today who preside as arbiters of literature and weigh the merits of men.

Third Policy Question
Wu Yan 吳戭

Embodying the primal principle is the duty of the sovereign; harmonizing the primal principle is the responsibility of the chief minister. Weighty indeed is the responsibility of the chief minister! It is through this that he assists in administering the myriad affairs of state, and through this that he pacifies the four quarters of the realm. That the sovereign's mind is rectified and the dignity of the state exalted, that worthy talents are employed and the realm is at peace—how could any of this not be rooted in obtaining the right man as chief minister? Among those in the past who discussed chief ministers, some praised them for their moral capacity, yet moral capacity is insufficient to encompass their duty; some spoke of them in terms of moral integrity, yet moral integrity is insufficient to encompass it; some cited them for their talent and ability, yet talent and ability are insufficient to encompass it. Only when the former Confucian scholar Zhen Xishan 真西山 (Zhen Dexiu 真德秀) examined them by means of four criteria was it fitting in principle. These four criteria are: first, rectifying oneself; second, correcting the sovereign's mind; third, taking counsel for the state; and fourth, employing men. During the Three Dynasties and earlier, as for men of the caliber of Gao Yao 臯陶, Bo Yi 伯益, Yi Yin 伊尹, Fu Yue 傅說, the Duke of Zhou 周公, and the Duke of Shao 召公, the manner in which they expressed agreement and dissent in deliberations at court, and praised and admonished through songs and chants, can generally be seen when examined in the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu). From the Three Dynasties downward, men such as Xiao He 蕭何, Cao Shen 曹參, Bing Ji 丙吉, and Wei Xiang 魏相 in the Han dynasty achieved illustrious merits. Yet if measured against these four criteria, although Xiao He and Cao Shen both had the merit of taking counsel for the state, they rose from the ranks of petty scribes and had never engaged in scholarly learning; since they themselves were not even rectified, how…

punctuated: 正君何？其用□□行，雖篤信而不能全信，衆則一無所□□，其於此四事，蓋未能全也。丙、魏雖同心□興之治，而吉忠厚長者，無大建明；相則廉正自持，居位數年，公卿各稱其職，尤能數以風雨逆賊上聞，庶幾格君者，但其進由外戚，大節虧焉。此其於四者，亦未能全也。歷考漢相能盡此者，但得一人焉，曰諸葛武侯。觀其開誠心，布公道，形之表奏，則忠懇足以悟上；發之教令，則感激足以動人。爵不以無功濫，刑不以貴勢撓。持心平無異衡石，用法信可質鬼神。考其四事，固無不備者，而其用人則尤可法焉。然而功業反不及蕭、曹之偉者，則時勢之難易耳，不足為相累也。至若房、杜、姚、宋之於唐，其名顯矣。然律以四事，則房、杜皆有開國之功，而玄齡持身甚敬，謀國甚忠，庶乎有古大臣風。其用人，則委諫諍於王、魏，付征伐於英、衛，使衆善畢舉於朝，
translation_en: … how could they rectify the ruler? As for their employing men [?], although [Xiao He] earnestly trusted [Cao Can?], he could not fully trust [others?], while the rest [or Cao Can?] had nothing at all [?]—thus in these four matters, they were unable to be complete. Although Bing Ji (丙吉) and Wei Xiang (魏相) were of one mind in [assisting the] pemerintahan of restoration, Bing Ji was a loyal, generous elder without great policy initiatives; Wei Xiang conducted himself with integrity and rectitude, and during his several years in office the chief ministers each fulfilled their duties, while he was especially able to repeatedly report anomalies of wind and rain and rebellious bandits to the throne, coming close to rectifying the ruler—yet his advancement came through the consort clan, so his great moral integrity was deficient. Thus in the four matters, they too were unable to be complete. Examining the Grand Councillors of the Han across history who could fulfill all of these, we find only one man: Zhuge, Martial Marquis (Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮). Observe how he opened his sincere heart and spread the public way: when expressed in memorials and petitions, his loyal earnestness was sufficient to enlighten his sovereign; when issued in instructions and ordinances, his stirring earnestness was sufficient to move the people. Ranks of nobility were not lavished on those without merit, and punishments were not bent for the noble and powerful. He held his mind as level as a balance beam and stone weight, and applied the law with a trustworthiness that could be vouched for before ghosts and spirits. Examining him against the four matters, there was indeed nothing in which he was not complete, and his employment of men is especially worthy of being taken as a model. That his achievements and enterprise nevertheless did not match the grandeur of Xiao He and Cao Can was simply a matter of the relative difficulty or ease of the times and circumstances, and is not enough to be a blemish on his statesmanship. As for Fang Xuanling (房玄齡), Du Ruhui (杜如晦), Yao Chong (姚崇), and Song Jing (宋璟) in the Tang, their fame was illustrious. Yet if measured by the four matters, Fang and Du both had the merit of founding the dynasty, and Xuanling conducted himself with great敬 (reverence) and planned for the state with great loyalty, coming close to having the style of the great ministers of antiquity. In his employment of men, he entrusted remonstrance to Wang Gui (王珪) and Wei Zheng (魏徵), and delegated military campaigns to the Duke of Ying (Li Shiji 李世勣) and the Duke of Wei (Li Jing 李靖), causing all men of worth to be promoted at court, …

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
其休休有容雖秦漢以下可及如晦雖曰
事日淺而觀玄齡許與及帝所親信則其
謀謨果有大過人者是其正己謀國用人
可謂無愧矣然而格君之功則槩乎未聞
也姚宋共成開元之治而姚也善於應變
其明决非同輩可及居相位則委任高齊
庶乎知大體者宋也持正守法百官各稱
其職刑賞無私深謀遠畧見於不賞邊功
是其正己謀國用人亦可謂無愧矣然而
===
格君之功亦槩乎未聞也歷考唐相能盡
此者但得一人焉曰陸宣公觀其居相位
四年小心精潔雖微賂必却其論諫必本
於仁義不雜以一毫功利之私惟欲以捄
德宗心術之弊凡所計畫未嘗有爽考其
四事無有不盡者而於養材用人之方尤
備舉不遺焉然而致治反在於姚宋之下
者則屬任之有久近耳不足為相恥也雖
然相以德而其本以學之數子者謂其不

As for Du Ruhui 杜如晦, although it is said that his time in service was brief, judging by Fang Xuanling's 房玄齡 high regard for him and the Emperor's close trust in him, his counsels and plans truly far surpassed those of others. Thus, in rectifying themselves, planning for the state, and employing men, they can be said to have had nothing to be ashamed of; yet as for the achievement of rectifying the ruler's mind, nothing at all has been heard of it. Yao Chong 姚崇 and Song Jing 宋璟 together accomplished the flourishing rule of the Kaiyuan 開元 era. Yao was skilled at adapting to changing circumstances, his clear decisiveness beyond the reach of his peers, and when he occupied the office of chief minister, he delegated responsibilities to Gao Zhongshu 高仲舒 and Qi Chuci 齊澣, coming close to one who understood the great essentials of governance. Song upheld rectitude and abided by the law; under him all officials were suited to their posts, punishments and rewards were impartial, and his deep counsel and far-sighted strategy were seen in his refusal to reward frontier exploits. Thus, in rectifying themselves, planning for the state, and employing men, they too can be said to have had nothing to be ashamed of; yet as for the achievement of rectifying the ruler's mind, nothing at all has been heard of it either. Examining the chief ministers of the Tang who were able to fulfill all of these, we find only one man: Lu Xuangong 陸宣公 (Lu Zhi 陸贄). Observing his four years in the office of chief minister, he was cautious and pure, refusing even the smallest bribe. His arguments and remonstrances were always rooted in benevolence and righteousness, unmixed with the slightest selfish consideration of utility or profit, desiring only to remedy the flaws in Emperor Dezong's 德宗 disposition of mind. In all that he planned, there was never an error. Examining him against the four tasks of a minister, there was none he did not fulfill completely, and in the methods of nurturing talent and employing men, he set them forth with particular thoroughness, omitting nothing. That his achievement of good order nonetheless fell below that of Yao Chong and Song Jing was merely a matter of the length of time he was entrusted with office; it is not enough to be a disgrace to him as a minister. Even so, a chief minister relies on virtue, and the root of virtue lies in learning. Regarding these several gentlemen, to say that they did not…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
學不可也謂其學之正則未也其學者雜
以智謀拳巧之術故足以蕆大功未學者
格致誠正之道故不足以全四事然要其
歸則以當時教化之不明耳使數子生於
文武成康之世被菁莪棫樸之澤則其功
業又豈臯陶伊傅之下哉愚深為之歎息
也
第四問
===
禦戎無上策自治為上策用兵無良計選
將為良計此非私言也古人論之已有成
說亦非迂談也前代行之屢有成效人知
三苗之徂征雖虞廷不能免而不知文德
誕敷終有以格七旬而致丕叙人知玁狁
之薄伐雖周宣不能無而不知方叔召虎
終有以任折衝而幹不庭則凡所以禦戎
之策用兵之計槩可見已下此若西漢之
南漠無庭西羌坐困所以備邊者雖不古

匈奴無庭西羌望國所以備邊者雖不古

學不可也，謂其學之正則未也。其學者，雜以智謀拳巧之術，故足以蕆大功；未學者，格致誠正之道，故不足以全四事。然要其歸，則以當時教化之不明耳。使數子生於文、武、成、康之世，被《菁莪》、《棫樸》之澤，則其功業又豈臯陶、伊、傅之下哉！愚深為之歎息也。

第四問

禦戎無上策，自治為上策；用兵無良計，選將為良計。此非私言也，古人論之已有成說；亦非迂談也，前代行之屢有成效。人知三苗之徂征，雖虞廷不能免，而不知文德誕敷，終有以格七旬而致丕叙；人知玁狁之薄伐，雖周宣不能無，而不知方叔、召虎，終有以任折衝而幹不庭。則凡所以禦戎之策、用兵之計，槩可見已。下此若西漢之南漠無庭、西羌坐困，所以備邊者雖不古
translation_en:
… lacked learning; yet to say that their learning was orthodox would not be true. What they did learn was mixed with the arts of shrewd calculation and clever expediency [?], and thus it sufficed to accomplish great feats; what they had not learned was the Way of investigating things, extending knowledge, making the intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind, and thus it was insufficient to fulfill the four duties of a chief minister in their entirety. Yet if we trace the ultimate reason for this, it was simply because moral transformation and instruction were not clarified in their times. Had these several men been born in the eras of Kings Wen, Wu, Cheng, and Kang of Zhou, and received the nurturing grace celebrated in the oaths "Jing'e" (Lush Tarragon) and "Yupu" (Thickets of Oak), how would their achievements and enterprises have fallen below those of Gao Yao, Yi Yin, and Fu Yue? I sigh deeply for them on this account.

Fourth Policy Essay

In defending against the western barbarians, there is no supreme strategy: governing oneself well is the supreme strategy. In employing military force, there is no finest plan: selecting capable generals is the finest plan. These are not merely my private words, for the ancients already had established doctrines when discussing them; nor are they impractical talk, for previous dynasties repeatedly achieved proven results when putting them into practice. People know that even the court of Yu (Shun) could not avoid the punitive expedition against the Three Miao, yet they do not realize that by broadly spreading civil virtue, it ultimately brought them to submission within seventy days and achieved grand order. People know that even King Xuan of Zhou could not dispense with the punitive campaign against the Xianyun, yet they do not realize that it was Fang Shu and Shao Hu who ultimately shouldered the task of repelling the enemy and rectifying the recalcitrant. From this, the general principles of strategies for defending against barbarians and plans for employing troops can all be seen. Coming down to later times, in the Western Han, when no royal court of the Xiongnu remained south of the desert and the Western Qiang were pinned down in exhaustion, the measures taken to prepare the frontiers, though not…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
若然亦可謂善矣建武以來西閉玉關不
置都護而南北單于侵冦迭至戊巳校尉
陷沒相仍較之西京誠有愧焉唐初之突
厥剪平馮智入侍所以柔遠者雖不古逮
亦不可謂不善矣天寶以後屯重兵於西
北列大鎮於朔方而回紇之騎近至涇源
吐蕃之酋雲擾郊甸視之貞觀不無嘅焉
是故善為計者勢欲其要則守禦之有方
兵欲其強則練習之有法收屯田之利省
===
餽運之艱使食無不足也簡拔於儲用之
先委任於推轂之際使將無不良也以良
將而握強兵因足食而乘要勢則夷雖為
患猶疥癬尔茍將弱而兵羸食耗而勢困
則邊雖無警可安枕乎方
今天下一家四夷賓服固得禦戎之上策一
無事乎用兵之良計矣然而鳥言獸面或
哨聚於山林豨突豕奔或猖狂於沙漠鼎
魚假息釜鬵何逃而況資以廟廊之勝算

患猶疥癬尒蕩將弱而兵羸食耗而勢困
則邊雖無警可安枕乎方
今天下一家四夷賓服固得禦戎之上策
無事乎用兵之良計矣然而烏言獸面或

急假息於何逃而況資以廟廊之勝算
punctuated: 若，然亦可謂善矣。建武以來，西閉玉關，不置都護，而南北單于侵冦迭至，戊巳校尉陷沒相仍，較之西京，誠有愧焉。唐初之突厥剪平，馮智入侍，所以柔遠者雖不古逮，亦不可謂不善矣。天寶以後，屯重兵於西北，列大鎮於朔方，而回紇之騎近至涇源，吐蕃之酋雲擾郊甸，視之貞觀，不無嘅焉。是故善為計者，勢欲其要，則守禦之有方；兵欲其強，則練習之有法；收屯田之利，省餽運之艱，使食無不足也；簡拔於儲用之先，委任於推轂之際，使將無不良也。以良將而握強兵，因足食而乘要勢，則夷雖為患，猶疥癬尔。茍將弱而兵羸，食耗而勢困，則邊雖無警，可安枕乎？方今天下一家，四夷賓服，固得禦戎之上策，一無事乎用兵之良計矣。然而鳥言獸面，或哨聚於山林；豨突豕奔，或猖狂於沙漠。鼎魚假息，釜鬵何逃？而況資以廟廊之勝算，
translation_en:
…equal to antiquity, yet it can still be called effective. From the Jianwu era (25–56 CE) onward, they closed the Jade Gate Pass in the west and did not establish a Protector-General (Duhu), yet raids by the northern and southern Chanyu arrived in succession, and the Wu and Ji Colonels (Wuji Xiaowei) were repeatedly overrun and lost; compared to the Western Capital [Western Han], this was truly shameful. In the early Tang, the Turks (Tujue) were wiped out and pacified, and Feng Zhi [Feng盎 / Feng Zhi's family of Lingnan?] entered court to attend the Emperor; aunque the means by which theyconciliated distant peoples did not reach the level of antiquity, it cannot be called ineffective. After the Tianbao era (742–756), heavy forces were garrisoned in the northwest and great defense commands were arrayed in Shuofang, yet Uyghur (Huihe) cavalry came as close as Jingyuan, and Tibetan (Tubo) chieftains swarmed like clouds to harass the imperial outskirts; looking at this in comparison to the Zhenguan era (627–649), one cannot but sigh.

Therefore, for those who are good at making plans: if they want the strategic position to be advantageous, there must be a proper method for defense; if they want the troops to be strong, there must be a proper system for training and drill; they reap the benefits of state farms (tuntian) and reduce the hardships of grain transport, ensuring that food supplies are never insufficient; they select and promote men before they are needed for service, and entrust them with full authority at the moment of commissioning them as commanders, ensuring that generals are never less than capable. When capable generals hold strong troops, and rely on sufficient food while occupying key strategic positions, then even if the barbarians cause trouble, it is merely like ringworm or scabies. If, however, the generals are weak and the troops feeble, the food depleted and the strategic position compromised, then even if there are no alarms on the frontier, how could one sleep in peace?

At present, all under Heaven is one family and the barbarians of the four quarters submit in allegiance; we have indeed attained the supreme strategy for defending against the barbarians, and have no need at all for good plans of deploying troops. Yet those with the speech of birds and faces of beasts at times whistle to gather in the mountain forests, and those who rush like boars and flee like swine at times run wild in the deserts. Like fish borrowing a few breaths in a cauldron, how can they escape the cooking pot? And how much more so when aided by the victorious calculations of the imperial court—…

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
亦何敢控草茅之鄙見也耶然竊謂南北
之勢既殊制馭之道當異炎荒際海皆吾
郡縣深山窮谷皆吾編氓使守令之撫養
有方邊閫之招徠以信何有於革其心必
不得已而加之以兵亦當召募土人任其
智勇則諳夷俗之情狀知山川之嚮道而
凡延頸就戮者可無俟乎歲月之久矣何
必遠徵師旅以輕褻
國威也哉若乃旌別之策桀黠之徒覘視窺
===
覦狡詐萬變使將帥之威武震揚邊庭之
要害嚴飭亦安所行其計必不得已而貸
之以恩亦宜先震以雷霆之威而後徐濡
以雨露之澤則威可以懾恩可以懷而凡
稽首來王者可保其無反側之虞矣夫豈
徒施惠利以上廑
聖筭哉狂瞽之言明者不棄惟執事其采擇焉

第五問
punctuated:
亦何敢控草茅之鄙見也耶？然竊謂南北之勢既殊，制馭之道當異。炎荒際海，皆吾郡縣；深山窮谷，皆吾編氓。使守令之撫養有方，邊閫之招徠以信，何有於革其心？必不得已而加之以兵，亦當召募土人，任其智勇，則諳夷俗之情狀，知山川之嚮道，而凡延頸就戮者，可無俟乎歲月之久矣，何必遠徵師旅以輕褻國威也哉？若乃旌別之策，桀黠之徒，覘視窺覦，狡詐萬變，使將帥之威武震揚，邊庭之要害嚴飭，亦安所行其計？必不得已而貸之以恩，亦宜先震以雷霆之威，而後徐濡以雨露之澤，則威可以懾，恩可以懷，而凡稽首來王者，可保其無反側之虞矣，夫豈徒施惠利以上廑聖筭哉？狂瞽之言，明者不棄，惟執事其采擇焉。
第五問
translation_en:
…how would I dare to offer the rustic views of a commoner from the thatched huts? Yet I would venture to say that since the strategic conditions of the south and the north are distinct, the ways of controlling and managing them ought also to differ. In the fiery wilderness of the south reaching to the sea, all are our prefectures and counties; in the deep mountains and remote valleys, all are our registered commoners. If the prefects and magistrates nurture them with proper method, and the frontier commanders win them over through good faith, what difficulty would there be in reforming their hearts? If, when there is no other alternative, we must resort to military force against them, we should also recruit local people and employ their resourcefulness and courage. Then, because they are familiar with the circumstances of the non-Chinese customs and know the routes and guides through the mountains and rivers, all those stretching out their necks to meet execution can be dealt with without waiting for months and years to pass. Why must we mobilize armies from afar and thereby lightly compromise the prestige of the state?

As for the strategy of distinguishing the good from the bad [or: the region of banners and felt in the north [?]], those fierce and crafty fellows spy and watch for opportunities with myriad shifting deceits. Yet if the martial might of our generals and commanders is resoundingly displayed, and the strategic passes of the frontier courts are strictly fortified, where would they be able to carry out their schemes? If, when there is no other alternative, we grant them grace and leniency, we ought first to overawe them with the might of thunderbolts and only afterward gradually moisten them with the beneficence of rain and dew. Then our might will be sufficient to cow them and our grace sufficient to win their attachment, and all who bow their heads to the ground and come to pay allegiance as to their king can be guaranteed to pose no worry of rebellion or duplicity. How could we merely dispense favors and benefits and thereby trouble the sacred calculations above? The words of the rash and blind are not discarded by the wise; may Your Excellency select from among them.

Fifth Question

punctuated: 布衣而詢以天下之務，經生而策以治世之宜，是執事欲待以政事之才，而不視為章句之腐者也。愚敢不陳所見以復明問乎？夫國以民為本，而任承流宣化之責者，守令也。守令得人，則齊民安業而内治可成矣。今苞苴之託，國有嚴刑；撫恤之恩，嵗有温詔。然而暴官汙吏屢逮於圜扉，啼飢號寒或興於委巷，是豈聖明任官愛民之初心哉？守令非人，而德澤壅於下流也。若夫民頼兵以為衛，而當撫馭折衝之寄者，將校也。將校得人，則軍旅精強而外侮可禦矣。今將校之任，患已預儲；軍旅之衆，時加簡閱。然而膏粱紈袴秉鉞邊疆，慵懦疲羸虛靡餽餉，亦豈聖世選將養兵之本意哉？將校非人，而士卒習於偷惰也。夫民貧而守令不恤，則自贍
translation_en: To inquire of a commoner about the affairs of the realm, and to examine a student of the classics on the proper measures for governing the world—this shows that Your Excellency wishes to treat us as talents fit for administration rather than viewing us as pedants bound to chapter and verse. How could I, in my ignorance, dare not set forth my views in reply to your enlightened question? Now, the state takes the common people as its foundation, and those who bear the responsibility of receiving the sovereign's grace and disseminating his transforming influence are the prefects and magistrates. When the right men are found to serve as prefects and magistrates, the common people are secure in their livelihoods and domestic governance can be achieved. Today, against the solicitation of bribes, the state has severe punishments; with the grace of relief and compassion, every year brings warm imperial edicts. Yet tyrannical officials and corrupt functionaries are repeatedly hauled into prison, and cries of hunger and wails of cold at times arise in the back alleys. How could this be the original intention of our sacred and enlightened ruler in appointing officials and loving the people? It is because the prefects and magistrates are not the right men, so that royal virtue and beneficence are blocked from flowing down to those below. As for the people relying on the military for their protection, those who bear the charge of pacifying, commanding, and repelling enemy assaults are the generals and officers. When the right men are found to serve as generals and officers, the military forces are well-trained and strong, and foreign aggression can be warded off. Today, out of concern for the posts of generals and officers, talent is already stored up in advance; the multitude of the military forces is periodically inspected and reviewed. Yet pampered scions in fine silks wield the battle-axes of command on the frontiers, while lazy, cowardly, exhausted, and frail troops vainly waste provisions and pay. How could this, either, be the fundamental intent of our sacred age in selecting generals and maintaining soldiers? It is because the generals and officers are not the right men, and the rank and file have grown accustomed to idleness and sloth. Now, when the people are impoverished and the prefects and magistrates show them no compassion, they scarcely have the means to support themselves…

text:

之險艱而為民衛哉大抵守令之貪墨者
類由於倖進而非德讓之循吏也將校之
不良者皆取之世胄而非詩書之元帥也
為今之計莫若盛科目之選嚴儒吏之銓
任用不雜以庸流勸懲一出乎公道則守

隆武學之制置武舉之科通知大義者方
===

寇鄧韓范之賢而兵不患於不精矣夫守

體民以給軍餉為先而水陸漕輓鱗集而

punctuated: 不暇，況能以翳桑之壺飧而為兵餽哉？兵驕而將校不戢，則橫暴方殷，況能蹈鋒刃之險艱而為民衛哉？大抵守令之貪墨者，類由於倖進，而非德讓之循吏也；將校之不良者，皆取之世胄，而非《詩》《書》之元帥也。為今之計，莫若盛科目之選，嚴儒吏之銓，任用不雜以庸流，勸懲一出乎公道，則守令皆龔、黃、卓、魯之循，而民不患於不安矣；隆武學之制，置武舉之科，通知大義者方許蔭襲，智勇兼畫者特加選用，則將校皆寇、鄧、韓、范之賢，而兵不患於不精矣。夫守令既□，則不徒安其民，而且能道民以養兵之道；將校既賢，則不徒精其兵，而且能訓兵以衛民之義。由是上下一心，兵民一體，民以給軍餉為先，而水陸漕輓鱗集而輻湊也；兵以恤民患為急，而干戈征伐虎視而鷹揚也。邊儲充牣，士飽而歌，得以防烽燧之虞；閭閻□□，民康而色，得以樂耕
translation_en: …have no spare capacity [to support themselves], how much less could they offer a pot of food like that at Yisang to provision the soldiers? When the soldiers are arrogant and the commanders and officers do not restrain them, their tyranny and violence are at their height; how much less could they tread the dangers and hardships of naked blades to defend the people? Generally speaking, prefects and magistrates who are corrupt and venal mostly advance through undeserved fortune rather than being upright officials of virtue and deference; commanders and officers who are incompetent are all drawn from hereditary lineages rather than being marshals versed in the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu). As a plan for the present, nothing is better than to exalt selection through the examination system and strictly conduct the appointment of Confucian officials, ensuring that appointments are not mixed with mediocre sorts and that encouragement and punishment proceed entirely from public justice; then prefects and magistrates will all have the uprightness of Gong [Sui], Huang [Ba], Zhuo [Mao], and Lu [Gong], and there will be no worry that the people are not at peace. If we elevate the system of military schools and establish the military examination (wuju) category, permitting only those who understand the great principles to inherit hereditary privilege, and specially selecting and employing those who combine wisdom and courage in their planning, then commanders and officers will all have the worthiness of Kou [Xun], Deng [Yu], Han [Qi], and Fan [Zhongyan], and there will be no worry that the troops are not elite. Once prefects and magistrates are [upright?], they will not merely bring peace to their people, but will also be able to guide the people in the way of sustaining the troops; once commanders and officers are worthy, they will not merely make their troops elite, but will also be able to instruct the troops in the duty of defending the people. From this, superiors and inferiors will be of one mind, and soldiers and civilians will form a single body. The people will put supplying military provisions first, and transport by water and land will gather like fish scales and converge like wheel spokes; the troops will treat relieving the people's distress as urgent, and in taking up shields and spears for punitive expeditions they will glare like tigers and soar like eagles. With frontier stores full to overflowing, the soldiers will be well-fed and sing, able to guard against the alarm of beacon fires; with the villages [at peace?], the people will be healthy and joyful in countenance, able to take pleasure in their work of plowing…

translation_en: … the pursuits of farming and sericulture, what worry would there be that soldiers and civilians do not mutually support one another? Encouraging and harmonizing them so as to form a plan for the state's lasting peace and enduring order truly goes no further than this. Alas! As the affairs of the realm turn over in my heart, there is much that I wish to say; yet beneath the windswept eaves and with only an inch of shadow on the sundial, I cannot set it all forth one by one. Should You take pity on my aspiration and grant my advancement, there are matters greater still than these of which I would speak before the enlightened Son of Heaven.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the seventh year of the reigning Emperor's restored Tianshun era (1463), the Ministry of Rites assembled the more than two thousand eight hundred tribute scholars presented from across the realm and examined them together. Prior to the date, the Minister of Rites, Your Servant Yao Kui 姚夔, and others memorialized to inform the Throne. The Emperor ordered that the examination be conducted according to precedent, and further proclaimed Your Servant Peng Shi 彭時 and Your Servant Qian Pu 錢溥 to serve as Examiners. Having received the imperial command, Your Servants proceeded to our posts and strove to uphold impartiality: the assignment of examination topics did not come from a single hand, and in evaluating the essays we sought agreement with the consensus of minds. Morning and night we worked with meticulous rigor, never daring to slacken in the slightest. By the time the examination compound was opened, we had obtained two hundred and fifty scholars—which is the quota set by imperial institution, and a flourishing selection indeed. The Ministry of Rites is now about to lead them forward and present them to the Emperor, to await…

translation_en: …the inquiry of the Emperor in person at the Palace Examination. Now, scholars are first nurtured in the schools, recommended from the provinces, selected by the Ministry of Rites, and then advanced to the court of the Son of Heaven. That the Emperor condescends to ask them pure questions, prepares the imperial cortege, has their names called out at the roll-call ceremony, and bestows gifts upon them in order to favor and honor them—is this merely to dazzle for a single moment? Indeed, we have heard it said by Shusun Mubo 叔孫穆伯, a minister of Lu in the Zhou dynasty, that establishing virtue, establishing merit, and establishing words are what it means to establish oneself. The multitude of scholars of the Zhou dynasty served as screens and bulwarks and as models for the states, truly flourishing in great numbers; and in ages below that, what can continue such flourishing is solely that this examination system is sufficient to obtain men of talent. For instance, Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒 and Jia Yi 賈誼 became illustrious through their policy essays, and Han Yu 韓愈, Ouyang Xiu 歐陽修, Su Shi 蘇軾, and Zeng Gong 曾鞏 ganó renown through their literature—was this not establishing words? For instance, Pei Du 裴度 and Lu Zhi 陸贄 served as Grand Councilors to the Tang, and Han Qi 韓琦, Fu Bi 富弼, and Sima Guang 司馬光 served as Grand Councilors to the Song—was this not establishing merit? As for virtue, in retirement they improved local customs through it, and in speaking they used it to [?]…

渠之張新安之朱元有臨川

其所以為盛則若不專於科

為科目光者寔由盛以致之

是雖不專於科目而其所以
爲科目光者寔由盛以致之
punctuated: 達其道，若宋有河南之程、橫渠之張、新安之朱，元有臨川之吳，皆假科目以發身者，而其所以為盛，則若不專於科目焉。何也？盖志於德者，功與言自立；而志於功與言者，非德亦無以行之。然則諸士子烏可恃此以自畫哉？職是而往，或以言揚，或以功懋，一皆本諸身而有其德，則天下後世知我朝得士之盛，無愧於前數君子。是雖不專於科目，而其所以為科目光者，寔由盛以致之。
translation_en: …transmit the Way—such as in the Song dynasty, the Chengs of Henan (Cheng Hao 程顥 and Cheng Yi 程頤), Zhang of Hengqu (Zhang Zai 張載), and Zhu of Xin'an (Zhu Xi 朱熹); and in the Yuan dynasty, Wu of Linchuan (Wu Cheng 吳澄)—all of whom relied upon the civil service examinations to launch their careers, yet that by which they achieved greatness seemed not to lie solely in the examinations. Why is this? Because when one sets one's mind upon virtue, merit and words are naturally established; whereas when one sets one's mind upon merit and words, without virtue there is no means to carry them out. This being so, how could all you scholars rely upon this achievement to set limits on yourselves? Going forward from this, whether you distinguish yourselves through words or exert yourselves in merit, if in every case you root it in your own person and possess that virtue, then the world and future generations will know that the flourishing of our Dynasty's acquisition of scholars is in no way inferior to those several gentlemen of former times. Although this does not lie solely in the examinations, that which brings glory to the examinations is truly brought about by such flourishing.

title: 天順七年會試錄
text:
雖然盛非特多之為盛也得
人以裨益於治化雖少亦以
為盛矣況皆濟濟然顯於其
位治日隆俗日美而世日熈
皡又何周士之多且盛者不
可以跂及耶會試錄成僭以
此共勉于後
===
翰林院侍讀學士奉直大夫
錢溥謹序

===
翰林院侍讀學士奉直大夫
錢溥謹序
punctuated:
雖然，盛非特多之為盛也，得人以裨益於治化，雖少亦以為盛矣。況皆濟濟然顯於其位，治日隆，俗日美，而世日熈皡，又何周士之多且盛者不可以跂及耶？《會試錄》成，僭以此共勉于後。
翰林院侍讀學士、奉直大夫錢溥謹序。
translation_en:
Even so, flourishing is not merely a matter of large numbers; when capable men are obtained to benefit governance and moral transformation, even if they are few, that is still considered flourishing. How much more so when all of them stand in dignified array and distinguish themselves in their offices, so that governance grows daily more prosperous, customs grow daily more refined, and the age grows daily more harmonious and serene—why then could the abundance and flourishing of the gentlemen of the Zhou dynasty not be matched on tiptoe? Now that the Record of the Metropolitan Examination is completed, I presumptuously offer these words at the end for our mutual encouragement.
Respectfully prefaced by Qian Pu 錢溥, Academician Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Fostering Uprightness.
